text:
Four decades after establishing roots in Columbus, a local manufacturer has made a determined foray into an increasingly electric future through construction of a new 295,000 square-foot manufacturing facility in Walesboro.

Toyota Material Handling North America (TMHNA) celebrated the opening of its new factory on Wednesday that officials said will position the Columbus-headquartered company to meet demand for the production of primarily electric forklifts into the future.

TMHNA employees, leadership from parent company Toyota Industries Corp. (TICO), city officials and representatives from the area’s entire federal congressional delegation, as well as Gov. Mike Braun came to commemorate the factory that TMHNA President and CEO Brett Wood hopes will be “the epicenter of electric forklift innovation for years to come.”

The types of products produced at the factory are used to move just about every product that arrives on doorsteps and retail shelves, from furniture to groceries to timber to metal.

TMHNA is investing nearly $100 million into the facility off Deaver Road, located just north of the one built 37 years ago. Wood characterized the investment as being one into the “heartland of America.”

While electric cars make up about 10% of the automotive industry in the US, electric forklifts are responsible for seven times that, Wood said.

When the planning process for the new facility began making its way through the local government process in 2023 and 2024, electric powered lift trucks comprised about 65% of the North American market.

TMHNA, made up of subsidiaries The Raymond Corporation and Toyota Material Handling, Inc., were compelled to expand its production of electric forklifts based upon forecasts that by 2035, electric-powered forklifts would make up 80% of the North American market.

In the time since the new facility has been brought online, that share has already trended past 70%.

Toyota Material Handling and Raymond, who merged in January 2025, are responsible for producing one-third of every forklift sold in North America, company officials said.

The new factory’s initial product, the electric Class 1 Stand-Up Counterbalanced forklift, was only produced at the TMHNA factory in Greene, New York until recently. The idea is that the shift in production location will permit the Greene factory to focus on products like reach trucks, order pickers and automation, while the new TMHNA factory in Columbus will enable increased capacity for counterbalance forklift production.

“Together, these investments make us an even more responsive and flexible supply partner,” remarked Tony Miller, TMHNA chief supply officer.

Production at the new facility started in July. New hires have already been made, and company officials said they were comprised mostly of local workers.

Miller discussed how he was asked to lead the company’s North American manufacturing strategy in 2022, at a time when COVID and resulting supply chain pressures produced record backlogs and extended lead times of many products across a variety of industries, forklifts included.

Out of that, it was determined another factory was needed to address demand and support future growth.

“We considered available workforce, supply partner proximity, long-term expansion opportunities and the support of state and local partners,” Miller said. “Every road led us right back here to Columbus, Indiana.”

The new factory, shown off during a tour, is a blend of automation and human craftsmanship, including quickly expanding assembly lines as needed. Sustainability is another feature, from the zero volatile organic compound power coat process to a design that allows for future rooftop solar installation.

The $100 million investment — the largest the company has ever made to increase its overall manufacturing footprint — has brought on an additional 140 jobs, bringing the total number of employees at TMHNA to over 2,100 people.

What began with a footprint in Columbus of 280,000 square feet in 1990 is now nearing 2 million square feet.

Mayor Mary Ferdon talked about how TMHNA has been “a team player” in Columbus over the course of the past nearly 40 years, reflected in its community service focus and the $3.64 million philanthropic impact the company has made in the last four years.

“Companies that stand out are the ones who recognize that people are their greatest asset,” Ferdon said. “… We’ve seen the invaluable effect of having TMH employees living and investing in Columbus and Bartholomew County, raising families, being good neighbors and volunteers, and helping create an environment which creates success.”

The mayor discussed how TMHNA is additive to the community’s STEM-centered identity, exemplified through the high percentage of engineers per capita that live in Columbus and Bartholomew Consolidated School Corporation’s STEM curriculum.

The mayor then read off a proclamation, acknowledging the long-standing community impact TMHNA has had on Columbus.

Gov. Braun described two of the city’s anchor companies in Cummins and TMHNA as making the state a leader in advanced manufacturing.

About a minute into the governor’s remarks, 2012’s dance-pop hit “Wild Ones” by Flo Rida inexplicably began blasting on speakers inside the TMHNA showroom, continuing on for about 2 minutes as organizers scrambled to get it to stop.

But in concert with the theme of the day, the short diversion from the festivities gave everyone attending a lift.

“I’d like to get a copy of that song,” Braun said.

title: Crusoe Supports Texas Data Center Audits & Responsible Growth Standards
description:
We support this demand for greater transparency and accountability, and commend Governor Abbott on these important steps.
We believe any company building infrastructure at this scale should welcome the kind of audit Governor Abbott is now requiring.
Water: Our facilities minimize water usage Water is a shared resource, and we treat it that way.
In fact Crusoe data center projects are often among the largest tax sources if not the single largest tax payer in the communities where we operate.
Governor Abbott is right to hold companies to a high standard, and we're glad to be judged against it.
text:
Earlier this week, Governor Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to audit every data center project in the state's interconnection queue, requiring clear disclosure of tax incentives, energy use, water use, and ownership before any new project moves forward.

We support this demand for greater transparency and accountability, and commend Governor Abbott on these important steps.

This isn’t a new position for us. Our position is consistent with the way we have always done business. As data center development has accelerated across Texas, so have questions from the communities hosting it: what effect will these sites have on their neighbors, who is actually paying for this growth, and who is watching to make sure the promises hold? We believe any company building infrastructure at this scale should welcome the kind of audit Governor Abbott is now requiring. These are fair questions, and every developer – Crusoe included – should be able to answer them clearly.

Energy: We pay our own way for power

For Crusoe, energy-first means planning a site's power from day one – building thoughtfully, in ways that benefit both the grid and the communities we enter, and not just building quickly. We seek out sources of abundant, underutilized energy so our workloads don't add pressure to local grids, and we've become a leader in deploying new power generation capacity to support digital infrastructure. We cover our own onsite generation and any infrastructure upgrades our projects require, so the cost of our growth doesn’t land on a neighbor's electric bill.

That's also why, earlier this year, we joined the White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge alongside Governor Abbott and more than 200 other developers, utilities, and states – standing with these leaders to keep investing in America's innovation economy, creating jobs, and responsibly building the power the nation needs, without asking ratepayers to foot the bill. In Abilene, our new campus will run entirely on on-site generation and battery storage, built and paid for by Crusoe.

Water: Our facilities minimize water usage

Water is a shared resource, and we treat it that way. Our closed-loop cooling systems recirculate water in a sealed loop, using virtually none of it during normal operations – a design choice that lets a 200-megawatt Crusoe data center use less water annually than ten average U.S. households. We don't think transparency about that number should be optional, and we don't wait for a regulator to ask for it.

Jobs: We prioritize hiring local residents

Our projects have created more than 13,000 positions to date across high-tech, construction, and skilled trades. We offer those roles to local workers in host communities first, backed by partnerships with regional vocational programs and local school districts. We believe a data center’s long-term economic impact should benefit every student, taxpayer, and business in a community.

Investments: Our projects boost the local economy

We've invested more than $20B to date at the local level, through job creation, local sourcing, and tax contributions that fund schools, emergency services, career training, water infrastructure, and roads. Abilene's economy has grown alongside our investment there – in the past year, the City has permitted more than 1,500 new homes to keep pace, on top of the tax revenue the campus contributes.

When we ask a community for a tax incentive to help build a project, we believe in being transparent about those agreements. What they actually create are enforceable commitments we're accountable for, not a one-way tax break. We think those commitments should be spelled out clearly to the community. Typically the tax receipts to communities remain very large even after tax abatements are agreed. In fact Crusoe data center projects are often among the largest tax sources if not the single largest tax payer in the communities where we operate. In Abilene alone, our flagship campus is expected to generate up to 32% of the City's and up to 25% of Taylor County's current budgeted property tax revenue once fully built out. Tax revenues from our project in Claude are expected to nearly double Armstrong County’s operating budget next year.

Ownership: Founded and headquartered in the United States

Crusoe was founded in the United States, in 2018, and remains headquartered here today. We are vertically integrated: we employ hundreds of American workers in Crusoe’s own manufacturing facilities located in Colorado, Oklahoma, and Louisiana to build much of the electrical equipment and switchgear that power our data centers. We're proud that Crusoe jobs are helping build the industrial capacity America needs to win the global race for AI leadership.

Accountability

None of this works as a one-time announcement. We often put our commitments into binding agreements with the communities where we build. We follow strict environmental and safety standards. We also hire local community liaisons so concerns don't have to travel far to reach someone who can quickly act on them.

We've held ourselves to this standard from the start because we don't think it should be possible to build infrastructure at this scale any other way. Governor Abbott is right to hold companies to a high standard, and we're glad to be judged against it.

Texas has been an important partner in Crusoe's growth. And we look forward to continuing that partnership – bringing economic development, jobs, and responsible growth to Texas communities, with commitments built to last for the long term.

title: Texas data center pause puts 20% of US pipeline at risk of delay: BNEF - Energy News Beat
description:
Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s directive pausing new data center interconnections to the ERCOT grid has placed nearly one-fifth of the entire U.S. data center development pipeline at risk of delays, according to analysis from BloombergNEF (BNEF).
BNEF tracks approximately 50 GW of Texas data center projects, of which more than 70% remain in early stages.
The pause specifically affects nearly 49.8 GW, representing almost 20% of the U.S. data center pipeline of about 253 GW.
BNEF forecasts only about 1.2 GW of total ERCOT data center capacity additions between the second quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027.
Delays in energization over this window could put billions of dollars of data center leasing revenue at risk.
text:
Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s directive pausing new data center interconnections to the ERCOT grid has placed nearly one-fifth of the entire U.S. data center development pipeline at risk of delays, according to analysis from BloombergNEF (BNEF). The move, announced August 3, 2026, requires a comprehensive audit of energy use, water consumption, financing, ownership, and community impacts before any additional projects can advance.

Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and ERCOT to verify and audit all data centers in the interconnection queue. Projects that fail to comply must be denied grid connection. The order pauses related transmission planning, including ERCOT’s “Batch Zero” large-load study process that was set to begin notifications around August 7. ERCOT confirmed it is postponing Batch Zero and will seek a good-cause exception at the PUCT’s August 20 open meeting.

The ERCOT queue holds roughly 474 GW of large-load interconnection requests—more than five times the grid’s record peak demand of approximately 91 GW— with about 90% attributed to data centers. BNEF tracks approximately 50 GW of Texas data center projects, of which more than 70% remain in early stages. The pause specifically affects nearly 49.8 GW, representing almost 20% of the U.S. data center pipeline of about 253 GW.

BNEF forecasts only about 1.2 GW of total ERCOT data center capacity additions between the second quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027. Delays in energization over this window could put billions of dollars of data center leasing revenue at risk. The firm estimates AI computing capacity can generate around $1.76 billion per gigawatt per month. Under a base-case assumption that 60% of the delayed capacity is AI-related, cumulative revenue losses could reach just over $8 billion by the first quarter of 2027. In a full-delay scenario with a 100% AI-compute mix, the figure rises toward $15 billion. Longer pauses raise the chance that the review extends into the 2027 Texas legislative session, where lawmakers could alter interconnection rules.

BNEF still projects roughly 8.25 GW of additional data center capacity coming online in ERCOT through 2030, lifting the total above 17 GW. However, the firm notes that the 2030 outlook could be revised significantly if Batch Zero proceeds smoothly—or if the audit introduces material delays. Many requested projects appear speculative; the gap between the 474 GW queue and more realistic tracked pipelines underscores the need for the verification process.

Impacts on Projects and Investors

The pause injects uncertainty into timelines for the bulk of early-stage projects. Real estate investors and developers holding land under option or purchase agreements tied to data center schedules face potential force majeure or change-in-law claims. Power generation and transmission investors financing infrastructure linked to large loads must reassess viability, security interests, and capital deployment. Hundreds of millions of dollars in grid deposits—often $50,000 per megawatt for Batch Zero eligibility—now sit in limbo without a clear path to approval.

Some market reaction was immediate. Shares of certain Texas-exposed powered-land developers and independent power producers declined sharply in the days after the announcement. Hyperscalers and technology companies planning Texas campuses or expansions must now evaluate new disclosure requirements on tax incentives, on-site generation plans, water sources and cooling technology, community mitigation measures, and ownership structures. Projects relying solely on behind-the-meter (on-site) generation rather than ERCOT interconnection are generally outside the pause’s scope and may continue advancing.

Industry groups such as the Data Center Coalition have urged a swift process that distinguishes serious, responsible projects from speculative ones, citing potential for substantial investment and job creation. At the same time, community opposition over water use in arid areas, noise, traffic, and quality-of-life effects has grown across counties and cities, contributing to the political pressure behind the audit.

Broader Implications for Consumers and the Energy System

Abbott framed the directive around protecting Texans’ safety, quality of life, affordable energy, grid reliability, and water resources. It builds on a June 2026 order requiring data centers to cover their own infrastructure costs so residential customers are not burdened. The audit examines whether projects provide their own power or depend heavily on the grid, projected electricity and water consumption, cooling methods, tax abatements or public assistance, and community safeguards.

For consumers, the pause aims to reduce near-term upward pressure on electricity rates and the risk of reliability shortfalls amid explosive load growth. ERCOT has previously warned that data center and other large-load demand could drive significant increases in statewide peak requirements. By filtering the queue, regulators hope to prioritize viable projects while preserving system stability.

Indirect effects could ripple into related infrastructure. Delayed grid connections may slow associated transmission investments and influence the timing of gas-fired generation or pipeline laterals planned to serve data center campuses, particularly in the Permian and other gas-rich regions where behind-the-meter solutions have proliferated. Texas already hosts a large share of announced behind-the-meter gas capacity for data centers, supported by existing pipeline infrastructure. A prolonged pause could shift more development toward these self-supplied models or to other states.

The action follows New York’s July 2026 temporary halt on certain hyperscale data center approvals and reflects a broader recalibration in both Republican- and Democratic-led states seeking to balance economic opportunity with grid, water, and community constraints. No fixed end date for the Texas review has been announced. ERCOT and the PUCT are implementing the directive while the industry assesses how long the uncertainty will last and what permanent policy changes, if any, may emerge in 2027.

As Texas remains one of the largest and fastest-growing U.S. data center markets, the outcome of this audit will shape not only local project pipelines but a meaningful share of national AI and cloud infrastructure deployment timelines.

text:
German energy developer RWE has agreed to surrender its offshore wind leases in the United States after securing a $1.22 billion settlement with federal authorities.

The deal resolves legal claims made by RWE U.S. Offshore against the federal government, effectively halting development across three key marine lease tracts.

The agreement covers offshore lease sites located off the coasts of New York, California, and Louisiana. RWE stated that while over $1 billion had been spent acquiring and planning the sites, permitting hurdles left no viable path forward in the American market for the foreseeable future.

This settlement represents the fifth major agreement between federal agencies and renewable energy companies seeking to cancel offshore wind developments.

Total federal commitments to buy out offshore wind lease agreements have now surpassed $3.9 billion across multiple corporate deals.

Under terms connected to the buyout, RWE will shift focus toward other American energy infrastructure investments.

The company plans to deploy capital into liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects and gas turbine infrastructure to support broader grid capacity expansion goals.

The cancelled projects include a major tract in the New York Bight, the Canopy Offshore Wind site located off northern California, and a designated parcel in the waters off Louisiana.

title: BMW-Backed Student EV Looks Like A Homemade Cybertruck But Ends The Day With ... - ТопЖир
description:

According to them, the result is a car that gains more energy than it consumes during a typical day of city driving.
Deep Orange 17 weighs only 1,212 pounds (550 kg), about four times less than many production cars of similar size.
Photos: Clemson University / BMW It is worth understanding that Deep Orange 17 is primarily a research platform, not a harbinger of an affordable production car.
The main lesson to be learned is that solar energy, even at the current level of technological development, can be not just decoration but a real power source for low-mobility vehicles.
text:
Solar panels on an electric vehicle are usually one of those features that actually turn out to be far less useful than they sound. The Deep Orange 17 project from Clemson University may change that perception. The team worked together with BMW to wrap more than 1,700 photovoltaic cells around a tiny electric coupe that looks like a homemade Cybertruck. According to them, the result is a car that gains more energy than it consumes during a typical day of city driving. But don’t get too excited — there are many nuances here.

What Is Luminetta and Who Is It For?

The prototype, developed by 16 graduate students together with BMW’s research team, is called Luminetta. The university says the car was designed for a daily commute of 12 miles (20 km). Of course, it is unclear how many people have exactly such a route, but it is obvious that it does not suit most. Nevertheless, the vehicle is designed to absorb sunlight both while parked and while driving.

Technical Solutions and Extreme Lightness

The main problem, of course, is that this is not an ordinary car at all. In metal, it is all solid flat angles and improvised panels. Deep Orange 17 weighs only 1,212 pounds (550 kg), about four times less than many production cars of similar size. Its multimaterial structure combines steel, aluminum, carbon fiber, and 3D-printed metal connectors. Regenerative braking, torque distribution, and optimized transmission control algorithms — everything is aimed at one goal: to use as little energy as possible.

Testing in Different Climatic Conditions

Together with partners from the Fraunhofer ISE Institute, Clemson researchers simulated solar radiation and weather conditions in four locations around the world: Greenville (South Carolina), Frankfurt (Germany), Madrid (Spain), and Mumbai (India). In these locations, according to the university, the solar system is capable of generating enough surplus electricity to add an average of 31 miles (50 km) of range each day. This is a groundbreaking achievement, despite all the caveats.

Of course, many other innovations will be needed to apply such technologies to a modern production car. But this prototype proves: it is technically possible to get more energy than is spent on very short… trips every day.

Photos: Clemson University / BMW

It is worth understanding that Deep Orange 17 is primarily a research platform, not a harbinger of an affordable production car. University projects of this kind exist to test bold ideas, and Luminetta does this job perfectly. The main lesson to be learned is that solar energy, even at the current level of technological development, can be not just decoration but a real power source for low-mobility vehicles. If such solutions are combined with more efficient photovoltaic cells, lighter materials, and smarter energy management, in the future we may see solar electric vehicles that truly do not need daily charging from the grid. Many obstacles will have to be overcome, but the first step has already been taken.

title: Africa wants more homegrown solar to boost self-reliance, but China's shadow remains
description:
Africa eyes solar production Africa’s largest economies are keen to build their own solar manufacturing capacity.
South Africa’s utility, Eskom, plans to develop a 1-gigawatt solar manufacturing facility to capture more value from its fast-expanding solar market and respond to changing electricity demand.
African power markets shift The increased interest in solar power represents a significant shift, said Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, even if actual manufacturing capacity remains limited.
Technology transfer remains limited China’s investment is helping Africa build manufacturing capacity and technical skills.
Chinese solar exports doubled in March reaching a new monthly record, as 50 countries set all-time records for Chinese solar imports in a single month, according to Ember, a think tank.
text:
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Africa’s largest economies are accelerating plans to build more domestic solar manufacturing capacity, a shift industry analysts say reflects both industrial ambition and growing unease over dependence on imports from China that dominate the global market.

Ethiopia, South Africa, Morocco and Nigeria have been stepping up efforts to localize manufacturing of equipment for solar power, from module assembly to more advanced manufacturing, according to industry experts.

However, they say China is likely to retain its dominant global role in making solar cells and other components. Its exports of such equipment have soared, partly due to a glut in supply back home.

Chinese renewable energy investment and related construction projects in Africa reached $66 billion between 2010 and 2024, according to the think tank ODI Global.

“Growing economies, coupled with recent energy shortages in countries like Zambia and the ongoing need to provide access to underserved populations, make it (Africa) a perfect market for China to channel its overcapacity in the sector,” said Olena Borodyna, a senior geopolitical risk advisor with the London-based think tank.

Africa eyes solar production

Africa’s largest economies are keen to build their own solar manufacturing capacity.

South Africa’s utility, Eskom, plans to develop a 1-gigawatt solar manufacturing facility to capture more value from its fast-expanding solar market and respond to changing electricity demand.

Production of solar panels in Nigeria, meanwhile, is expanding rapidly, with local assembly capacity rising from about 120 megawatts to roughly 300 megawatts in the last two years. Its annual solar imports, mostly from China, also put it near South Africa’s level.

The homegrown manufacturing push is tied to structural shifts in Africa’s power markets. Rising adoption of rooftop and distributed solar systems in South Africa is reducing national grid demand, squeezing utilities’ revenues and prompting interest in diversification.

South Africa is already the continent’s largest importer of solar equipment, bringing in more than 3 gigawatts annually, also largely from China. Industry analysts say this scale of demand makes it one of the continent’s strongest candidates for localized production.

African power markets shift

The increased interest in solar power represents a significant shift, said Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, even if actual manufacturing capacity remains limited. He said nations pursuing solar manufacturing tend to already have industrial capacity and strong domestic demand.

“Morocco has doubled production to around 1 gigawatt a year. South Africa maintains a similar capacity. Egypt has gigawatt-scale projects coming online,” he said.

“A few years ago, local solar manufacturing was barely on the agenda anywhere in Africa,” Clarke said “It is now becoming a recognized pillar of industrial policy and green economic development.”

The need for more solar or other renewable power has soared. The industry group GOGLA estimates that more than 10 million solar kits were sold across Africa in 2025, serving roughly 148 million people. This was a 10% increase compared to 2024, with much of that growth concentrated in East and West Africa.

The solar build-out is within a highly concentrated global supply chain dominated by China. Africa has effectively no commercial-scale solar cell manufacturing, meaning emerging assembly plants still must rely on imported Chinese components.

“Most new factories assemble imported Chinese components rather than produce the high-value solar cells and other upstream materials, leaving Africa dependent on foreign technology for the most sophisticated parts of the supply chain,” Clarke said.

Technology transfer remains limited

China’s investment is helping Africa build manufacturing capacity and technical skills.

It’s a vital opportunity for technology transfer and job creation, ODI Global’s Borodyna said, “given China’s expertise in building out these technologies at scale.”

“China will play a huge role in the build-out of manufacturing capacity across the continent, as well as continue solar exports to the continent,” she said.

Experts say the continent has yet to receive the deeper sharing of knowhow needed to develop its own fully integrated solar industry.

Reliance on China for solar supply is likely to remain high in regions including Africa, said Hannah Pitt, with the think tank Rhodium Group’s energy and climate practice.

Trade restrictions in the U.S. and Europe have led Chinese companies to invest more in other regions such as Africa and Southeast Asia, according to Rhodium Group. Ethiopia is a favored destination, with more than half of the announced investments since 2018 coming from Chinese sources, alongside Japanese investments.

Investments in South Africa, Nigeria and Morocco were mostly led by domestic companies or joint ventures with local participation, the think tank said.

Saturated Chinese markets push solar manufacturing overseas

Extensive state support and years of steady investments in green technology manufacturing have resulted in an oversupply of solar power equipment and falling prices in China, a key factor in its huge global market share, said Lauri Myllyvirta with the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

With the market oversupplied, several major Chinese solar manufacturers, including Longi and Jinko, made losses in the first three months of 2026. For such companies, shifting overseas may be the only way to stay in business.

Chinese firms pledged as much as $250 billion in overseas green manufacturing projects between 2011 and the first half of last year, according to an estimate by Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab’s “China’s Green Leap Outward” report.

Chinese solar exports doubled in March reaching a new monthly record, as 50 countries set all-time records for Chinese solar imports in a single month, according to Ember, a think tank.

“In terms of producing and manufacturing things — like solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles — really China is by far the lead in this race,” said Li Shuo, director of the Asia Society Policy Institute’s China Climate Hub. “I personally expect the dominance of China to be further cemented and not weakened over the coming years.”

___

Chan reported from Hong Kong. Associated Press journalist Anton L. Delgado contributed from Bangkok.

title: Amazon data center plant in Texas could become America's biggest polluter
description:
The natural gas plant powering a sprawling Amazon data center project in Texas could become the largest climate polluter in the country, despite the company’s commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2040.
As part of a planned data center campus in Pecos County, the tech giant is investing in an on-site natural gas power plant, the company has confirmed.
The company has emphasized that the power plant would not raise rates for Texas residents.
The site is reportedly Amazon’s first major investment in off-grid power for a data center.
This week, the state of Texas pause new data center projects until state electricity regulators could complete an audit of each proposed facility.
text:
The natural gas plant powering a sprawling Amazon data center project in Texas could become the largest climate polluter in the country, despite the company’s commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2040.

As part of a planned data center campus in Pecos County, the tech giant is investing in an on-site natural gas power plant, the company has confirmed.

The plant is permitted to release 33 million tons of carbon dioxide per year, according to documents obtained by The New York Times and the climate research outlet Distilled.

If the final plant matches those specifications, it would be the largest single source of climate pollution in the country, according to the Times, more than doubling the emissions from Alabama’s James H. Miller Jr. Power Plant, a coal facility which emits about 16 million tons of carbon dioxide annually. (Power plants don’t always emit the maximum they are allowed to, and the Amazon facility is still in early-stage construction.)

The company has emphasized that the power plant would not raise rates for Texas residents.

“Amazon believes in paying the full costs of powering our operations,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement to The Independent on Saturday. “Our new planned data center campus in Pecos County does just that: it’s powered by new on-site generation that won’t raise electricity costs for Texas families and designed to transition to grid-connected service as interconnection timelines allow.”

Amazon is “exploring opportunities for solar energy and battery storage on site,” according to the company. The Pecos project is expected to create “thousands of new jobs,” Amazon said.

The site is reportedly Amazon’s first major investment in off-grid power for a data center.

This puts them in league with “hyperscalers” including Microsoft, Google and Meta, which have all invested in fossil fuel power sources this year as tech companies race to get enough data centers online to meet the ravenous demand for artificial intelligence.

The data campus is the latest complication in Amazon’s highly touted climate commitments.

title: Trump Refunds to Cancel Offshore Wind Projects Total $4B - Rigzone
description:

In return for focusing on fossil fuels, the US will reimburse TotalEnergies “dollar-for-dollar, up to the amount they paid in lease purchases for offshore wind,” according to the Interior Department’s statement.
New York along with six other Northeastern states filed suit in June against the Trump administration to challenge the TotalEnergies settlement.

text:
The Trump administration has agreed to roughly $4 billion in settlements this year to cancel planned offshore wind projects, including a $1.22 billion deal with German utility RWE AG announced Thursday, with billions more in projects still at risk.

In addition to RWE, the Trump administration has reached agreements with five other developers, including TotalEnergies SE, to surrender offshore wind leases and redirect reimbursed funds to fossil fuel projects and other investments favored by President Donald Trump. More than 20 leases valued at nearly $2 billion remain outstanding, according to estimates from ClearView Energy Partners, making more agreements likely in the coming months.

“The Trump administration is pulling all the levers it can to constrain the offshore wind industry to the few projects already under construction or in service,” said Timothy Fox, an analyst at ClearView Energy. “And they seem likely to succeed.”

Since returning to office last year, Trump has followed through on his campaign pledge to block wind power, a source of renewable energy he has derided for years. He issued an executive order that halted leases and project reviews for wind on federal lands and waters, a move that was declared illegal by a federal judge in December.

Some of the announced lease buybacks involved projects that were already struggling to advance, said Seth Kaplan, a vice president at Grid Strategies LLC. More than 15 gigawatts of offshore wind capacity across 16 projects was withdrawn from grid operators’ interconnection queues last year alone, according to the consulting firm.

“Companies saw the way things were going and made decisions accordingly,” Kaplan said. “If a developer sees the handwriting on the wall about where things are going they will pullback on spending.”

The administration’s latest strategy appears to be paying companies to walk away from their offshore wind leases for projects that haven’t started yet.

Advertisement - Scroll to continue

“Rather than waiting years for the projects to materialize, the Trump administration is prioritizing investments in existing infrastructure and functioning supply chains that can create jobs now and deliver economic benefits faster,” said an Interior Department spokesperson.

In March, the department agreed to pay TotalEnergies and its partners almost $1 billion to redirect funds from wind farms off the coasts of New York, New Jersey and North Carolina to oil and natural gas investments in the US.

In return for focusing on fossil fuels, the US will reimburse TotalEnergies “dollar-for-dollar, up to the amount they paid in lease purchases for offshore wind,” according to the Interior Department’s statement.

New York along with six other Northeastern states filed suit in June against the Trump administration to challenge the TotalEnergies settlement.

TotalEnergies Chief Executive Officer Patrick Pouyanné said in the statement that considering “the development of offshore wind projects isn’t in the country’s interest, we have decided to renounce offshore wind development in the United States.”

California said in June it plans to challenge the administration’s agreement to pay $120 million to Golden State Wind for a lease off the state’s coast with the funds to be reinvested in fossil-fuel projects. Golden State Wind said it has decided not to pursue any new offshore wind projects in the US.

“The real question is what happens to the progress that was made before Trump came into office,” Fox said. “After he leaves, there may be few, if any, projects to follow.”

name: American Energy
title: Some data centers are building their own power plants. In Oklahoma, most want to plug into the grid
description:
“You’re going to be building your own data centers, and you’re going to be building your own electric plants,” said President Donald Trump.
The legislature also passed Senate Bill 480 last year, allowing data centers to build power plants behind the meter, bypassing utilities.
But so far, most data centers with plans in Oklahoma are opting to plug into the grid.
Why Oklahoma isn’t seeing an influx of behind-the-meter projects for data centers Google and Oklahoma Gas & Electric announced a deal in the spring to power the tech company’s three data centers in Muskogee and Stillwater.
Large proposed data centers, including the Luther Horizon Technology Park, Project Mustang in Claremore, IREN’s Kiowa Data Center and more, plan to work with local utilities.
text:
Oklahoma passed a law last year allowing energy-hungry facilities to build their own power. But as data center announcements sprout up across Oklahoma, most include plans to work with local utilities.

Last month, Governor Kevin Stitt and some Oklahoma electric utilities signed a federal pledge to protect household ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge directs data center developers to pay their own way and invest in surrounding communities.

Part of the document states companies must buy the massive amount of electricity they require, add more power to the grid or supply it on-site.

“You’re going to be building your own data centers, and you’re going to be building your own electric plants,” said President Donald Trump. “You’re essentially becoming a utility.”

The pledge is one of many ways officials are responding to public pushback against hyperscale data centers.

Oklahoma has its own version of a ratepayer protection pledge, a law requiring electricity suppliers to create separate terms and conditions for large-scale energy consumers like data centers and increase transparency. State regulators are currently reviewing large-load tariffs from utilities intended to prevent households from shouldering grid connection costs for companies like Google and Meta.

The legislature also passed Senate Bill 480 last year, allowing data centers to build power plants behind the meter, bypassing utilities. Representative Brad Boles, R-Marlow, co-authored the legislation.

“What we realized is in Oklahoma, our state law is kind of vague; it doesn’t really say that companies can provide their own power generation,” Boles, who is running for a seat on the Corporation Commission, said. “It doesn’t say they can’t either, but it doesn’t say that they can.”

“ So we wanted to provide clarity that if a large load comes to Oklahoma and they want to provide their own power generation, that they would have the ability to do that,” he said.

The bill was expected to generate billions of dollars in private investment and alleviate pressure from the electric grid. Growing demand, supercharged by large-load consumers like data centers, is expected to outpace supply within the Southwest Power Pool’s territory. The organization operates the electric grid in Oklahoma and 16 other states.

But so far, most data centers with plans in Oklahoma are opting to plug into the grid. Experts say the state’s grid system is likely more reliable than depending on behind-the-meter generation. Building a power plant is costly and can take years to complete.

“ I don’t readily, actually, believe that any data center company wants to also be in the power business,” said Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin.

Still, some AI companies are investing in behind-the-meter natural gas plants in states like neighboring Texas to accelerate the pace of buildout. Those plants are expected to emit significant amounts of pollution, an analysis from the Texas Tribune and Floodlight shows.

Why Oklahoma isn’t seeing an influx of behind-the-meter projects for data centers

Google and Oklahoma Gas & Electric announced a deal in the spring to power the tech company’s three data centers in Muskogee and Stillwater. Google is building two solar farms to add energy generation.

Christi Woodworth, OG&E’s chief communications officer, said companies are eyeing the state’s relatively low electricity costs and reliability.

“They’ve got to make a decision about if they want to build or bring their own generation,” she said. “That effectively puts them on an island, right? They take on all of that risk themselves, and they have to decide if that’s something that they want to do.”

“The folks we’re talking with are very interested in connecting to the grid.”

The company is in “a handful” of other discussions with large-load projects, Woodworth said, but no plans are public yet.

Last year, officials announced a project in Chickasha and celebrated the state’s new behind-the-meter law. The Chickasha Airport Industrial Park could one day be home to a data center and power plant, but no firm plans have been made public. A manufacturing firm in the Tulsa Port of Catoosa announced early this year it plans to build its power on-site. A news release says the company specializes in aerospace, energy and advanced manufacturing.

Large proposed data centers, including the Luther Horizon Technology Park, Project Mustang in Claremore, IREN’s Kiowa Data Center and more, plan to work with local utilities.

The Kiowa facility is the state’s largest proposed data center, according to energy analytics firm Cleanview. In an email, Jason Date, associate director of development, said the company plans to secure its power through Public Service Company of Oklahoma.

“Like the vast majority of homes and businesses, IREN’s facilities use grid power because it is the most efficient and reliable way to source electricity,” he said.

A delay in critical infrastructure delivery is also an obstacle for data center developers. Getting a natural gas plant, the typical energy source for behind-the-meter data center projects, can currently take years.

“If you’re not in line right now, you’re probably not getting one until the 2030s,” Rhodes said.

Some companies instead are turning to used products to avoid the mile-long backlog.

“ I’ve heard of companies looking to buy used cruise ship engines,” Rhodes said. “I heard one the other day of someone trying to string together a bunch of used helicopter engines.”

Oklahoma’s behind-the-meter law requires developers to have natural gas as part of their plant. Other sources, including solar and wind, could be used in conjunction. When asked about the natural gas requirement, Boles said it was included to support the oil and gas industry.

“We felt like, as Oklahomans, it’s important to ensure that natural gas has a seat at the table,” he said.

According to an analysis from Cleanview, Oklahoma has fewer than 30 data centersplanned for the state as of early August. Texas has hundreds in its queue, Rhodes said, meaning more developers are racing to supply power. Should tech companies continue showing interest in Oklahoma, it’s possible more behind-the-meter projects could be announced.

Boles said he expects more interest in the future.

“Like anything, it takes time,” Boles said. “If you’re to build a facility with behind-the-meter, it may take three to five years to get the power infrastructure built.”

“I think we’re not going to really know for sure how many companies are utilizing this until a few years down the road.”

title: Africa wants more homegrown solar to boost self-reliance, but China's shadow remains
description:
Africa eyes solar production Africa’s largest economies are keen to build their own solar manufacturing capacity.
South Africa’s utility, Eskom, plans to develop a 1-gigawatt solar manufacturing facility to capture more value from its fast-expanding solar market and respond to changing electricity demand.
Rising adoption of rooftop and distributed solar systems in South Africa is reducing national grid demand, squeezing utilities’ revenues and prompting interest in diversification.
African power markets shift The increased interest in solar power represents a significant shift, said Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, even if actual manufacturing capacity remains limited.
Chinese solar exports doubled in March reaching a new monthly record, as 50 countries set all-time records for Chinese solar imports in a single month, according to Ember, a think tank.
text:
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Africa’s largest economies are accelerating plans to build more domestic solar manufacturing capacity, a shift industry analysts say reflects both industrial ambition and growing unease over dependence on imports from China that dominate the global market.

Ethiopia, South Africa, Morocco and Nigeria have been stepping up efforts to localize manufacturing of equipment for solar power, from module assembly to more advanced manufacturing, according to industry experts.

However, they say China is likely to retain its dominant global role in making solar cells and other components. Its exports of such equipment have soared, partly due to a glut in supply back home.

Chinese renewable energy investment and related construction projects in Africa reached $66 billion between 2010 and 2024, according to the think tank ODI Global.

“Growing economies, coupled with recent energy shortages in countries like Zambia and the ongoing need to provide access to underserved populations, make it (Africa) a perfect market for China to channel its overcapacity in the sector,” said Olena Borodyna, a senior geopolitical risk advisor with the London-based think tank.

Africa eyes solar production

Africa’s largest economies are keen to build their own solar manufacturing capacity.

South Africa’s utility, Eskom, plans to develop a 1-gigawatt solar manufacturing facility to capture more value from its fast-expanding solar market and respond to changing electricity demand.

Production of solar panels in Nigeria, meanwhile, is expanding rapidly, with local assembly capacity rising from about 120 megawatts to roughly 300 megawatts in the last two years. Its annual solar imports, mostly from China, also put it near South Africa’s level.

The homegrown manufacturing push is tied to structural shifts in Africa’s power markets. Rising adoption of rooftop and distributed solar systems in South Africa is reducing national grid demand, squeezing utilities’ revenues and prompting interest in diversification.

South Africa is already the continent’s largest importer of solar equipment, bringing in more than 3 gigawatts annually, also largely from China. Industry analysts say this scale of demand makes it one of the continent’s strongest candidates for localized production.

African power markets shift

The increased interest in solar power represents a significant shift, said Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, even if actual manufacturing capacity remains limited. He said nations pursuing solar manufacturing tend to already have industrial capacity and strong domestic demand.

“Morocco has doubled production to around 1 gigawatt a year. South Africa maintains a similar capacity. Egypt has gigawatt-scale projects coming online,” he said.

“A few years ago, local solar manufacturing was barely on the agenda anywhere in Africa,” Clarke said “It is now becoming a recognized pillar of industrial policy and green economic development.”

The need for more solar or other renewable power has soared. The industry group GOGLA estimates that more than 10 million solar kits were sold across Africa in 2025, serving roughly 148 million people. This was a 10% increase compared to 2024, with much of that growth concentrated in East and West Africa.

The solar build-out is within a highly concentrated global supply chain dominated by China. Africa has effectively no commercial-scale solar cell manufacturing, meaning emerging assembly plants still must rely on imported Chinese components.

“Most new factories assemble imported Chinese components rather than produce the high-value solar cells and other upstream materials, leaving Africa dependent on foreign technology for the most sophisticated parts of the supply chain,” Clarke said.

Technology transfer remains limited

China’s investment is helping Africa build manufacturing capacity and technical skills.

It’s a vital opportunity for technology transfer and job creation, ODI Global’s Borodyna said, “given China’s expertise in building out these technologies at scale.”

“China will play a huge role in the build-out of manufacturing capacity across the continent, as well as continue solar exports to the continent,” she said.

Experts say the continent has yet to receive the deeper sharing of knowhow needed to develop its own fully integrated solar industry.

Reliance on China for solar supply is likely to remain high in regions including Africa, said Hannah Pitt, with the think tank Rhodium Group’s energy and climate practice.

Trade restrictions in the U.S. and Europe have led Chinese companies to invest more in other regions such as Africa and Southeast Asia, according to Rhodium Group. Ethiopia is a favored destination, with more than half of the announced investments since 2018 coming from Chinese sources, alongside Japanese investments.

Investments in South Africa, Nigeria and Morocco were mostly led by domestic companies or joint ventures with local participation, the think tank said.

Saturated Chinese markets push solar manufacturing overseas

Extensive state support and years of steady investments in green technology manufacturing have resulted in an oversupply of solar power equipment and falling prices in China, a key factor in its huge global market share, said Lauri Myllyvirta with the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

With the market oversupplied, several major Chinese solar manufacturers, including Longi and Jinko, made losses in the first three months of 2026. For such companies, shifting overseas may be the only way to stay in business.

Chinese firms pledged as much as $250 billion in overseas green manufacturing projects between 2011 and the first half of last year, according to an estimate by Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab’s “China’s Green Leap Outward” report.

Chinese solar exports doubled in March reaching a new monthly record, as 50 countries set all-time records for Chinese solar imports in a single month, according to Ember, a think tank.

“In terms of producing and manufacturing things — like solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles — really China is by far the lead in this race,” said Li Shuo, director of the Asia Society Policy Institute’s China Climate Hub. “I personally expect the dominance of China to be further cemented and not weakened over the coming years.”

___

Chan reported from Hong Kong. Associated Press journalist Anton L. Delgado contributed from Bangkok.

title: Big tech, residents clash over data centers - Lowell Sun
description:
Politically, the data center debate is gathering momentum.
From Lowell to Westfield: Data centers in Mass.
The parcels either contain or are colocated to generators of the scale needed to power data centers, perhaps even artificial intelligence.
Healey advocates accountability Healey has previously said Massachusetts was “leading the country” on issues related to data center growth.
“For more than a decade, the Markley data center has been a steady, reliable part of Lowell,” the website said.
text:
Markley Lowell is currently ground zero in the commonwealth for the growing anxiety nationwide about the impact of data centers on communities, including water usage, utility bills and air and noise pollution. Even the massive size of these facilities can overwhelm neighborhoods.

Some communities are fighting back by filing lawsuits, protesting and demanding political action from their elected officials.

In April, a coalition of 10 Lowell residents filed suit in Middlesex Superior Court against the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection and Markley Group LLC.

The 94-page filing challenges the final decision by MassDEP in authorizing Markley’s operation of 27 industrial diesel backup generators and 16 cooling towers in the middle of a densely populated residential community prior to final plan approval, a process the suit called a “flawed air quality plan.”

A spokesperson for the agency said MassDEP rigorously reviewed Markley Group’s air permit application to make sure it met all compliance, reporting and environmental justice requirements.

“We remain committed to enforcing all Massachusetts environmental laws and ensuring Markley abides by the terms of the permit,” MassDEP said by email shortly after the suit was filed.

The case was heard July 29, with Judge William Barrett presiding. Plaintiff Alex Solange, who attended the hearing, said the judge listened to both sides.

“I think he was really listening and asked a lot of questions,” Solange said by phone Friday. “He said he’s going to think about it.”

Air quality is just one concern of neighbors — noise is another.

Two additional residents are plaintiffs in a class action lawsuit against Markley alleging that through its operation and maintenance of the 352,000-square-foot data center, Markley “continues to emit unreasonable and excessive noise onto the Plaintiffs’ properties thereby causing property damages through private nuisance and negligence.”

That case has not yet been heard.

Politically, the data center debate is gathering momentum. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul halted construction of large data centers for one year pending an environmental review in New York, and activist organizations like the Party for Socialism and Liberation have held protests and door-knocking campaigns in impacted communities.

From Lowell to Westfield: Data centers in Mass.

Markley’s Lowell location is in addition to the company’s almost 1 million-square-foot facility located above Macy’s in Boston’s Downtown Crossing.

Resident concerns in Lowell echo those in communities like Westfield, in which residents are digging in to do battle against an approved $4 billion data center.

Both communities passed moratoriums, halting future growth. The existing and proposed facilities are not impacted, raising further questions about the limits to local control and whether communities are prepared for the deep pockets and complex legal structures that drive this form of high-tech growth.

From ‘carrier hotels’ to AI

Like Markley Boston, Markley Lowell is a colocation data center that rents secure space to local and regional organizations to run their own technology. Those companies include the Red Sox, universities and even games of chance. The Massachusetts State Lottery Commission named Markley Boston as its colocation service provider in 2021.

Markley recently expanded its footprint in Lowell, purchasing multiple properties in and around its existing facility at 1 Markley Way in the city’s Sacred Heart neighborhood. The parcels either contain or are colocated to generators of the scale needed to power data centers, perhaps even artificial intelligence. The company’s website recently added “Now available for your generative AI workloads.”

The data center company has not divulged its long-term development plans for any of its sites, but power generation that doesn’t negatively impact rate payers may be part of that strategy, which would be in keeping with Gov. Maura Healey’s data center framework, which was released in June.

Healey advocates accountability

Healey has previously said Massachusetts was “leading the country” on issues related to data center growth.

The governor said the hold on applications for the 20-year sales- and use-tax exemptions for qualified data centers, which she agreed to as part of a 2024 economic development law, will remain in effect “until we have strong protections in place for our residents and communities against higher gas and electric bills.”

“I’ve been clear if data centers are going to come, they need to come with accountability to the community,” she said following a July 10 event in Lowell. “They have to be able to generate their own energy. It has to be clean energy. They can’t hurt the environment. They can’t hurt our water supply. They can’t cause environmental pollutions.”

Markley Lowell launches info campaign

In response to growing pushback from both residents and city leadership, Markley Lowell launched a website, “Keeping Lowell in the Loop” that makes the argument that the company has improved both the neighborhood and the Gateway City’s prospects through strategic investments.

“For more than a decade, the Markley data center has been a steady, reliable part of Lowell,” the website said. “It brought a long-empty factory back to life and quietly keeps the systems our community depends on running every day.”

Elsewhere, it says, “The City Council’s moratorium puts Lowell’s jobs, services, and one of its largest investments at risk. It doesn’t have to.”

Its “Facts, not fiction” section disputes resident claims of excessive water use and noise and air quality concerns. It does not address gas and electricity rates.

Like many large corporate developments in most municipalities, Markley received a 20-year $77 million tax break from the city of Lowell through 2035.

In the data center ecosystem, Markley Lowell’s 14-acre site, and current 40 megawatts of power, pales in comparison to the proposed almost 3 million-square-feet and 300-megawatt facility in Westfield, but both projects speak to the rising angst among voters of all persuasions of what this inexplicable and propulsive growth means for their future.

“People are really angry about what the city allowed this guy to do,” Solange said, referring to President Jeff Markley, who sued the city over the moratorium applying to its most recent purchases. According to Jeff Markley, Markley Lowell and the city have since agreed to dismiss the lawsuit “by joint stipulation.”

“We’re going to speak in the voting booth this November,” Solange said.

title: California needs a community solar plus storage program | Your Turn
description:
Here’s how it works: Californians subscribe to local, small-scale community solar projects on unused farmland or warehouse rooftops.
A community solar plus storage program in California would directly benefit low-income communities and communities of color that are on the front lines of extreme weather, climate disasters, and pollution.
Community solar plus storage is a localized solution that provides more clean energy to the grid.
The problem is, we don’t currently have a workable community solar plus storage program in our state.
Legislation that’s currently in front of the California Senate — AB 1813 — would strengthen the community solar plus storage program that’s lacking.
text:
Over the past several years, leaders at CAUSE (Central Coast Alliance United for a Sustainable Economy) have been working to retire the Ormond Beach Generating Station, which is currently being paid to remain available as an emergency “break-the-glass” reliability resource.

Since March 2024, taxpayers have been paying approximately $13 million per month — or $150 million annually — through the Electricity Supply Strategic Reliability Reserve program to keep the plant available, despite minimal actual operation. Not only a costly expense, this dirty resource burdens the residents and communities living right next door.

Rather than asking taxpayers to pay for polluting power plants that provide little actual utility, we should be investing in local resources like community solar plus storage, which can help our state meet skyrocketing electricity needs while reducing dependence on aging gas peaker plants.

Here’s how it works: Californians subscribe to local, small-scale community solar projects on unused farmland or warehouse rooftops. They receive a credit back on their monthly utility bill. There’s no up-front costs and no fee to cancel.

A community solar plus storage program in California would directly benefit low-income communities and communities of color that are on the front lines of extreme weather, climate disasters, and pollution. Nationally, nearly two million Latino families live within a half-mile radius of existing oil and gas facilities. It is not a coincidence that communities of color also see higher rates of cancer and asthma.

These same polluting practices from oil and gas companies cause more and more damage to our climate, while our communities face raging wildfires, shrinking water supply, and extreme heat waves that hit hardest to those who work long hours outdoors, lack access to emergency information, and are excluded from disaster aid due to their immigration status.

Our communities every day are facing multiple and intersectional issues all at once, and so we must hold the state responsible for its promise to us: move California away from relying on large fossil fuel plants and instead invest in distributed, community-scale clean energy resources that strengthen reliability and resilience.

Residents and communities living next to legacy, polluting fossil fuel should not be forced to breathe in particular matter, while at risk of medical debt compounded with rising utility bills. Air pollution from fossil fuel use is already estimated to cause between $430 billion and $870 billion in health expenses every year in the United States. A cleaner, renewable grid reduces pollution-related deaths by 53,000 per year and prevents family trips to the emergency room.

Community solar plus storage is a localized solution that provides more clean energy to the grid. The problem is, we don’t currently have a workable community solar plus storage program in our state. Low-income Californians can’t benefit from the promise of solar if they don’t own homes or can’t afford the investment of putting solar panels on their roofs.

Legislation that’s currently in front of the California Senate — AB 1813 — would strengthen the community solar plus storage program that’s lacking. Passing this legislation would enable us to catch up with the more than 20 other states that have community solar programs. It would benefit low-income communities and communities of color that have too often been sidelined in the transition to clean energy.

Over time, the power of community organizing can overcome corporate interests seeking to slow progress. In April 2025, we achieved the passage of a city resolution in which the Oxnard City Council said it opposed future extensions of the Ormond Beach Generating Station. More recently, we heard that the water board has reaffirmed its commitment to retirement by the end of this year.

We will continue to organize to hold state officials and city councilmembers accountable to using their power to shut this power plant down for good.⁠ At the same time, we’ll continue to advocate for adding more clean energy to the grid that will benefit communities not only in the Central Coast, but across all of California.

Passing AB 1813 will mean that low-income communities who have been on the front lines of pollution and locked out of the promise of clean energy for far too long will finally be able to reap the benefits of lower bills and cleaner air. That’s a result that’s worth fighting for.

Lucia Marquez is the Associate Policy Director with The Central Coast Alliance United for a Sustainable Economy (CAUSE).

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Right-leaning legal activists along with Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence company have brought sweeping challenges against a cornerstone of legal enforcement in the United States: the right of private groups, people and local governments to sue over violations of many major laws.

Their argument, supported by the Trump administration, is that the Constitution reserves tremendous power for the president and federal agencies to decide how — or whether at all — to enforce federal law. They contend Congress should never have handed that power to others through so-called citizen suits that are part of environmental, campaign finance and certain other laws.

Environmentalists say it would be devastating to lose this essential, decades-old tool that is used to impose fines and halt lawbreaking by bad actors. Citizen suits, for example, have extracted millions from heavily polluting oil and gas operations, and ensured that lead pipes in Flint, Michigan, would be removed after its water crisis.

Legal experts say four pending federal cases — one of them filed last week — are moving forward at a time when the conservative majority on the Supreme Court gives opponents of citizen suits a greater chance than ever of success. The hard part for those opponents now is winning early federal cases and creating disagreement between the country's appeals courts, which may help convince the Supreme Court the issue is important enough for a nationwide ruling.

Back in 2000, a Supreme Court opinion opened the door for that possibility.

“Many of us who worked in this area have been waiting basically 26 years for this shoe to drop,” said Richard Lazarus, a Harvard professor with decades of experience in environmental law.

A more inviting Supreme Court could take up the issue

Lazarus was referring to former moderate Justice Anthony Kennedy's comments in a Clean Water Act case that citizen suits raised “difficult and fundamental” questions about whether they improperly dilute executive power. The late conservative Justice Antonin Scalia wrote in a dissenting opinion in the same case that citizen suits turn “over to private citizens the function of enforcing the law.” He avoided explicitly saying they were constitutional.

“The court is more like Scalia’s court since he died than it ever was when he was there,” said Lazarus.

He observed that those who lost cases where Scalia dissented are rushing back to today's court hoping for a more favorable result.

The critical issue for citizen suits is who — the government or private citizens — collects fines and has control. A person filing a citizen suit must tell the government ahead of time. The government can stop the suit if it sufficiently pursues the case itself, but its options are limited and the person suing can stay involved. Citizen suits can force compliance with the law and result in fines, which go to the U.S. Treasury.

Prominent law firms and companies are pushing against citizen suits

Efforts to increase presidential power and limit who can sue have grown in recent years. They gained vital federal support this summer.

That’s when the Pacific Legal Foundation, a right-leaning organization with recent Supreme Court success, chose a routine citizen suit in Tennessee federal court for a broader constitutional challenge.

They signed on as attorneys for Springfield, a town of roughly 19,000 north of Nashville, that was in the early stages of fighting allegations brought by Tennessee Riverkeeper that it had let too much sewage flow from its treatment plant into a nearby creek, violating the Clean Water Act.

It was the thirty-first citizen suit Tennessee Riverkeeper had filed under the Clean Water Act since 2010. Pacific Legal argued this was part of the problem — a private group of unelected activists had repeatedly forced others to expend resources defending themselves.

It’s better when “the government is the one wielding the power because the government remains accountable to the people,” said Sean Radomski, a Pacific Legal Foundation attorney on the case.

Radomski isn’t targeting every lawsuit a person can bring under federal law — he takes exception to those where fines go to the Treasury and where he says people are improperly taking on the government's powers. Civil rights lawsuits, for example, where damages are paid directly to those wronged, wouldn't be touched. Nor would many procedural challenges.

Elon Musk's AI company is also getting into the fight

Musk-led xAI argued many similar points in its ongoing bid to rid itself of the NAACP’s lawsuit accusing it of operating dozens of gas turbines near Memphis to power a data center without first getting permits. The civil rights group told a Mississippi federal court that the turbines are a pollution threat to those who lived nearby, many of whom are Black. One of their demands was to halt the gas turbines until the company complied with the law.

The Trump administration intervened in support of Musk’s company, arguing that turning off the power to artificial intelligence that supports the Department of War would harm national security. Because the Trump administration wants the suit dismissed, the NAACP shouldn’t be allowed to proceed with it — prudent enforcement requires balancing interests, including national security, the DOJ said.

Laura Thoms, director of enforcement at Earthjustice, which is representing the NAACP, said the government traditionally gets involved in cases to enforce the law, not to argue that it doesn’t matter if the law is broken.

“This administration has determined that the company should be allowed to continue to pollute and that therefore, they should have the unilateral and unreviewable authority to veto our citizen suit,” she said.

Changing the law would have profound consequences at a critical time

Citizen suits were written into foundational environmental laws because Congress understood that the federal government had limited resources to go after polluters and that the politics of some cases could be dicey — the government sometimes is the polluter. That’s why outside groups are necessary to fulfill the law’s purpose, according to Lazarus.

Some argue that dynamic is especially important now. The Trump administration has slashed air and water protections and promoted fossil fuels. They’ve also constrained enforcement that could slow energy projects to only the most extreme cases, such as an “imminent and substantial threat to human health,” according to a federal guidance memo. Environmentalists say citizen suits are vital for filling the enforcement gap this administration created.

Leaner budgets in many states make the problem worse.

Thoms said the potential for corruption could increase, too — the president could unilaterally waive laws to benefit friends.

She said that those who live in states with strong protections may be fine if citizen suits end, but other areas will be “sacrifice zones” where citizens have few options to fight pollution in their backyard. And the unprotected are more often poor and majority-minority communities.

Many experts are skeptical of the challengers’ claims of a powerful president that gets to unilaterally shape enforcement even outside of criminal law. They argue the country’s history is rife with examples of that task falling to private individuals, too — a contention the challengers reject.

David Adelman, a law professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Law, said before the current conservative majority on the Supreme Court, he would have thought there was a close to zero percent chance the challenges would succeed.

“But this court has been so protective of the executive branch’s complete control of implementation of federal law,” he said, “that it’s not implausible that something like this could prevail.”

When Texas’s privately-run electrical grid collapsed amid a battery of winter storms in February of 2021, it plunged over 4.5 million people into darkness, and contributed to hundreds of deaths due to the lack of water, food, and heat.

A similarly tragic story almost unfolded in July of this year — had in not been for the deployment of a jaw dropping amount of solar power infrastructure that kept the grid from collapsing under the strain.

New reporting by the Texas Tribune details the state’s rapid adoption of solar energy, specifically solar panels and storage batteries. The paper notes that when the organization that manages state’s electrical grid — the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) — broke record energy demands on both July 21st and 22nd, it hardly registered as an event, because its solar infrastructure ensured there was a 20,000 megawatt buffer padding the grid’s capacity.

“We hit an all time peak, and we had no issue hitting that peak,” Thomas Gleeson, chair of Texas’s Public Utility Commission, told the Tribune.

Unsurprisingly, those moments of peak demand coincided with oppressive summer temperatures, with the heat index reaching 116 degrees Fahrenheit in Dallas on July 22nd. The Tribune notes that at various points, solar power accounted for over 45 percent of the state’s total electrical generation, breaking state records both for total electricity generated by solar panels and for total electricity discharged from solar batteries.

As the power grid’s capacity grows, so too will the demand. Though ERCOT is standing strong for now, the state estimates that by 2032, statewide electric demand will be nearly double what it was on July 22nd.

To combat that reality, the utility firm says it has some 460 gigawatts of generation cued up for development, around 70 percent of which is made up of solar infrastructure.

Of course, it will also help if Texas governor Greg Abbott sticks to his recently enacted data center moratorium, which put the brakes on over 474 gigawatts worth of impending electrical stress, at least temporarily. Long-term, it’s unlikely that Texas will refuse the nearly 1,800 data center projects looking to call the state home — an unending game of chicken between the tech industry and a utility provider scrambling to keep up with growing demand.

text:
The Rivian R2 is, frankly, the most important vehicle Rivian (RIVN) has ever built. It's the car that's supposed to push Rivian over the edge on cost, scale, and, importantly, profits.

Rivian's first-gen R1S and R1T EVs earned acclaim but bled money at their high price points. The R2 is Rivian's answer: a midsize electric SUV built on a platform using a cheaper bill of materials, aimed squarely at the Tesla (TSLA) Model Y, and priced to move volume — $61,000 in test-car trim and as low as $45,000 for the base model coming next year.

The R2 is make-or-break for California-based Rivian. But after a few days behind the wheel of the Performance model, the verdict is clear: The company nailed it.

The R2 look

The R2's styling is familiar, in the best way. The cube-like, squared-off design that people love in the R1 carries over, but the R2 just looks better. Maybe it's the smaller footprint, shorter rear hatch, and tighter proportions that give it a cleaner, more coherent stance than the larger R1S.

And the interior makes you feel right at home. Anyone who's sat in an R1 will recognize the layout — crisp, high-resolution screens for both infotainment and the driver cluster. But the fit and finish definitely punches above its weight. This is a $60,000-ish car, not Mercedes or BMW money, yet it feels premium.

Special touches include soft-touch materials, real stitching, an interesting denim-like fabric across the dash, nice switchgear, and a key fob that doubles as a durable carabiner. Storage is excellent, down to a pull-out tray in the center console sized for a tissue box.

The back seat is a highlight. Without the R1's third row eating into legroom, the R2's second row gets more foot space and stretch-out room.

The cargo hatch is spacious, the panoramic glass roof is expansive, and the whole cabin is remarkably quiet. Driving around New York City — bumps, ruts, sirens, chaos — the R2 remains serene inside.

R2 on the road

The R2 in Performance trim means dual motors making 656 horsepower and 609 lb-ft of torque, good for a 0-to-60 time Rivian measured at blistering 3.6 seconds — that's Porsche 911 territory. The power is immediate, smooth, and effortless.

But the suspension is the star. This isn't air suspension — it's semiactive adaptive damping, and you can dial it through the drive modes. I left it in the softest comfort setting and never looked back.

The car rides beautifully — planted, well-damped, no excessive body roll, no wafting or wallow. It turns in cleanly and stays composed. Over broken pavement, it absorbs the hit and moves on rather than bouncing you down the road.
