text:
The study also found that relatively small, inexpensive interventions can have significant effects

Canada’s clean energy transition is creating thousands of new jobs, but structural barriers are preventing many qualified workers from entering the sector, according to new research from the Trellis Foundation and the University of Victoria.

The study draws on the experiences of 119 applicants to the Trellis Foundation’s bursary program, which supports women pursuing careers in the clean energy transition. Rather than identifying a lack of interest in clean energy careers, the research concludes that financial hardship, credential recognition, workplace culture, and traditional hiring practices are limiting participation at a time when demand for skilled workers continues to grow.

Rebecca Black, executive director of the Trellis Foundation, said the research was designed to better understand why people who want to work in the clean energy sector are struggling to find pathways into those careers.

“We have all these students looking for jobs in the sector, and there seems to be a disconnect,” Black said. “We wanted to understand what those disconnects are between the companies and utilities that are hiring and the people who want to work in the sector.”

The findings suggest the issue is not a shortage of interest or talent. Instead, researchers identified systemic barriers affecting women and people with intersecting identities, including newcomers to Canada, Indigenous people, racialized Canadians, LGBTQ+ individuals, and young workers. Financial insecurity, difficulties obtaining recognition for international credentials, exclusionary workplace cultures, and traditional education and hiring pathways all contribute to the problem.

Black said employers also have opportunities to broaden recruitment by reconsidering conventional hiring practices. Lengthy lists of required qualifications, for example, may discourage otherwise capable applicants from applying, particularly women.

The report recommends expanding mentorship programs, recognizing transferable skills alongside formal credentials, supporting more flexible education pathways, and treating bursaries and mentorship as essential workforce infrastructure rather than optional initiatives.

The findings come as Canada’s energy sector prepares for significant growth in electricity demand driven by electrification, renewable energy development, grid expansion, battery storage, and building decarbonization. At the same time, a growing number of experienced workers are approaching retirement, increasing pressure on employers to recruit and retain skilled employees.

Black said the discussion should be viewed primarily as an economic and workforce issue rather than a political debate over diversity initiatives.

“When we have gaps, we need to look at who can fill them,” she said. “There are a lot of people who can fill them, just not necessarily through the transition that has traditionally happened into the sector.”

The study also found that relatively small interventions can have significant effects. A modest bursary can help students remain in school instead of taking on additional work, while mentorship and networking opportunities provide valuable connections between students and employers.

Black said the Trellis Foundation is already building mentorship programs and working with industry partners to test more inclusive approaches to workforce development.

She hopes the organization’s work will eventually become unnecessary.

“The best outcome of something like the Trellis Fund is that we see the systemic change that we need,” she said. “These pilot projects wouldn’t need to happen anymore because we’ve seen scaled-up versions of inclusive policies that allow these sectors to attract and retain the people they need.”

Canada’s clean energy transition will require more than new technologies and infrastructure, Black said. It will also require building a workforce capable of delivering them.

By Nora Eckert

DETROIT, Aug 6 (Reuters) – Ford Motor said on Thursday that its upcoming midsize electric pickup truck would be priced starting at about $28,000 ​and named Fathom, as the Michigan automaker ‌looks to offer an affordable model in a market full of pricey EVs.

• Ford has approached development and manufacturing of this vehicle from the ground up, assembling a specialized team in California aimed ‌at ​competing with rivals like Tesla and ⁠China’s BYD.

• The automaker ⁠has established a new assembly-tree manufacturing process at its Louisville Assembly Plant.

• Three lines, for the front, rear and structural battery and seating, will run ​simultaneously and join at the end instead of having one traditional, long conveyor belt. The new system ⁠is meant to improve efficiency ⁠and reduce costs.

• Ford reset its EV ​strategy after a $19.5 billion writedown late last year, in which ​it axed several planned models as well as ‌its larger, more expensive Lightning electric pickup truck.

• Fathom is part of a limited group of vehicles, gasoline-powered, hybrids and EVs included, that are available under $30,000. Data ⁠from car-shopping website Edmunds, updated through May 2026, shows 36 models are available for under a starting price of $30,000 in ⁠the U.S.

• Fathom ‌would become one of Ford’s least ⁠expensive models, rivaling its Maverick pickup, which ​starts ‌at just below $30,000, according to Edmunds.

• Pre-orders ​for Fathom ⁠will open in early 2027, with customer deliveries beginning in autumn 2027. The sub-$30,000 pickup truck is expected to be the first of a family of models based on Ford’s new EV platform.

(Reporting by Nora Eckert; Editing ​by Jamie Freed)

text:
Engineers are crucial to the electric grid, but it worked so well for so long that it became a victim of its own success– many engineering students started to see it as boring and looked elsewhere for careers they perceived as more exciting.

All that is starting to change, and Clemson University is using that momentum to recruit students and prepare the grid workforce of the future.

Factors that include rising energy demand from data centers, electrification of the manufacturing sector and extreme weather are putting unprecedented stress on the grid. At the same time, utilities are facing a wave of workforce retirements.

Clearly, those are problems for society. But for power engineering students, they become interesting challenges to solve and the foundation for meaningful careers.

For the Clemson faculty members who teach those students, it is an opportunity to foster a passion for power engineering in the next-generation workforce.

Ramtin Hadidi, an associate professor of electrical and computer engineering, said he is seeing an uptick in interest in the grid among students.

“There was a period of time when this was not a popular topic,” Hadidi said. “Students said, ‘Oh, power, everybody knows how it works. There’s nothing to research about that.’ It was not an enticing topic. Computers and the internet were enticing. Now power engineering is back on top. Students like to know more about it and work in this field.”

The next generation of power engineers will need more than a traditional electrical engineering background.

Clemson faculty members said that while strong fundamentals in power systems will continue to be critical, students will also need to understand power electronics, computing, communications, controls, artificial intelligence and the practical realities of keeping electricity reliable.

That is why Clemson is combining classroom instruction with hands-on labs, industry-connected projects and facilities such as the Duke Energy eGRID, where students can see how real grid equipment behaves under real-world conditions.

It’s a combination that has attracted top students, including a Fulbright Scholar.

“You have to teach fundamentals at the right level but also make it interesting,” said Johan Enslin, a professor of electrical and computer engineering. “I don’t think you should just give them differential equations until it’s over their heads. I think it’s important to make it fun for them in class.”

Kevin Tomsovic, the Duke Energy Endowed Chair in Smart Grid Technology, said power engineering gives students a wide range of problems to solve, from helping data centers manage their electricity use to keeping the full grid working together.

It’s also an opportunity to work in a field that provides a critical service to society.

“I’m happy to be part of the utility industry, because I think it’s a service field,” Tomsovic said. “We’re providing critical services, and it’s good for society. The system runs well, and everybody’s better off.”

title: Vineland, N.J. data center makes case for on-site power generation during 6-hour hearing
description:
Representatives for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data center in Vineland, New Jersey, on Wednesday defended a proposal to house liquefied natural gas and utilize fuel cell technology to power the 300-megawatt facility.
During a six-hour hearing before the city’s planning board, DataOne pleaded their case for the project’s second phase: a new proposal to use Bloom Energy fuel cells to power the site.
The fuel cells use a chemical reaction to convert natural gas into electricity.
While the new energy plan is projected to emit fewer pollutants than the natural gas engines, it would increase the amount of water required to cool the data center.
However, that water generation was only possible through the use of diesel or natural gas engines proposed in the original plan.
text:
This story is part of the WHYY News Climate Desk, bringing you news and solutions for our changing region.

From the Poconos to the Jersey Shore to the mouth of the Delaware Bay, what do you want to know about climate change? What would you like us to cover? Get in touch.

Representatives for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data center in Vineland, New Jersey, on Wednesday defended a proposal to house liquefied natural gas and utilize fuel cell technology to power the 300-megawatt facility.

The project, with the first phase already approved and under construction, is being developed by DataOne for the Nebius Group to support AI infrastructure as part of a $17 billion deal with Microsoft.

During a six-hour hearing before the city’s planning board, DataOne pleaded their case for the project’s second phase: a new proposal to use Bloom Energy fuel cells to power the site. If approved, it would be Bloom Energy’s largest single-site fuel cell project to date. Currently, the company’s largest fuel cell project is an 80-megawatt installation in South Korea.

DataOne’s attorney Michael Fralinger said the fuel cells, which do not utilize combustion, release fewer carbon emissions than traditional power generation. The fuel cells use a chemical reaction to convert natural gas into electricity. Fralinger also said on-site generation takes strain off the electrical grid and won’t impact ratepayers’ bills.

“This particular project has been deliberately designed and structured so that its energy requirements are not subsidized by existing electric or natural gas customers,” Fralinger said at the planning board hearing, which included six hours of witness testimony and cross examination. “All of the financial risk for this project is being borne by the project.”

The planning board, after ending the hearing at midnight, must reconvene to allow for additional comment and decide whether to approve the plan. Members of the public were not afforded the chance to speak during the lengthy and detail-oriented meeting, and many walked out as it neared the midnight hour.

“People in the room felt that he was going at a certain pace and focusing on extraneous details to basically run out the clock and to get it to a point where people were just like, ‘This is so boring, I don’t want to be here anymore,’” said Zac Landicini, who lives about 3 miles from the data center and has been advocating against its development.

The acceleration of power-hungry artificial intelligence has boosted demand for data centers. President Donald Trump’s administration last year announced plans to accelerate AI development with limited regulatory oversight.

DataOne said its facility will benefit Vineland by hiring more than 200 permanent, full-time workers, and by becoming one of the largest taxpayers in the city. The city’s mayor and City Council president have voiced support for the project, and have approved a tax exemption for the company as part of a five-year plan.

Residents have voiced concerns about the potential impact on air quality and water supplies, which in some areas of the country have been threatened. Some residents have also complained about whining metallic construction noises, leading to a class-action lawsuit that claims construction and operational noise will impact property values.

Much of the meeting was focused on DataOne’s plans to generate the majority of its energy on site, utilizing natural gas accessed through an already-existing gas pipeline that runs from the facility. The proposal would also make way for a 1.5-million gallon LNG storage tank on site in the event access to the natural gas pipeline is interrupted.

Eric Reaman, president and CEO of Cashman Preload Cryogenics, which is the manufacturer of the tank, said LNG cannot ignite inside the tank without coming in contact with a source of ignition. He also said there’s no oxygen inside the tank necessary to trigger a fire or explosion. Reaman said the tank is built with fire resistant concrete, and equipped with leak and heat detection monitors as well as an automatic shut-off system in case of emergency.

DataOne’s application previously proposed the use of 32 high-efficiency natural gas engines, of which five would be utilized for back-up generation, as well as six diesel generators for emergency power. During the hearing, Fralinger said DataOne scrapped the plan to use engines because of public outcry over potential air emissions.

The company is now seeking approval to use Bloom Energy fuel cells, which turn natural gas into electricity through an electrochemical reaction without releasing high amounts of air pollutants like nitrous oxides and sulfur dioxides. During the hearing, Marisa Blackshire, Bloom Energy’s vice president of environment and regulatory law, said the technology is quieter than a hair dryer and has such a low emission profile it’s exempted from New Jersey’s air permit requirements.

“The nature of the electricity generation being that it comes from a noncombustion reaction dictates that we have very low criteria pollutant emissions,” she said.

However, during cross-examination, Blackshire confirmed that the facility in Vineland would still emit about 2.19 billion pounds of climate-warming CO2 a year.

While the new energy plan is projected to emit fewer pollutants than the natural gas engines, it would increase the amount of water required to cool the data center.

Hyperscale data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons of drinking water per day to cool the facilities and their servers to prevent overheating. In some areas, that has drained residents’ well water supplies.

Previously, DataOne said the facility wouldn’t consume water from the region’s aquifer because it would use waste heat to generate its own water supply by utilizing thermal energy to extract moisture from the air. However, that water generation was only possible through the use of diesel or natural gas engines proposed in the original plan.

Instead, the new plan would use more than 400 fans to cool the data center, and during particularly hot days, a misting spray would be utilized to further cool the system. Though DataOne will use a closed-loop system that reuses water, the water from the misting spray would evaporate. An engineer testified that the project would require about 8 million gallons of water a year drawn from the city’s water supply. The proposed Bloom units would also require an undetermined amount of water on start-up, which would be reused.

name: Indiana Environment
title: The problem with going solar in Indiana
authors: Gabriel Bosslet, Matthew Will, Danielle McGrath, Sean Mobley
description:
The average Indiana home uses ~900 kilowatt-hours of energy per month.
Indiana high court sides with utilities on solar power, ending benefits for small owners To cover 100% of those energy needs, a family would need an 8-kilowatt solar system, which costs around $25,000 to install.
This greatly changes the financial math for solar energy in Indiana.
Rather than reducing the previous $152 monthly energy bill for a solar owner to $17, this net metering boondoggle means that the average solar owner in Indiana still pays $85 monthly.
Those savings become profits for Indiana electric utilities and their (mostly) out-of-state shareholders.
text:
Over the past year, I have been noodling over the possibility of installing solar panels on my roof. This simple curiosity eventually turned into action — I got several quotes for what solar installation might cost. It was at that point that I discovered a 2017 Indiana state law that makes installing solar financially difficult for individual homeowners but quite profitable for electric companies.

I like the idea of being more self-sufficient. I like the fact that, once installed, solar panels provide pretty much free energy for my home that is healthier for our planet. And solar technology has become much better and more affordable over time. As climate author Bill McKibben put it on a podcast: “Sometime earlier this decade, we passed some invisible line where it became cheaper to produce energy from the sun and the wind than from setting stuff on fire.”

While it has become less expensive, installing a solar harvesting system is not cheap in the short term; especially after federal lawmakers abruptly eliminated the 30% residential tax credit at the end of last year. I would have to pay a lot up front for the ability to harvest free photons that would otherwise just warm up the shingles on my roof. Under fair economic conditions, that upfront cost pays for itself over time through drastically lower monthly power bills, eventually earning back every dollar spent and saving money for years to come.

Let’s look at what this should look like for an average Hoosier household.

The average Indiana home uses ~900 kilowatt-hours of energy per month. At an average cost of $0.15 per kWh, that equates to an average electricity bill of $135 per month (plus a $17 monthly customer fee, totaling $152 monthly) .

Indiana high court sides with utilities on solar power, ending benefits for small owners

To cover 100% of those energy needs, a family would need an 8-kilowatt solar system, which costs around $25,000 to install.

With fair energy policy, this system would essentially eliminate a family’s electricity charges, leaving them with only the mandatory monthly fee to the electric company required to be connected to the grid. That would drop their $152 monthly energy bill to $17.

At this savings rate, the payoff horizon is 15.4 years. Assuming a 30-year solar panel lifespan, a solar household would save around $23,650 in energy bills over the last 14.6 years of the system. All while releasing zero carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

While that is how it should happen, a 2017 state law ensures that is not how it works in Indiana. Here’s why.

On a sunny afternoon in July, a home solar array typically makes far more power than the house needs, sending the extra electricity back to the neighborhood power lines. At night, when the sun is shining in Australia instead of Indiana, the family has to pull electricity back off the grid to keep the lights on.

Think of the power grid like a bank account: with a solar system you make energy “deposits” during the day, and make energy “withdrawals” at night. The system that tracks these deposits and withdrawals is called “net metering”.

In most states, if you deposit 20 kWh of power during the afternoon (as is usual on a typical sunny day), you get a full 1-to-1 credit to withdraw those same 20 kWh later that night. While states like Florida, Ohio, and Iowa protect 1-to-1 net metering as a matter of property rights and energy freedom, Indiana’s Senate Enrolled Act 309 created an artificial government price control that penalizes Hoosier families for investing in their own homes.

Passed in 2017, the law allows electric companies to harvest those same 20 kWh of afternoon power from you and immediately sell them to your neighbors for $3.00 (the full $0.15/kWh retail price), while crediting you just $0.70 (the discounted $0.035/kWh wholesale rate). When you pull that same power back out of the grid that night, they charge you $3.00 once again. That leaves the homeowner getting back less than 25% of the energy value they deposited just hours earlier.

This greatly changes the financial math for solar energy in Indiana. Rather than reducing the previous $152 monthly energy bill for a solar owner to $17, this net metering boondoggle means that the average solar owner in Indiana still pays $85 monthly. That pushes the payoff horizon to over 31 years, which exceeds the lifespan of the panels entirely. Instead of saving tens of thousands of dollars, Hoosier families actually end up taking a $900 net loss on their investment.

The $23,650 of potential savings that SEA 309 takes from solar households does not disappear into thin air. Those savings become profits for Indiana electric utilities and their (mostly) out-of-state shareholders. Funded out of the pockets of Hoosiers. It’s time for the General Assembly to repeal SEA 309, restore fair 1-to-1 net metering, and give Hoosier families the right to benefit from their own private property investments.

title: RWE relinquishes North Coast offshore wind lease, part of $1.22 billion Trump admin deal
description:

RWE is one of two companies, alongside Vineyard Offshore, that hold wind leases off California’s North Coast through its RWE U.S. Offshore subsidiary.

This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone.
text:
On Thursday, renewable energy company RWE announced that it entered into a $1.22 billion agreement with the Trump administration to relinquish its offshore wind leases. RWE is one of two companies, alongside Vineyard Offshore, that hold wind leases off California’s North Coast through its RWE U.S. Offshore subsidiary.

According to a press release published by RWE Thursday morning, the company’s settlement with the U.S. Department of Interior will “resolve claims against the U.S. government and relinquish its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.”

“RWE U.S. Offshore secured these leases from the U.S. government with a long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity in American waters and invested more than $1 billion toward the leases and the development of these projects,” RWE’s release reads. “These leases provided legal rights to develop offshore projects and represented years of planning, investment, and partnership with federal agencies.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future. The settlement resolves RWE U.S. Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds. The company determined that this resolution best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

The news did not come as a shock.

“Today’s news is disappointing but not surprising,” Environmental Protection Information Center Executive Director Tom Wheeler told the Times-Standard via an emailed statement Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration has used its full weight to hamper offshore wind development. Elsewhere, other offshore wind companies have already caved to the pressure. The winners today are the fossil fuel industry and the losers are Humboldt County and the planet. But tomorrow is a new day. The Trump Administration will end. And the promise of offshore wind remains: clean, reliable energy built locally by well-paying blue-collar jobs. The Trump Administration can delay, but it cannot suppress the future.”

RWE’s press release says that the agreement will allow the company to “redeploy its capital to accelerate value-accretive opportunities that deliver reliable and affordable energy.” That “redeployment” is described as including “$900 million to acquire an indirect 16% stake in the Louisiana LNG Project” — a large-scale natural gas development that has been criticized as a major source of greenhouse gas pollution — and other natural gas projects throughout the U.S.

“While RWE’s shareholders get their bag, the rest of us get the finger. We the people are paying for this buyout, and what we get in return is more expensive energy, backwards climate policy and greater harm to our communities,” Assemblymember Chris Rogers told the Times-Standard via email Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration is again using taxpayer dollars to settle personal vendettas and line the pockets of his friends and donors by protecting oil profiteers from the competition of clean, affordable and renewable energy.

‘Every American should be enraged.’

U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-San Rafael), ranking Democratic member of the U.S. House of Representatives’ Committee on Natural Resources, released a statement Thursday morning just before noon, calling the DOI and RWE’s agreement a “fake settlement” and saying that “the deals are deeply corrupt and illegal” and “when the accountability comes, and I promise you accountability is coming, everyone involved in them will answer for it.”

“The most corrupt, lawless administration in American history is once again flouting the law and attempting to use over $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to kill off clean energy projects slated to create thousands of good jobs and lower electricity bills for Californians,” Huffman said. “Trump is strongarming companies into taking these illegal deals and abandoning offshore wind projects that would put huge amounts of cheap electricity on the grid and lower electricity prices. Instead, he is pressuring them to invest not only in dirty fossil fuel projects, but in LNG export facilities that push domestic energy prices even higher at a time when American families are reeling from skyrocketing costs caused by his reckless war of choice in Iran.

“One of the projects illegally canceled in this fake settlement is off the coast of Humboldt County in my district. The benefits of that project were tremendous — revitalizing the economy of a rural community, creating thousands of quality jobs and lowering utility bills for families all across California. Like a mob boss, Trump tightened the screws on RWE and, shamefully, the company capitulated and went along with this sham deal that robs the American people and makes a mockery of RWE’s stated commitments to clean energy. When these illegal, fake settlements are reversed by the courts and/or future congressional action — and they will be — RWE and others who participate in these charades will own every bit of the shame they deserve.”

Huffman said that the total cost to the taxpayers for paying companies to abandon offshore leases already ads up to “the tune of about $4 billion” noting that such settlements have thus far employed funding intended for the payout of federal lawsuits and settlements.

“Trump is using the Judgment Fund as a slush fund to pay for it. This is the same pot of taxpayer money Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche tried to use for his so-called ‘Anti-Weaponization Fund’ to pay off convicted J6 felons,” Huffman said. “Once again, we see this administration’s priorities laid bare: treating a fund that exists to resolve valid claims and liabilities as a massive personal slush fund Trump can use to reward criminals, kill off clean energy projects and do virtually anything else that serves his personal and political interests.”

Spokesperson Anthony Martinez from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office provided the Times-Standard with the following statement: “The pattern is impossible to ignore. After getting beaten in court again and again, Trump has stopped trying to win on the merits and continues to make backroom deals to kill clean energy projects — a gift to his fossil fuel industry donors at the expense of America’s economic security.

“While China and other global competitors race to dominate the technologies that will power the future, California is building a modern grid, energy independence and an energy future that Trump is too small to understand.”

“This action by the Trump Administration is utter BS,” Sen. Mike McGuire (D-Healdsburg) said in an emailed statement delivered around 1 p.m. “The overall California RWE wind project would have advanced clean, reliable wind energy — enough to power 5 million homes — and created good rural jobs for the North Coast. Seemingly ripped from a script of VEEP, Trump is now forcing RWE’s hand to reinvest in the same fossil fuels which delivered the climate crisis to our door. This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone. Total buffoonery.”

The Interior Department provided a statement from Secretary of the Interior and Chairman of the National Energy Dominance Council Doug Burgum Thursday afternoon.

“Americans deserve an energy system built on common sense, not one dependent on costly subsidies or technologies that can’t meet our country’s current demand,” said Burgum. “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”

name: Louisiana American Energy
title: Trump administration will buy back company's offshore wind leases off 3 states in a $1.2B deal
description:
The Republican administration has been buying back offshore wind leases from energy companies as it seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.
RWE announced it is investing $900 million in a liquified natural gas project in Louisiana and spending $300 million on natural gas turbines.
The administration adopted this strategy after federal courts thwarted Trump’s efforts to stop offshore wind development through executive action.
Chicago-based Invenergy agreed in June to end its four offshore wind leases that were very early in development in exchange for reimbursements of lease fees totaling $765 million.
States that are losing offshore wind energy are suing.
text:
An offshore wind company said Thursday that it reached a $1.2 billion deal with the Trump administration to walk away from projects under development off New York, California and Louisiana.

RWE U.S. Offshore said its leases represented years of planning, investment and partnership with federal agencies, but it determined there was no path forward to permit the projects for the foreseeable future. In exchange for $1.22 billion, RWE is relinquishing the wind power leases.

President Donald Trump, who often talks about his hatred of wind power, has said his goal is to not let any “windmills” be built. The Republican administration has been buying back offshore wind leases from energy companies as it seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels. Offshore wind produces electricity cleanly. Oil, coal and natural gas emit carbon pollution when burned.

RWE announced it is investing $900 million in a liquified natural gas project in Louisiana and spending $300 million on natural gas turbines. The company is developing 15 natural gas peaking projects across the United States.

This latest deal brings the total amount spent on these agreements to roughly $3.9 billion. The administration adopted this strategy after federal courts thwarted Trump’s efforts to stop offshore wind development through executive action.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said Thursday that Americans “deserve an energy system built on common sense, not one dependent on costly subsidies or technologies that can’t meet our country’s current demand.” He said he welcomes RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen the nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power and help keep electricity affordable.

But Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., said the lease buybacks are effectively bribing companies to step away from clean energy that can displace more expensive fossil fuel plants, which in turn will raise costs for consumers.

title: Dwindling Colorado River creates water, power challenges for the western US
description:
A recent study from NASA found that since 2002, Colorado River reservoirs and aquifers have lost a total of 52 cubic kilometers of water.
The shrinking resource has created a conundrum for the seven states that rely on the river: Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming.
In those states, the Colorado River provides water for farming, municipal use, industrial use and human consumption.
Arizona, California and Nevada, collectively known as the Lower Basin states, are subject to cuts of their river water use under a new federal plan.
Colorado River water also powers hydroelectric dams at Lake Mead and Lake Powell, a source of renewable power for the region.
text:
As the Colorado River dwindles, it threatens to reduce the availability of both water and electricity in the western U.S.

Last week, the federal government came up with a plan to manage the river water, but critics on both sides of the aisle warn that deep cuts to water use could be harmful in the states that depend on it.

The river has been in a drought for more than 25 years, and its levels have fallen over time. A recent study from NASA found that since 2002, Colorado River reservoirs and aquifers have lost a total of 52 cubic kilometers of water.

That drought, intensified by climate change, is one factor constraining the water supply. Another is heavy usage, especially for agriculture, including crops such as hay, which are particularly water-intensive.

The shrinking resource has created a conundrum for the seven states that rely on the river: Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming.

In those states, the Colorado River provides water for farming, municipal use, industrial use and human consumption.

Arizona, California and Nevada, collectively known as the Lower Basin states, are subject to cuts of their river water use under a new federal plan.

Arizona is being particularly hard hit.

“The most junior water right in the Lower Basin, where most of the water is used, is the water that supplies the Central Arizona Project Canal, the CAP, the Central Arizona Water Conservation District, that takes water and is a critical supplemental source to Phoenix and Tucson,” said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University, in an interview prior to the announcement last week.

Colorado River water also powers hydroelectric dams at Lake Mead and Lake Powell, a source of renewable power for the region.

Recently, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation projected that Lake Powell could near a level that would threaten power production.

Schmidt said that if water levels in the reservoirs get below a certain threshold, “hydropower gets compromised at both dams.”

Malcolm Woolf, president and CEO of the National Hydropower Association, described the situation as adding “to the power challenges that that region is already facing.”

But he said the impacts of less power generation from the dams are expected to be a handful of electricity price surges, rather than blackouts.

“It definitely is going to have an impact, but it’s probably just a few hours in those hottest summer months,” Woolf said.

Meanwhile, the seven states that rely on the Colorado River have endured lengthy negotiations on how to cut their water use in the years ahead, as interim guidelines from 2007 expire at the end of this year.

When the states were unable to come to a consensus, the Interior Department last week proposed its own plan, which could result in potentially steep cuts for the Lower Basin states.

The department’s proposed cuts of up to 3 million acre-feet per year could be far steeper than the cuts proposed by the states themselves.

However, the 3 million figure is a maximum, and the Trump administration has stressed that it intends for its plan to be flexible, depending on water conditions.

And the department has yet to reveal near-term plans for how significant the cuts will be in 2027 and 2028.

Nevertheless, the potential for significant cuts garnered pushback from impacted states.

Arizona’s Department of Water Resources said in a statement that a cut of 3 million acre-feet per year “would devastate Arizona’s water users and its economy.”

Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs (D) said in a statement that the plan “contains unacceptable options that include the federal government forcing Arizona to take the majority of draconian water cutbacks.”

She said for 2027 and 2028, her administration “will be working around the clock advocating for an approach that protects the stability of the system, distributes water reductions equitably, and ensures water security for all Colorado River water users.”

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) said in a statement that the plan “seeks to impose unrealistic reductions on Nevada and our water users.”

He added that it “could have devastating economic and environmental impacts on Nevada.”

text:
The Tennessee Valley Authority confirms it's in active talks with industry partners to bring new nuclear generation to North Alabama's long-dormant Bellefonte site, though the utility says no final decision has been made.

The statement comes after TVA interim CEO Mike Skaggs told a nuclear industry conference in Knoxville that the federal utility is in "fast-paced" negotiations to build small modular reactors at Bellefonte, according to the Chattanooga Times Free Press. Skaggs said TVA is working with North Carolina-based GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy to build small reactors at Bellefonte, in addition to the Clinch River Nuclear Site in Oak Ridge, Tenn.

In a statement to FOX54, the utility said:

TVA is a nuclear leader and is actively and working with industry partners to evaluate potential locations to bring new nuclear energy to the Tennessee Valley. We are collaborating with manufacturers and others as part of our commitment to safe, reliable, and resilient nuclear technology. These negotiations are progressing quickly and involve some of the most complex energy agreements in our history.

Through this work, TVA aims to position new nuclear facilities within the Valley, support the growth of the U.S. nuclear industry, and help meet emerging energy needs — including those of data centers — while establishing a model for future nuclear development.

TVA's current goal is to preserve the Bellefonte site for future development. Small modular reactors (SMRs) are among the technologies being considered as we evaluate potential generation options, however, it is important to note that no decision has been made.

GE Vernova Hitachi is one partner that TVA is in discussions with to potentially place multiple BWRX-300 units at the Bellefonte site. TVA is a leader in nuclear energy, and we look forward to continuing to work with the Administration to unleash American energy and provide energy security for the nation.

About the Bellefonte site

Bellefonte sits in Hollywood, roughly 45 miles east of Huntsville in Jackson County. TVA halted work on the plant in 1988 after spending 14 years and billions of dollars on the facility. The plant was one of 10 large-scale reactors TVA never finished out of 17 originally planned.

FOX54 first reported on the prospects of the plant in March, though the TVA would not confirm Bellefonte as a site at that time. The Trump administration has negotiated a $40 billion trade deal between Japan and the U.S. involving major Japanese investment in advanced reactors.

Skaggs, a former TVA nuclear executive who came out of retirement to lead the agency, described the ongoing negotiations as among the biggest and most complex energy contracts TVA has worked through, saying the probability of the projects moving forward "is pretty good."

TVA is separately in discussions with Houston-based Entra1 Energy about building small modular reactors near its unfinished nuclear site in Hartsville, Tenn., the Chattanooga Times Free Press reported.

text:
On Thursday, renewable energy company RWE announced that it entered into a $1.22 billion agreement with the Trump administration to relinquish its offshore wind leases. RWE is one of two companies, alongside Vineyard Offshore, that hold wind leases off California’s North Coast through its RWE U.S. Offshore subsidiary.

According to a press release published by RWE Thursday morning, the company’s settlement with the U.S. Department of Interior will “resolve claims against the U.S. government and relinquish its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.”

RELATED: Trump administration pays another offshore wind project to pull out of California

“RWE U.S. Offshore secured these leases from the U.S. government with a long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity in American waters and invested more than $1 billion toward the leases and the development of these projects,” RWE’s release reads. “These leases provided legal rights to develop offshore projects and represented years of planning, investment, and partnership with federal agencies.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future. The settlement resolves RWE U.S. Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds. The company determined that this resolution best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

The news did not come as a shock.

“Today’s news is disappointing but not surprising,” Environmental Protection Information Center Executive Director Tom Wheeler told the Times-Standard via an emailed statement Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration has used its full weight to hamper offshore wind development. Elsewhere, other offshore wind companies have already caved to the pressure. The winners today are the fossil fuel industry and the losers are Humboldt County and the planet. But tomorrow is a new day. The Trump Administration will end. And the promise of offshore wind remains: clean, reliable energy built locally by well-paying blue-collar jobs. The Trump Administration can delay, but it cannot suppress the future.”

RWE’s press release says that the agreement will allow the company to “redeploy its capital to accelerate value-accretive opportunities that deliver reliable and affordable energy.” That “redeployment” is described as including “$900 million to acquire an indirect 16% stake in the Louisiana LNG Project” — a large-scale natural gas development that has been criticized as a major source of greenhouse gas pollution — and other natural gas projects throughout the U.S.

“While RWE’s shareholders get their bag, the rest of us get the finger. We the people are paying for this buyout, and what we get in return is more expensive energy, backwards climate policy and greater harm to our communities,” Assemblymember Chris Rogers told the Times-Standard via email Thursday morning. “The Trump Administration is again using taxpayer dollars to settle personal vendettas and line the pockets of his friends and donors by protecting oil profiteers from the competition of clean, affordable and renewable energy.

‘Every American should be enraged.’

U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-San Rafael), ranking Democratic member of the U.S. House of Representatives’ Committee on Natural Resources, released a statement Thursday morning just before noon, calling the DOI and RWE’s agreement a “fake settlement” and saying that “the deals are deeply corrupt and illegal” and “when the accountability comes, and I promise you accountability is coming, everyone involved in them will answer for it.”

“The most corrupt, lawless administration in American history is once again flouting the law and attempting to use over $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to kill off clean energy projects slated to create thousands of good jobs and lower electricity bills for Californians,” Huffman said. “Trump is strongarming companies into taking these illegal deals and abandoning offshore wind projects that would put huge amounts of cheap electricity on the grid and lower electricity prices. Instead, he is pressuring them to invest not only in dirty fossil fuel projects, but in LNG export facilities that push domestic energy prices even higher at a time when American families are reeling from skyrocketing costs caused by his reckless war of choice in Iran.

“One of the projects illegally canceled in this fake settlement is off the coast of Humboldt County in my district. The benefits of that project were tremendous — revitalizing the economy of a rural community, creating thousands of quality jobs and lowering utility bills for families all across California. Like a mob boss, Trump tightened the screws on RWE and, shamefully, the company capitulated and went along with this sham deal that robs the American people and makes a mockery of RWE’s stated commitments to clean energy. When these illegal, fake settlements are reversed by the courts and/or future congressional action — and they will be — RWE and others who participate in these charades will own every bit of the shame they deserve.”

Huffman said that the total cost to the taxpayers for paying companies to abandon offshore leases already ads up to “the tune of about $4 billion” noting that such settlements have thus far employed funding intended for the payout of federal lawsuits and settlements.

“Trump is using the Judgment Fund as a slush fund to pay for it. This is the same pot of taxpayer money Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche tried to use for his so-called ‘Anti-Weaponization Fund’ to pay off convicted J6 felons,” Huffman said. “Once again, we see this administration’s priorities laid bare: treating a fund that exists to resolve valid claims and liabilities as a massive personal slush fund Trump can use to reward criminals, kill off clean energy projects and do virtually anything else that serves his personal and political interests.”

RELATED: California investigates Trump administration’s deal to end an offshore wind project

Spokesperson Anthony Martinez from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office provided the Times-Standard with the following statement: “The pattern is impossible to ignore. After getting beaten in court again and again, Trump has stopped trying to win on the merits and continues to make backroom deals to kill clean energy projects — a gift to his fossil fuel industry donors at the expense of America’s economic security.

“While China and other global competitors race to dominate the technologies that will power the future, California is building a modern grid, energy independence and an energy future that Trump is too small to understand.”

“This action by the Trump Administration is utter BS,” Sen. Mike McGuire (D-Healdsburg) said in an emailed statement delivered around 1 p.m. “The overall California RWE wind project would have advanced clean, reliable wind energy — enough to power 5 million homes — and created good rural jobs for the North Coast. Seemingly ripped from a script of VEEP, Trump is now forcing RWE’s hand to reinvest in the same fossil fuels which delivered the climate crisis to our door. This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone. Total buffoonery.”

The Interior Department provided a statement from Secretary of the Interior and Chairman of the National Energy Dominance Council Doug Burgum on Thursday afternoon.

“Americans deserve an energy system built on common sense, not one dependent on costly subsidies or technologies that can’t meet our country’s current demand,” said Burgum. “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”

People still smoke indoors at the bar in Atomic City, Idaho, population: 52. The walls are plastered with one-dollar bills and a “Don’t Tread On Me” flag.

“Where were you Monday?” bar and nearby race track owner Vickie O’Haro asks one of her regulars who typically comes in every day.

O’Haro knows her customers’ orders without asking: cold beers or shots called “atomic bombs” — fitting since her regulars mostly work down the road at Idaho National Laboratory, or INL, America’s nuclear energy testing grounds since 1949.

A March Gallup poll shows a majority of Americans still oppose a nuclear energy plant in their area, but that’s not the case here.

“ I live 10 miles away, and I'm fine,” O’Haro said. “I'm not glowing in the dark, you know? There's nothing to be scared of.”

New nuclear power has stalled out for decades, largely due to public opinion.

But, now, the industry is having a moment. President Donald Trump fast-tracked new projects, and now a new generation of small nuclear reactors is poised to come online in the next few years.

Three companies at INL, plus one in central Utah, switched on new types of reactors this summer.

“ I think it's actually pretty cool to be happening in my backyard,” O’Haro said.

Zoom out, and INL is a pretty big backyard. It’s 900 square miles of remote, sagebrush-filled high desert, almost the size of Rhode Island.

And it’s in an unassuming building there that one startup, Deployable Energy, recently took its test reactor “critical.” That means it had a sustained chain reaction for the first time, proving the design works and could someday generate electricity.

Standing in the control room, Lance Maul, chief operating officer at Deployable Energy, described this as a “real moment in history for the nation.”

“This could be a real turning point for the energy future,” said Maul, who has an Australian accent and was sporting a man bun and a scraggly beard, which he referred to as his “criticality beard” — he and other employees swore not to shave until the reactor went critical, but he decided to keep it as a “memento.”

Maul said the goal isn’t your 20th-century reactor: massive, expensive nuclear plants. It’s micro reactors, which could power 1,000 homes versus 1 million.

“It’s something deployable,” Maul said. “It's something that you can put on the back of a truck. It is a fundamentally different proposition.”

Nuclear optimists like Maul see a future where these reactors are mass-produced and power remote communities, military bases and AI data centers. They see them as a solution to meet America’s rising energy demand without emitting carbon.

Trump is also a fan. Last year, the Department of Energy sped up reactor permitting. That means getting rid of hundreds of pages of regulations, without telling the public, NPR reporting has shown.

“I have no confidence in the Department of Energy and its oversight of this at all,” said Edwin Lyman, nuclear power safety director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, a national nonprofit science advocacy group.

He said he worries about reduced standards around radiation, security and environmental contamination.

Plus, the federal commission that oversees commercial nuclear development has lost hundreds of staff, especially safety experts, due to cuts by the Trump administration and resignations, according to reporting from ProPublica. Companies now testing their reactors will seek approval from that commission.

“I don't think cutting corners when you're talking about nuclear safety is a good idea,” Lyman said. “I'm concerned about its impact on the communities around INL.”

But at the bar in Atomic City, where lab workers drink after a long day, O’Haro said she’s not worried.

“It’s safe. If it wasn’t safe, my guys would tell me that we weren’t safe,” she said, before turning up the country music playing in the background.

Despite the majority of Americans opposing new nuclear plants near them, polling also shows growing support for the U.S. “emphasizing” nuclear power more broadly.

text:
DENVER - Today, Governor Polis took Executive Action to strengthen Colorado’s economy, boost investment and infrastructure in the state, and create good-paying jobs by creating a statewide permitting portal and directing certain agencies to streamline permitting to make it easier and faster for important industries to secure permits in Colorado.

“Slow, burdensome, and bureaucratic permitting hurts our economy, slows investment in the state, and reduces opportunity for Coloradans. Colorado is the best state for innovative industries like clean energy, semiconductors, and other advanced manufacturing, and we can create good jobs and attract more businesses in these growing industries to Colorado by making permitting easier, faster, and more convenient. In April, I directed state agencies to speed up permitting, and today we are building on that work to ensure companies interested in Colorado are not deterred by a confusing and slow permitting process,” said Governor Polis.

The Governor’s Executive Action directs state agencies to work together to build a single statewide online platform to streamline permitting for industries important to Colorado’s economy – by starting with a pilot for the semiconductor industry. By December 15, 2026, agencies will provide a joint report on progress on the pilot permitting portal. The goal would be to then expand the pilot to more industries.

Agencies are also directed to make permitting for these industries more efficient by digitizing and streamlining processes, setting goals to track permit processing timelines, and reducing regulatory complexity – all while still protecting the environment and public health. These modernization improvements apply to the Air Pollution Control Division (APCD), Energy and Carbon Management Commission (ECMC), Hazardous Materials and Waste Management Division (HMWMD), and Water Quality Control Division (WQCD). These agencies and divisions oversee a number of different permit categories, with examples including:

Air Quality, including for construction of new facilities and factories for advanced manufacturing and more

Water Quality, also for construction of new facilities and more

Hazardous Waste Management

Geothermal Development and Operations

Ultimately, Colorado strives to be a leader in delivering major projects faster, better, and cheaper while making more efficient use of taxpayer resources and providing exceptional customer service to the residents, businesses, and communities that interact with State government.

title: Buick's Elegant Electra SUV Goes Global As GM Inks 20-Year Deal With China - CarBuzz
description:
Maybe the Electra will return to the US someday, but for now, the nameplate is focused on the China market, where Buicks have been popular with government officials for decades.
John Roth, President of GM China, said the new JV extension sets up SAIC-GM for long-term growth potential, even beyond China.
GM has manufacturing operations in all those regions mentioned, so you can expect SAIC-GM vehicles developed and engineered in China to be built in those plants at some point.
This could allow for affordable vehicles with GM technology built in Mexico to enter the US market.
CarBuzz traded messages with GM's communications team, and the response was unequivocal: There are no plans to bring the Electra E7 to the US, or any other SAIC-GM vehicles.
text:
It's been four years since Buick promised to electrify its entire lineup by 2030, with a new brand identity led by the Electra battery-electric vehicle coming to the North American market by 2024. Clearly, that didn't happen, although the General Motors near-luxury brand did find sales success in the US with its stylish, inexpensive Envista crossover, powered by a three-cylinder internal combustion engine.

In the ensuing four years, GM found itself with more EVs than it could sell in the US, as political winds shifted and the loss of $7,500 federal tax credits hurt EV sales, meaning Buick would not get a modern-day Electra with a plug. Of all the EV names out there, could any top Electra? Meanwhile, the dramatic, all-electric Buick Wildcat (pictured above) remains just a concept.

Maybe the Electra will return to the US someday, but for now, the nameplate is focused on the China market, where Buicks have been popular with government officials for decades. Incidentally, China's last emperor, Pu Yi, purchased a Buick in 1924, and it became the first car to enter the Forbidden City.

GM Strengthens Ties With China As Electra Travels The World

Today, Electra represents a complete line of premium new-energy Buicks offered in China, including the all-electric E4 crossover coupe, E5 midsize crossover, and Encasa premium MPV, as well as the L7 extended-range EV and E7 plug-in hybrid midsize crossover. It's this last vehicle, the E7, that drew attention this week at the end of a GM press release about its SAIC joint venture in China being extended 20 more years.

That's probably a smart move for the General in the world's largest car market, though it's unclear how it might affect the company in the States, where China may as well be a four-letter word these days. GM said the E7 has become Buick's best-seller in that region, delivering more than 10,000 units in its first month this past spring, and that the E7 "also represents SAIC-GM’s growth opportunities beyond China."

As such, starting in October, SAIC-GM will begin exporting the E7 "to select global markets," representing the joint-venture's first premium new-energy vehicle heading overseas. But, as previously mentioned, China and the US don't exactly mix right now.

JV Is Targeting Several Key Markets, Including Mexico

That got us wondering: which overseas markets are targeted, and might the US be in line to get the Electra E7 PHEV? That seems unlikely, given the total potential 45% tariff rate on hybrids and ICE vehicles from China, not to mention the punishing 125% tariff on EVs.

But another paragraph in the GM statement got us thinking the idea isn't so crazy. John Roth, President of GM China, said the new JV extension sets up SAIC-GM for long-term growth potential, even beyond China. “We see meaningful opportunities to compete in select international markets: the Middle East, Africa, South America, Mexico, and Asia-Pacific,” Roth said.

Laying A Foundation For A Future In The US?

GM has manufacturing operations in all those regions mentioned, so you can expect SAIC-GM vehicles developed and engineered in China to be built in those plants at some point. No, the US is not mentioned – but Mexico is. So, perhaps GM and its JV partner are laying the foundation for tooling up capacity in Mexico, in hopes that trade tensions with China ease up. This could allow for affordable vehicles with GM technology built in Mexico to enter the US market. Yes, it sounds highly unlikely now, but not impossible in the future.

CarBuzz traded messages with GM's communications team, and the response was unequivocal: There are no plans to bring the Electra E7 to the US, or any other SAIC-GM vehicles. But the joint venture clearly wants to expand its reach via exports and is now looking at several major regions.

CarBuzz Insight – Why This Matters:

Together, SAIC-GM has delivered 20 million vehicles in China since the JV was formed in 1997, and there were years when those thriving operations were generating income while GM's operations in North America and elsewhere were losing money.

name: Indiana American Energy
title: Op-Ed: Smart, affordable energy built Iowa. Iowa's voters must protect It in November | Opinion
description:
The voters of the 1st District are being asked to ignore the reality of the Democrat Party’s dystopian energy policy.
Mariannette Miller-Meeks supports policies similar to those expressed in the Affordable, Reliable, Clean Energy Security Act (ARC-ES) that will stop this risk to Iowa voters in its tracks.
She led efforts to protect hydraulic fracturing from federal bans, recognizing that affordable energy and national security start with American hands-on American resources.
Bohannan, by contrast, opposed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s push for American energy production.
Iowa built the template for affordable renewable energy before renewable energy was a virtue signal.
text:
Iowa was first.

In 1983, before climate anxiety became injected into the American bloodstream by Washington, D.C. consultants, Iowa passed the nation’s first Renewable Portfolio Standard. It wasn’t driven by ideology — it was pro-agriculture and smart market-hedging behavior. A farming state hedged against energy price volatility the way farmers hedge against weather: practically, locally, without waiting for permission from the federal government.

The result is that Iowa today generates more than 60% of its electricity from wind and still pays roughly 13.5 cents per kilowatt-hour, well below the national average of about 18 cents. When energy policy is written by people who pay energy bills, good things happen.

Christina Bohannan has a different model in mind, and it’s a model invented by people who know a lot more about making lattes in Brooklyn than bringing in the corn in Clinton County.

The Democratic candidate for Iowa’s 1st Congressional District carries the endorsement of the League of Conservation Voters; the same national figures who have spent a decade-plus promising the American public a painless energy transition that was all pain and no transition.

States like Massachusetts, Connecticut, and California have followed the League’s lead most faithfully. The result is that all three states now pay the highest electricity rates in the continental United States. Bohannan’s own platform calls for turning Iowa into an energy basket case under the same progressive orthodoxy that has driven costs skyward elsewhere. The voters of the 1st District are being asked to ignore the reality of the Democrat Party’s dystopian energy policy.

It is worth being clear about what is at stake locally. Iowa’s average residential electricity bill sits around $110–$120 a month, industrial rates hover near 6.5 cents per kilowatt-hour, and agricultural operations — the lifeblood of the 1st District — depend on affordable, reliable power for irrigation, drying, refrigeration, and processing. When electricity prices rise, family farms get squeezed, manufacturers stop expanding, and co-ops pass higher costs straight to America’s grocery stores.

Bohannan and her ilk will likely argue that more renewables are always better, and that Iowa should move from 60% renewables toward 100%. But it’s the 40% from coal and natural gas that keeps electricity from spiking when the wind isn’t blowing, and that’s the rub.

In states like California still smitten with net-zero mandates, regulations are blocking dispatchable carbon generation before sufficient replacement capacity is available; tight supplies can produce wholesale prices as high as $2,000 per megawatt-hour—enough to cause a farm manager to dream of a new career.

Mariannette Miller-Meeks supports policies similar to those expressed in the Affordable, Reliable, Clean Energy Security Act (ARC-ES) that will stop this risk to Iowa voters in its tracks. Bohannan’s donors, on the other hand, have misled and gaslit the country’s electorate for years regarding energy policies. They think that ‘watch the world burn’ policies will advantage them in the end, even in the face of rising utility bills in every state where they have had their way.

Miller-Meeks has a record that mirrors Iowa’s practical success and common sense:

She opposed President Biden’s attacks on American energy like the ban on LNG exports and the slashing of onshore drilling permits.

She stood against Biden’s electric-vehicle mandate that would force Americans to ditch gasoline-powered vehicles.

She led efforts to protect hydraulic fracturing from federal bans, recognizing that affordable energy and national security start with American hands-on American resources.

She sponsored the Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity Act to harden the grid that rural cooperatives and municipal utilities rely on. This is the critical infrastructure that keeps Iowa farms and small towns powered when the wind dies, or the sun sets.

Bohannan, by contrast, opposed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s push for American energy production. She has pledged to “fight” for the same green expansion that her League of Conservation Voters backers define as rejecting fossil fuels entirely. Iowa already leads the nation in wind without that ideology.

Iowa built the template for affordable renewable energy before renewable energy was a virtue signal. The question in the 1st District on Nov. 3rd is not complicated: do you want a representative who protects the energy economy and every citizen affected by it, or someone who will buckle every time a coastal donor knocks on their office door?

Farmers understand hedging because they invented it. They understand that wind works only when it blows and solar works only when the sun shines. When grid purchases are forced regardless of the weather, prices start to skyrocket. ARC-ES codifies the common-sense test Iowa has already passed: Is it affordable? Is it reliable? Is it clean? Those are the only metrics that matter when the dryer is running, the tractor needs diesel, and the plant needs steady power at 3 a.m.

Iowa has not yet been corrupted by 21st-century green cultism. Send a representative back to Washington, D.C., who knows how to win a fight and will always fight for energy abundance instead of energy rationing.

description:
Ford has finally released the closely guarded name of its forthcoming midsized electric pickup truck, and it’s not what anyone thought.
It’s Fathom, as in the new Ford Fathom EV with an MSRP of $28,3501, going mano-a-mano against gasmobiles for the attention of budget-centric drivers.

The Affordable EV With An MSRP Of $28,3501 Interested?
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Wait, the Ford what? Yes, it’s true. Ford has finally released the closely guarded name of its forthcoming midsized electric pickup truck, and it’s not what anyone thought. Some Ford followers have been guessing Ranchero since last year, though Ranger seems a better fit. The answer is, neither. It’s Fathom, as in the new Ford Fathom EV with an MSRP of $28,3501, going mano-a-mano against gasmobiles for the attention of budget-centric drivers.

Finally, The Ford Fathom EV Is Here

Ford has been dropping hints about the new Fathom EV over time, spreading word that it tasked a secretive “skunkworks” team with developing an affordably priced EV from the ground up. The team was housed in California, far away from the humdrum of activity in Detroit. Earlier this year Ford let the secret fully out of the box, disclosing that the team’s first project is a midsized electric pickup truck with an affordable price tag. The company also staged an open house at the California complex to show off the team’s state-of-the-art, EV-centric equipment and systems.

That’s where things stood at the beginning of this summer. The only big mystery was the name of the truck. Now there is still a big mystery, and that is why Ford tapped Fathom over every other possible name under consideration, of which there were hundreds.

Fathom sounds a bit like Phantom, though the reference to early 20th century automotive culture is probably an illusion. In a long form press statement explaining the “naming journey,” Ford notes that the team turned the clock back almost as far as the Model T, trying out Galaxie and Taurus (oh god, not the Taurus) for size along with the Ranchero.

Either way, with the Fathom, Ford aims to scoop up drivers who feel like Ford gets them.

“The blueprint for Ford’s new midsize electric truck — from the engineering to its name — came from one place: a deep understanding of the person who would drive it,” Ford insists, adding, “Their day. Their challenges. Their goals. Even their wallet.”

“Which meant the name had to do more than sound good. It had to capture a mindset, shifting the focus from specs to a spirit of adaptability,” Ford elaborated in a press statement.

“What communicates depth below the surface? How do we communicate an emotional feeling of a vehicle that’s more than it appears to be?” Ford asks in a burst of existential enthusiasm.

What’s In A Name?

Hmmm…Fathom…I’m still not convinced. Maybe it’s that flat “a” in the first syllable, followed by an “um” that strikes a note of uncertainty. Ford followers, what do you think? Is this what you expected?

Nevertheless, Fathom it is. Ford cites the dictionary definition:

fath·om | \ ˈfa-thəm

noun 1: a unit of length equal to six feet, used chiefly in measuring the depth of water 2: archaic the span of a person’s outstretched arms

verb 1: to measure the depth of; to sound 2: to penetrate and come to understand

If you’re wondering why Ford didn’t simply borrow from its F-series, that’s a good question. The company did get off to a good start with its F-150 Lightning full-sized electric pickup, but the decision was made to go off in a new direction.

“But we’ve been committed to doing things differently with this truck from the beginning. It’s in its DNA. And so, we wanted to choose a name — to give the vehicle personality, a soul, and make it a character in our customer’s life,” Ford explains.

Apparently that took some doing. Kind of like growing a new human being inside of you. Coincidentally or not, Ford indicates that it took the team nine months to settle on a name.

The Affordable EV With An MSRP Of $28,3501

Interested? Ford won’t start taking pre-orders until early next year, but starting now you can sign up here for a pre-order invitation. Ford provides more details about the new EV here, and you can presumably get even more particulars by filling out this form.

A quick rundown of the juicy bits:

The MSRP of $28,3501 is a starting price that applies to a “standard-range” battery

Bidirectional charging is included, meaning you can run home appliances and other gear from the EV battery, and potentially participate in your local utility’s demand-response programs

BlueCruise, Apple CarPlay, and Android auto capability come with every Fathom, and BlueCruise is integrated with Apple Maps.

A digital key is part of the package

Of course, the 800-pound elephant in the room is the price of gas at the pump, which has rocketed upwards since February 28, when US President Donald Trump decided to attack Iran, motivating that nation to effectively shut down the key Strait of Hormuz shipping route. The lifetime cost of owning an EV (TCO or Total Cost of Ownership) already compared favorably against gasmobiles before February 28, due to the relatively low cost of electricity and the potential for saving money on maintenance. Now the TCO is better than ever (try this handy cost calculator to see for yourself).

Next Steps For The US EV Market

Now that the Tesla Cybertruck is safely out of the running in the electric pickup truck space, Ford has a chance to pick off some of the leavings. Pickup trucks are hugely popular in the US whether or not one really needs a pickup truck to go about one’s daily business.

With an MSRP below $30,000, the automaker also has an opportunity to help restore EV sales momentum in the US. Interest in EVs fell off a cliff last year after the Republican majority in Congress axed the $7,500 federal EV tax credit last September. However, some bright spots persist, and activity has been stirring in the startup field, particularly in the area of pickups.

Keep an eye on Rivian, which somehow managed to secure a $4.5 billion (that’s billion with a “b”) Energy Department loan to build a new factory in Georgia. The Jeff Bezos-backed venture Slate Auto is also still on track to move its stripped-down pickup into the market.

Another up-and-comer is the Scout Motors affiliate of Volkswagen, though the company offers an extended-range version for its forthcoming vehicles in the form of a gas engine to recharge the battery as needed. As of this writing, the range-extended iteration has attracted more reservations than the 100% battery pickup.

TELO Trucks is also still in there pitching a city-sized pickup, seen just last month pulling a full sized battery-enabled RV from the manufacturer Pebble.

text:
The Columbia Climate School and the Department of Earth and Environmental Engineering (EEE) of the Columbia Engineering School are delighted to announce that Yan Yao has joined our faculty, effective July 1. A leading researcher in electrochemical energy storage, Yao brings a distinguished record of developing next-generation batteries and sustainable energy materials.

“The clean energy transition depends on breakthroughs in safer, more sustainable energy storage,” said Alexis Abramson, dean of the Columbia Climate School. “Professor Yao’s research advances solutions to some of the field’s most pressing challenges, from reducing reliance on critical minerals to developing more circular materials systems. His work reflects the interdisciplinary innovation that drives the Climate School’s mission.”

Yao joins Columbia from the University of Houston, where he was the Hugh Roy and Lillie Cranz Cullen Distinguished Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering and a principal investigator at the Texas Center for Superconductivity. His research group has advanced the science of solid-state batteries, organic and sustainable electrode materials and multivalent (magnesium) battery chemistries, developing safer, lower-cost, and more environmentally responsible energy storage technologies.

At Columbia, Yao’s program will bridge fundamental electrochemistry and real-world energy systems. His work will advance solid-state and other next-generation batteries for grid and transportation applications; develop sustainable electrode materials that reduce dependence on critical minerals; and explore battery life cycle and recycling strategies that help close the materials loop.

“We’re thrilled to have Yan Yao joining our faculty,” said Shih-Fu Chang, dean of Columbia Engineering. “His research in battery storage, particularly alternatives to lithium-ion, and experience launching start-ups will help advance Columbia’s ability to make an impact and build a more sustainable future.”

Yao’s appointment deepens collaboration across Columbia with a joint appointment between the School of Engineering and Applied Science and the Columbia Climate School, and as a member of the Columbia Electrochemical Energy Center. His arrival advances the university’s shared mission to develop innovative solutions at the intersection of energy, sustainability and the environment.
