text:
PREVIOUSLY

SOLD! BOEM Names California North Floating and RWE Offshore Wind Holdings as Provisional Winners of Two Offshore Wind Leases Off the Humboldt Coast

LoCO Interview: Meet the Folks at RWE, One of the Energy Companies Working to Bring Floating Offshore Wind Facilities to Humboldt’s Coast

German Offshore Wind Developer Sells its Humboldt County Lease Back to the Trump Administration, Promises to Develop Natural Gas in the United States Instead

###

The latest offshore wind lease ended due to pressure from the Trump Administration is a site off Humboldt Bay, a deal that has drawn ire from North Coast elected officials.

The Trump administration will pay German energy company RWE $1.22 billion to vacate three leases, off the coasts of Eureka, New York and Louisiana, in a settlement with the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The local lease is one of two sites in federal waters off Humboldt Bay that was auctioned off to energy developers.

The settlement follows a concerted effort by the Trump Administration to halt or stymie offshore wind projects across the country, met with lawsuits from developers.

The administration has bought back leases from several companies, with costs the Associated Press has totaled at over $4 billion.

RWE said the company invested over $1 billion and years of planning across three leases and their respective projects.

“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future,” RWE said in a press release.

“The company determined that this resolution best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

Similar to other energy companies, RWE pointed to investments in natural gas in their press release, something celebrated by officials in the Trump Administration.

“Americans deserve an energy system built on common sense, not one dependent on costly subsidies or technologies that can’t meet our country’s current demand,” DOI Secretary Doug Burgum said in a statement.

“We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future,” he said.

But Democratic elected officials who represent Humboldt County are pissed off by the settlement.

“The most corrupt, lawless administration in American history is once again flouting the law and attempting to use over $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to kill off clean energy projects slated to create thousands of good jobs and lower electricity bills for Californians,” Rep. Jared Huffman said in a statement.

“One of the projects illegally canceled in this fake settlement is off the coast of Humboldt County in my district. The benefits of that project were tremendous — revitalizing the economy of a rural community, creating thousands of quality jobs, and lowering utility bills for families all across California. Like a mob boss, Trump tightened the screws on RWE and, shamefully, the company capitulated and went along with this sham deal that robs the American people and makes a mockery of RWE’s stated commitments to clean energy. When these illegal, fake settlements are reversed by the courts and/or future congressional action — and they will be — RWE and others who participate in these charades will own every bit of the shame they deserve,” he said.

“The deals are deeply corrupt and illegal. When the accountability comes, and I promise you accountability is coming, everyone involved in them will answer for it,” he said.

State representatives involved in supporting the project in Humboldt County, poised to boost California’s renewable energy goals, were similarly unhappy.

“While RWE’s shareholders get their bag, the rest of us get the finger,” said Assemblymember Chris Rogers, in a statement from a spokesperson. “We the people are paying for this buyout, and what we get in return is more expensive energy, backwards climate policy, and greater harm to our communities.”

“The Trump Administration is again using taxpayer dollars to settle personal vendettas and line the pockets of his friends and donors by protecting oil profiteers from the competition of clean, affordable, and renewable energy. Every American should be enraged.”

State Senator Mike McGuire said the action is “utter BS.”

“The overall California RWE wind project would have advanced clean, reliable wind energy—enough to power for 5 million-homes—and created good rural jobs for the North Coast. Seemingly ripped from a script of VEEP, Trump is now forcing RWE’s hand to reinvest in the same fossil fuels which delivered the climate crisis to our door. This is yet another example of how off the rails the Trump Administration has gone. Total buffoonery,” he said in a statement from a spokesperson.

The state of California has goals to reach a 100% zero-carbon electricity grid, with offshore wind representing a key piece in delivering the goal of 25,000 megawatts by 2045.

After the federal government cancelled an over $400 million grant to develop the Humboldt Bay Offshore Wind Heavy Lift Multipurpose Marine Terminal, an essential piece of infrastructure that would be used to assemble and deploy wind turbines, the state has filled the hole with funding of its own.

Humboldt Bay Harbor District Executive Director Chris Mikkelsen told the Outpost the district will continue forward with plans to develop the terminal, a project in the environmental review stage.

“We’re operating under very strong direction under the state of California,” he said.

While it’s too soon to say how exactly the end of one lease will effect the terminal, he remains optimistic. It’s possible the projects can be scaled smaller, he said, or built over time as the appetite grows and communities get more comfortable with the prospect. Maybe the timeline will be stretched out five years.

“One president can’t change the demand for energy that we as Americans have. We know we have to get energy from new sources,” he said.

“The winners today are the fossil fuel industry and the losers are Humboldt County and the planet,” said Tom Wheeler, executive director of Arcata-based Environmental Protection Information Center, in a statement.

“But tomorrow is a new day. The Trump Administration will end. And the promise of offshore wind remains: clean, reliable energy built locally by well-paying blue collar jobs. The Trump Administration can delay but it cannot suppress the future,” he said.

text:
Energy storage developer Syntropic Power is working to commercialize the sodium-ion battery technology of UNIGRID, possibly creating another alternative to lithium-ion in the U.S. stationary battery market.

This joint effort, announced this week, will integrate UNIGRID's sodium chromium oxide (NCO) chemistry into Syntropic's energy storage system hardware. The partnership is targeting 1 GWh of NCO-based energy storage by 2027 through a Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC)-free supply chain, according to a release.

According to research firm Wood Mackenzie’s U.S. Energy Storage Monitor Q2 2026 report, BESS developers with mature pipelines are securing supply agreements with domestic manufacturers. Over the next two to four years, sourcing components free from Foreign Entities of Concern is emerging as a critical market bottleneck.

North Carolina-based Syntropic states it will incorporate both its residential “Tenet” storage system and its “GridSpan” platform designated for large-scale stationary applications. Syntropic will design, manufacture and deploy these battery energy storage systems based on the independently validated cell chemistry of California-based UNIGRID.

The company claims the combination of sodium chromium oxide is distinct from other conventional chemistries utilized by prominent Chinese manufacturers that combine sodium nickel iron manganese oxide (NFM) or sodium iron pyrophosphate.

UNIGRID highlights “ultra-low cost” as a primary benefit of chromium, which is one of the most widely used industrial metals after aluminum. Unlike many critical minerals, chromium is non-toxic for safe handling and not classified as a hazard.

According to UNIGRID, its advantages in BESS development include high power output and narrow voltage curves for system integration. By replacing iron, nickel and manganese with exceptionally abundant trivalent chromium, UNIGRID claims this offers both affordability and system stability, preventing internal decomposition that generates oxygen and heat.

“UNIGRID’s NCO chemistry combines high round-trip efficiency, high power capability, strong cycle life performance and distinctive thermal safety behavior, providing the foundation for a GridSpan platform designed to operate without active cooling,” said Matt Huber, chief technology officer of Syntropic Power, in a statement.

Huber notes that the battery testing trials commissioned by Syntropic in New York at the Rochester Institute of Technology Battery Development Center on UNIGRID’s NCO cells provided the independent data needed to measure the performance metrics for stationary energy storage. Key takeaways included a mere 2.3% capacity loss across varying temperature ranges, alongside "highly beneficial behavior" during charging sessions.

The data reportedly revealed that after 1,000 cycles at full depth of discharge, the batteries sustained over 99% of their original capacity.

“As surging power demand from AI and electrification collides with extreme weather and rising energy costs, the modern grid requires unmatched reliability and thermal resilience,” said UNIGRID CEO Darren H. S. Tan. “Partnering with Syntropic allows us to scale this robust technology to deliver the dependable power infrastructure North America urgently needs.”

name: Clean Energy
title: How Africa can power its trillion-dollar critical minerals revolution - African Business
description:
The pillars are: Advancing Mineral Development; Developing Human and Technological Capabilities; Building Strategic Value Chains, and Promoting Prudent Mineral Stewardship.
Ivorian Minister of Mines, Petroleum, and Energy, Mamadou Sangafowa, at a recent forum organized by the AfCFTA noted that “Africa is ready to make critical minerals a lever for industrial transformation,” adding that the world was entering an era that is built on critical minerals.” Special Adviser to Nigeria’s Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Kehinde Bamigbetan, while commenting on how the continent could position itself as a global leader in critical minerals, pointed out that collaboration was critical.
This, he, however said was already happening with the formation of the Africa Minerals Strategy Group (AMSG).
On investments badly needed to unlock Africa’s critical minerals potential, Bamigbetan said investment in infrastructures was essential.
To realise its potential and power its critical minerals revolution, greater investment is needed in exploration, mining infrastructure, processing facilities, transport networks, and supporting industries across the continent.
text:
The global race for critical minerals is reshaping economies, industries and geopolitical alliances, placing Africa at the centre of one of the most significant economic opportunities of the 21st century.

That is why Africa needs to avoid repeating mistakes of resource extraction without sustainable development, opaque arrangements, and missed opportunities, which it made in the past by focusing on value-adding activities.

Home to vast reserves of lithium, cobalt, graphite, manganese, rare earth elements, and other strategic minerals, the continent possesses the resources needed to power the world’s clean energy transition, advanced manufacturing, and digital economy.

Today, 30% of the world’s critical mineral deposits are estimated to be found in Africa. From the Democratic Republic of Congo, which has cobalt, copper in abundance, to South Africa (platinum, manganese, chrome), Zambia (copper, cobalt), Zimbabwe (lithium), and Guinea (bauxite, iron ore), Africa possesses some of the world’s richest deposits of critical minerals that are invaluable to the global energy transition and industrial revolution.

Yet, despite these critical resources, it continues to capture only a fraction of the value generated from its mineral wealth because of limited investment in exploration, processing, infrastructure, and industrial value chains. This situation perpetuates an extraction model that shifts job creation, industrial capacities, and technological know-how outside the continent.

Fragmentation due to isolated national approaches further weakens Africa’s bargaining power in global mining value chains, reducing its strategic influence when it should be maximised by building regional value chains.

The region’s political commitment to address this situation is reflected in the 2025 Africa Union’s Green Mineral Strategy, which is structured around four pillars designed to realise its vision. Each pillar supports a set of integrated outcomes to achieve resource-based development and regional integration. The pillars are: Advancing Mineral Development; Developing Human and Technological Capabilities; Building Strategic Value Chains, and Promoting Prudent Mineral Stewardship.

These pillars are focused on attracting investment, and creating the enabling infrastructure and policy environment for investments in the sector to thrive, building relevant skills and technological base to leverage green mineral opportunities; leveraging the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to build regional and continental mineral value chains as means of enhancing value addition and promoting regional integration and addressing the environmental, social and governance (ESG) concerns of mineral extraction, emphasising responsible natural resource governance.

But beyond policy declarations, the real challenge lies in translating these ambitions into tangible investments, modern infrastructure, and integrated value chains that keep more of Africa’s mineral wealth on the continent.

Nigeria’s Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Dele Alake, stressed the need for African leaders to prioritise local processing of their mineral resources.

According to him, this is essential to creating jobs, strengthening industries and unlocking greater economic value across the continent.

He also called for Africa to take greater control of how its mineral wealth is assessed by adopting the Pan-African Resource Reporting Code (PARC), which he said would enable the continent to determine the value of its resources using standards developed by Africans.

As Chair of the Africa Mineral Strategy Group, Alake reaffirmed his commitment to working with governments and stakeholders across the continent to ensure Africa’s mineral resources drive sustainable economic growth, create jobs and deliver lasting prosperity for its people.

Ivorian Minister of Mines, Petroleum, and Energy, Mamadou Sangafowa, at a recent forum organized by the AfCFTA noted that “Africa is ready to make critical minerals a lever for industrial transformation,” adding that the world was entering an era that is built on critical minerals.”

Special Adviser to Nigeria’s Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Kehinde Bamigbetan, while commenting on how the continent could position itself as a global leader in critical minerals, pointed out that collaboration was critical. This, he, however said was already happening with the formation of the Africa Minerals Strategy Group (AMSG).

“Today, AMSG has 33 member-countries and has passed resolutions on the policy of value addition. Individual countries are implementing value addition policies by placing bans on the export of raw minerals.

About 13 countries have enacted strict curbs or bans on unprocessed materials like lithium, gold, cobalt, and manganese to force local refining, create domestic jobs. These include Guinea, Malawi, Namibia and Zimbabwe.

“In Nigeria, applicants for mining licences must include plans for local processing. This policy has stimulated over 10 mineral processing projects worth billions of dollars particularly for gold, lithium and rare earth elements,” he added.

On investments badly needed to unlock Africa’s critical minerals potential, Bamigbetan said investment in infrastructures was essential.

“Transportation is key to the mining value chain, so the road, rail and water infrastructures need to be provided. Investment in geological data will improve investor confidence and boost foreign direct investment,” he added.

In his contribution, a Geologist, Salawu Olamide, pointed out that the most important investments needed to revolutionise the sector are in mineral exploration, geological mapping, modern exploration equipment, transport infrastructure (roads, railways, ports), reliable power supply, and mineral processing facilities.

“Africa must also invest in training and upskilling personnel to effectively operate the latest exploration and mining technologies, while strengthening research and innovation. These investments will attract investors, improve operational efficiency, increase local value addition, and create sustainable jobs across the mining value chain,” he added.

Additionally, closing these gaps will require coordinated action by governments, investors, mining companies, technology providers, and development partners – the sort of collaboration that the Africa Business and Investment Summit (ABIS) seeks to catalyse by connecting the key stakeholders needed to transform Africa from a raw materials supplier into a global industrial powerhouse.

Convened by Africa’s most prestigious awarding institution, the Millennium Excellence Foundation, founded in Ghana in 2000, the ABIS is the flagship investment forum of Millennium Excellence Week America 2026.

Scheduled to hold at the MGM National Harbor, Washington DC, over two intensive days, August 27th and 28th 2026, precisely, the Summit is structured to move participants from vision to commitment: from the strategic framing of Africa’s investment landscape, to the bilateral meetings, signed agreements and diaspora investment pathways that turn intention into action.

The ABIS provides a platform to bring together the key stakeholders needed to advance this agenda. By connecting investors, policymakers, mining companies, technology providers, and industry leaders, the summit facilitates partnerships, promotes investment opportunities, and encourages collaboration across the critical minerals value chain. Through these engagements, ABIS supports the development of sustainable investment partnerships that can strengthen Africa’s mining sector and contribute to long-term economic growth.

Unlocking this opportunity requires more than the availability of mineral resources. It depends on collective efforts from governments, investors, mining companies, technology providers, financial institutions, and skilled professionals. By strengthening technical expertise, improving infrastructure, and creating an enabling investment environment, Africa can build competitive mineral value chains that generate long-term economic returns for the continent while supporting global supply needs.

The benefits extend far beyond the mining sector. Increased investment in critical minerals has the potential to create employment, develop local industries, improve infrastructure, attract foreign direct investment, strengthen regional trade, and enhance Africa’s economic position in global markets.

As demand for critical minerals continue to rise, Africa is well positioned to play a leading role in supplying these resources that are essential for industrial development, clean energy technologies, manufacturing, and digital innovation.

To realise its potential and power its critical minerals revolution, greater investment is needed in exploration, mining infrastructure, processing facilities, transport networks, and supporting industries across the continent. Africa must move beyond being a supplier of raw materials and become a key player in mineral processing, value addition, and downstream manufacturing.

The ABIS platform offers governments, investors, development finance institutions, mining companies, technology providers, policymakers, and the African diaspora a unique platform to forge the partnerships that will define the continent’s critical minerals future. Every stakeholder has a role to play in transforming Africa’s vast mineral wealth into industrial growth, quality jobs and shared prosperity. The time to move from dialogue to decisive action is now, and broad participation at ABIS will be instrumental in achieving this.

title: Ford Fathom Will Show Whether Ford's EV Reset Can Build an Entire Generation of Vehicles
description:
The Ford Fathom may become the second kind.
Fathom Is Ford’s Replacement Baseline After an Abandoned EV Generation The historical weight of Fathom begins with what Ford discarded to create it.
Future automotive archaeology may trace several Ford vehicles back to this awkwardly named pickup, just as the present Z still carries evidence of decisions made during Nissan’s previous recovery.
Fathom’s Most Dangerous Competitor Is the Calendar Chinese automakers have changed the acceptable speed of vehicle development.
Armen Hareyan Sees Fathom as a Test of Ford’s Manufacturing Reset Torque News publisher Armen Hareyan sees Fathom as evidence that Ford is changing the economics behind its electric vehicles.
text:
Some vehicles are remembered for what they sold. Others are remembered for what they taught the company that built them.

The Ford Fathom may become the second kind.

Years from now, engineers and automotive historians may look back at this truck as the point where Ford’s first electric strategy ended and a different company began taking shape underneath it. Success would make Fathom the foundation beneath a family of affordable electric vehicles. Failure would preserve it as evidence that Ford understood what was wrong, spent billions rebuilding its development system and still could not move quickly enough.

That gives Fathom a significance far beyond its $28,350 starting price.

Vehicles born during periods of corporate recovery often carry their influence far beyond one model cycle. The Nissan 350Z became the basis for the 370Z and, eventually, today’s Nissan Z. Its architecture survived because the original car restored something Nissan needed and gave later engineers a workable foundation to improve rather than replace. Similar patterns appear throughout automotive history. A company reaches a crisis, concentrates its resources, creates one unusually consequential product, and then spends years uncovering everything that product made possible.

Fathom could occupy that role for Ford.

The truck is the first production vehicle from a clean-sheet electric program created after Ford concluded that its previous approach was structurally uncompetitive. Jim Farley has described internal combustion thinking inside Ford as a barrier to Model E, acknowledged that the company canceled an entire generation of planned electric vehicles, and explained why the replacement team had to be separated from Detroit’s established development culture.

Fathom is therefore the first public artifact of Ford’s attempt to replace the system that produced the Mustang Mach-E and F-150 Lightning.

Fathom may need the truck beside it before the name fully makes sense.

Ford spent nine months narrowing hundreds of possibilities. Two copywriters independently proposed Fathom, engineers were asked for their preferences, and the finalists were tested with focus groups. Inside Ford, the name was presented alongside years of customer research, product planning, engineering decisions, and a complete explanation of what the truck was supposed to represent.

The public received the process in reverse. Ford revealed the name, its symbolism, and its starting price before showing the finished vehicle. That left buyers trying to connect an abstract word to a truck they could not yet see.

I am still unsure whether Fathom immediately communicates the character of a pickup, but Ford has given the name room to acquire meaning through the product. Bronco, Mustang, Ranger, and Maverick became powerful names because vehicles, owners, and years of history filled them with associations. Fathom will have to earn its meaning in the same way.

The name may shape the first reaction. The platform will shape the legacy.

The Reveal Is Only the Middle of a Vehicle’s Development

A vehicle is designed three times.

First comes the private idea inside the studio and engineering organization. Then comes the product the company can manufacture, certify, service, and sell. Finally, the public gives it a reputation that may survive long after the original engineering team has moved on.

The reveal sits in the middle of those processes.

Fathom is already developing its third identity before Ford has finished showing its second. The company has confirmed a standard-range starting price of $28,350, a $1,595 destination charge, seating for five, more passenger space than a Toyota RAV4, a frunk, a bed, bidirectional power, a digital key, a large display and the hardware needed for BlueCruise. Ford has not announced the EPA range, battery capacities, charging curve, payload, towing rating, trim walk, production mix or how many base trucks it intends to build.

That makes $29,945 a consequential promise rather than a complete product.

A base vehicle that exists primarily in advertisements is a marketing artifact. A base vehicle built in meaningful volume, protected from five-figure markups and supported with available replacement parts could reset what American buyers expect from an affordable EV.

Would you place a Fathom order if Ford guaranteed the advertised price in writing, or has the Lightning and Maverick experience made any launch price difficult to trust?

Fathom Is Ford’s Replacement Baseline After an Abandoned EV Generation

The historical weight of Fathom begins with what Ford discarded to create it.

Jim Farley told T. Rowe Price that his internal combustion organization had “such strong prejudice” that Model e could never receive a competitive platform. He said Ford consequently created a separate California team, brought in talent from Tesla and Apple, and gave it a blank sheet of paper.

Farley stopped short of calling that sabotage. The distinction matters because sabotage implies deliberate intent.

His description remains extraordinary. Ford’s profitable legacy organization was being asked to help build a competitor to the products and processes that sustained it. Its supplier relationships, development systems, factory assumptions and engineering habits continued pulling the EV program toward internal combustion architecture.

Ford did more than delay a few vehicles after recognizing the problem. Farley said the company canceled a next-generation electric Lightning and multiple planned SUVs. Ford had become emotionally attached to those products, but its teardowns of Tesla and BYD vehicles showed that the underlying engineering and cost structure could not compete.

Fathom therefore carries a heavier responsibility than replacing the Lightning or confronting Slate. It is the first physical evidence that Ford can apply what it learned after discarding an entire development generation.

The Universal EV Platform is designed around that reset. Ford says the architecture will support a family of affordable vehicles, while its new production system builds the front, rear, and structural battery assembly on three parallel branches before joining them. The company expects comparable range from a battery as much as one-third smaller than those used by competitors.

Ford’s Long Beach team says it can move certain ideas from concept into testing in hours or days rather than weeks or months. That is promising, although rapid experiments inside a development center are different from rapidly releasing durable production vehicles through a global supplier, factory, regulatory and service network.

Fathom is the first production baseline for finding out whether those gains survive contact with the rest of Ford.

The Vehicles That Rebuild Companies Often Shape What Comes Next

When an automaker is forced to rethink its costs, priorities, and identity, one vehicle can carry far more weight than its first-year sales suggest. It can become the engineering baseline that later products refine for years.

The Nissan 350Z is one of the clearest examples. It emerged from Nissan’s late-1990s survival crisis, before the 2008 recession, but followed the same pattern: concentrated resources, a clearer product mission, and an architecture strong enough to support several generations.

The 350Z gave Nissan an attainable performance car, restored some of the company’s emotional credibility, and became the starting point for the 370Z and today’s Nissan Z. Its influence lasted because the original car gave later engineers a workable foundation to improve rather than replace.

Fathom could occupy a similar role for Ford.

Advertising

The 350Z was born from Nissan’s late-1990s survival crisis rather than the recession that began in 2008. Nissan’s official business-plan history identifies the Nissan Revival Plan as its fiscal 2000 and 2001 effort to revive the company. By May 2002, Nissan said it had reduced the number of platforms used at its Japanese plants from 24 to 15 while preparing the Z as part of a new product wave.

The resulting 350Z did more than revive a famous badge. It gave Nissan an attainable performance car, restored some of the company’s emotional credibility and became the starting point for a long engineering genealogy. Nissan sold more than 250,000 examples before replacing it with the 370Z. The present Z still carries elements of the previous model’s chassis, with Nissan concentrating its investment on the areas that would deliver the most noticeable benefits.

Fathom could become Ford’s version of that moment.

A compact electric truck and a rear-drive sports car have little in common as products. Their strategic roles may prove similar. Each arrived after a company discovered that its existing cost structure and development assumptions could no longer sustain the desired product.

The first Fathom does not need to become Ford’s definitive EV. It needs good enough bones for Ford to build a better second vehicle, a cheaper third vehicle and an improved second-generation truck without returning to another blank sheet.

Future automotive archaeology may trace several Ford vehicles back to this awkwardly named pickup, just as the present Z still carries evidence of decisions made during Nissan’s previous recovery.

Fathom’s Most Dangerous Competitor Is the Calendar

Chinese automakers have changed the acceptable speed of vehicle development.

ABI Research says leading Chinese new-energy vehicle companies can operate on software-defined vehicle design cycles as short as 18 months, compared with more than 48 months for many established manufacturers. Reuters has documented how Chinese companies compress development through vertically integrated suppliers, rapid decisions, extensive simulation, concurrent engineering and teams that continue work across time zones.

Ford cannot solve that gap by copying a feature from BYD or buying a Xiaomi for its CEO to study. It needs a development system that can learn, release, measure, and revise before two or three competing Chinese product cycles pass.

This is where vehicle development archaeology becomes useful. A platform has several clocks running at once:

The architecture clock determines how long the hard points, electrical system, and manufacturing assumptions survive. The program clock determines when another body style reaches production. The refresh clock determines how quickly hardware weaknesses are corrected. The software clock determines whether existing vehicles improve after sale. The retail clock controls when buyers can order, receive, and repair them.

Ford’s old system allowed those clocks to drift apart. A vehicle could be technically ready while software lagged, advertised as affordable while available trims became expensive, or sold nationally while local dealers lacked knowledge and parts.

Fathom’s descendants will show whether UEV synchronizes those clocks or merely accelerates the engineering team at the beginning.

The first truck could sell well and still fail as a platform if no affordable descendants follow. It could have a difficult first year and still become historically important if Ford learns quickly and turns the same architecture into better vehicles.

That is why first-year sales alone will provide an incomplete verdict.

Ford Accidentally Conducted Two Public Test on Launch Day

The Fathom discussions divided into two distinct audiences.

The general automotive audience asked: What is this?

Those readers attacked the name, the missing vehicle, and an announcement that sold a lifestyle before showing the machine. Some speculated that Ford wanted to place a $28,350 marker in the market before customers committed to Slate. Ford has not confirmed that motive, so it remains an inference rather than a fact.

The Lightning community asked: Why should we trust you?

Its most visible responses focused on dealer markups, reservation prices that changed before delivery, salespeople who understood less about EVs than their customers, unnecessary service products and frustration that Ford canceled a full-size electric truck many owners still love.

The first can be repaired with a convincing product reveal. The second requires structural changes to ordering, pricing, delivery and service.

Ford previously tried to create a Model e dealer-certification program with charger, infrastructure and training requirements. It ended the program in 2024 after only about half of its U.S. dealers enrolled, opening EV sales to the full network. Farley had also estimated that Ford’s franchise system added roughly $2,000 per vehicle compared with Tesla’s direct-sales model.

Ford cannot erase its franchise contracts and state dealer laws with a software update. Federal competition authorities have argued that state prohibitions on manufacturer-direct sales should be eased, but those restrictions remain deeply embedded across the country.

A workable intermediate model is possible. Ford could establish a binding online order price, publish a list of participating no-markup dealers, protect customer orders from being reassigned, guarantee meaningful base-trim allocation and let local dealers earn money through delivery, accessories and competent service. Regional EV parts and repair centers could support smaller dealers that cannot justify every battery, body and diagnostic capability individually.

The dealer issue should not consume the entire Fathom story. It can still falsify the affordability claim.

A $29,945 truck that routinely reaches customers at $40,000 is a $40,000 truck.

Five Tests Will Show Whether Fathom Actually Succeeded

Price Integrity

Ford should disclose how many standard-range base trucks it plans to produce and later publish the percentage sold within a reasonable margin of MSRP.

The average transaction price matters more than the lowest number on the configurator. So do destination charges, mandatory accessories, activation fees, financing costs and dealer adjustments.

Platform Multiplication

UEV is supposed to support a family rather than one pickup. The strongest evidence of success will be the second and third products, how quickly they arrive and how many expensive components they share.

A platform that requires substantial reinvention for every body style has failed its central purpose, even when engineers continue calling it universal.

Iteration Speed

Ford should make Farley’s public candor measurable through a UEV development ledger.

Advertising

That ledger could report major software releases, production changes, wiring and part-count reductions, charging improvements, warranty trends, and which components carry into the next UEV vehicle. It would give buyers evidence that the architecture is learning rather than waiting for a conventional mid-cycle refresh.

Ford does not need to release proprietary drawings. It can show the rate of improvement.

Repairability and Parts Support

The unicastings and structural battery that lower factory complexity could move costs into the collision-repair and insurance system.

Ford says it developed the castings with its crash, insurance and repair experience in mind. It also says the battery pack will be serviceable, although individual cells cannot be replaced because they serve a structural role.

Those claims need real numbers after launch: average collision-repair time, total-loss frequency, battery repair cost, parts fill rate and how far an owner must travel for qualified service.

Factory simplicity loses some of its value when ordinary damage creates extraordinary repair bills.

Owner Continuity

Ford needs to treat first-generation customers as participants in the platform’s development rather than the cost of reaching the second generation.

That means maintaining software, replacement parts, diagnostic knowledge, and honest communication after the next UEV product arrives. Lightning owners are already warning Ford that a new product announcement does not erase their experience with the previous one.

A platform becomes valuable when its learning compounds. Abandoned owners represent lost learning and lost trust.

Armen Hareyan Sees Fathom as a Test of Ford’s Manufacturing Reset

Torque News publisher Armen Hareyan sees Fathom as evidence that Ford is changing the economics behind its electric vehicles.

Detroit (has) finally stopped trying to win the EV game with bigger batteries. I think this shows that Ford is starting to win the EV game with smarter factories.

His point establishes a tougher measure of success. An attractive launch price can disappear with trim changes, limited production, or retail markups. A manufacturing advantage can spread across an entire vehicle family.

Fathom will become historically important if Ford carries its savings into the vehicles that follow. Faster development, broader platform use, and lower production costs would show that Ford created a repeatable system. That legacy would matter far more than the performance of one truck during its first model year.

Ford’s Quality Story Has Improved, but Fathom Raises a Harder Question

Ford deserves credit for recent progress.

It ranked first among mainstream brands in the 2026 J.D. Power Initial Quality Study, improving to 152 problems per 100 vehicles from 193 one year earlier. Ford attributed the gain to breaking down silos, bringing experienced engineers into early design reviews, involving suppliers sooner and expanding automated software testing.

The same reporting found that Ford still led the industry with 51 recalls at that point in 2026, mostly involving older vehicles. Initial quality also measures the first 90 days. It cannot answer every question about durability, repair cost or parts availability years later.

Fathom will test whether Ford’s new quality system and its new EV architecture reinforce each other.

A shorter wiring harness, fewer fasteners and fewer individual body pieces reduce the number of opportunities for defects. They also concentrate more functions into fewer assemblies. A failure inside a consolidated component may affect more systems or cost more to replace.

The useful question therefore goes beyond whether Fathom launches with fewer defects. Ford needs to show that it fails gracefully, can be diagnosed quickly, and can be repaired without turning every problem into a module, casting, or battery-pack replacement.

Fathom Does Not Need to Change Everything

Ford’s promotional material says, “This changes everything.”

That is too much responsibility for one vehicle, particularly one we have barely seen.

Fathom needs to change one thing first: Ford’s ability to turn a clean-sheet EV into a repeatable product family without letting legacy complexity grow back into the system.

The name may remain awkward. A good product can earn an awkward name over time. A weak product can destroy a brilliant one.

If UEV produces several affordable vehicles, gets materially better with each release and lets Ford respond within the pace set by China, future automotive writers may treat Fathom as the point when Detroit rebuilt its EV foundation.

If the base version becomes impossible to buy, dealer margins erase the factory savings, collision repairs become prohibitive or the architecture remains trapped under one truck, Fathom will mark a different moment.

It will be the point when Ford finally understood the depth of its problem and still could not move quickly enough to escape it.

Lightning, Mach-E and Maverick buyers, what would Ford have to prove before you trusted another launch price or placed a Fathom reservation?

About The Author

Noah Washington is an automotive journalist based in Atlanta, Georgia, covering sports cars, luxury vehicles, and performance culture. His reporting focuses on explaining the engineering, design philosophy, and real-world ownership experience behind modern vehicles.

Noah has been immersed in the automotive world since his early teens, attending industry events and following the enthusiast communities that shape how cars are built and driven today. His work blends industry insight with enthusiastic storytelling, helping readers understand not just what a car is, but why it matters.

Noah is also a member of the Southeast Automotive Media Association (SAMA), a professional organization for automotive journalists and industry media in the Southeast.

His coverage regularly explores sports cars, luxury vehicles, and performance-driven segments of the automotive industry, including the evolving culture surrounding Formula Drift and enthusiast builds.

text:
The Trump administration is paying yet another company more than $1 billion to give up the rights to produce wind off the U.S. coast, the firm announced Thursday.

RWE U.S. Offshore, a subsidiary of German energy company RWE, issued a press release saying it will receive $1.22 billion in settlement funds and give up its rights to build wind farms off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.

The company said it had previously invested more than $1 billion toward its efforts to build wind farms off the U.S. coasts.

Unlike the Biden administration before it, the Trump White House has taken a hostile approach to wind power, especially offshore wind, and has sought to block wind projects, including those previously approved.

As part of this endeavor, it has reached several similar agreements with companies, paying them to give up their leases to build wind offshore, spending billions in total on the effort.

RWE says it will continue to invest in U.S. energy, particularly natural gas. It said it will spend $900 million to take a 16 percent stake in a Louisiana liquefied natural gas project, and it is signing a $300 million deal related to gas turbines.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer criticized the deal as an example of corruption and said it would make electric bills more expensive.

“Everything the Trump administration does can be summed up in four words: CORRUPTION AT YOUR EXPENSE,” the New York Democrat wrote in a post on X.

“Trump is again spending billions of taxpayer money to limit the U.S. energy supply in favor of exporting more energy to countries like China. This will only make your utility bill MORE expensive,” he added.

In response, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum defended the deal and criticized Democrats.

“Wrong on every count, @SenSchumer,” Burgum wrote in his own social media post.

“1. ZERO taxpayer money will be spent. It’s a dollar-for-dollar repurposing of RWE’s own money. 2. The REAL CORRUPTION was you and Joe Biden forcing Americans to bankroll Green New Scam subsidies for expensive, unreliable, weather dependent, foreign sourced energy,” he added. “3. The Trump administration believes in energy ADDITION. Your climate extremist energy ‘transition’ was actually energy SUBTRACTION—which drove up electric bills. 4. Thanks to @POTUS companies are investing in affordable, reliable, secure American energy, increasing production, creating jobs, and lowering costs.”

text:
WASHINGTON — RWE Americas, a subsidiary of the German multinational RWE AG, has agreed to relinquish its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana as part of a settlement of claims against the federal government.

Under the terms of an agreement with the Department of Interior, the government will repay RWE Americas the approximately $1.22 billion it invested in the leases.

In return, the company has agreed to continue to fund a number of fossil fuel-related projects in the U.S., including infrastructure needed to support the liquid natural gas industry in Louisiana, and a pipeline that will serve 15 different LNG projects.

In announcing the settlement, RWE Americas said its offshore leases had provided it with legal rights to develop large-scale wind energy projects and “represented years of planning, investment, and partnership with federal agencies.”

However, it said, “after careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future.”

As a result, it said, it determined that the resolution announced Thursday “best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”

About $900 million of the settlement funds will be used by RWE to acquire an indirect 16% stake in the massive, still-under-construction production and export terminal located in Calcasieu Parish near Lake Charles, Louisiana.

To support the expansion of its growing flexible power generation work in the U.S., RWE Americas has also signed a $300 million turbine reservation agreement securing future generating capacity to meet growing U.S. electricity demand.

A portion of the remaining money will be invested in the aforementioned pipeline development.

“These investments will help deliver affordable, reliable energy solutions while supporting American jobs, enhancing grid reliability, and strengthening energy security,” the company said in a press release.

In addition, RWE Americas has announced plans to invest approximately $19.6 billion in the U.S. over the next six years to grow its generation capacity from approximately 13 GW across 27 states today to 22 GW by 2031.

In 2025, RWE Americas commissioned 2 GW of new power generation capacity in the United States.

RWE said despite abandoning its U.S. wind ambitions, it remains focused on growing its offshore activities globally.

RWE is one of the world’s leading offshore wind developers with 18 offshore wind farms currently in operation, four under construction, and additional projects in development – including 6.9 GW of capacity secured in the United Kingdom’s most recent offshore wind auction.

text:
The Ford Fathom will be Ford Motor Co.'s first vehicle built on its new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform — a midsize truck that'll start at $28,350 plus $1,595 destination and come with a standard-range battery.

It's not a heritage name like Bronco or Maverick from deep in the 123-year-old Dearborn automaker's archives. But perhaps that's the point: Ford is doing something different with this all-electric truck. Executives say it needs to because it's struggled to win mass consumer acceptance of its first-generation EVs, and because Chinese automakers are expanding globally and rapidly with subsidized, low-cost electrified models customers want.

"That owner's motivations," Kay Hart, general manager of Model e, Ford's EV division, said in a blog post about the target buyer of the Fathom, "look a little different from the traditional truck customer's, and defining them guided every decision on the first vehicle built on our Universal EV Platform. Which meant the name had to do more than sound good. It had to capture a mindset, shifting the focus from specs to a spirit of adaptability."

Customers can sign up for Fathom updates, though pre-orders won't open until early next year. First deliveries are expected later in 2027. Timing for a true reveal hasn't been shared, though customers already have spotted camouflaged pre-production models on the roads.

Naming the vehicle was a nine-month process, Hart said. The company evaluated archived names: Galaxie, Taurus and Ranchero. Each, Hart said, came with a specific implication that might not fit with the new electric truck.

Two Ford copywriters separately brought Fathom forward among hundreds of other options. The naming team asked engineers to pick their favorites. One engineer who fit the vehicle's customer profile chose the winner before every meeting.

"Long before it meant depth, fathom described the span of a person's outstretched arms, roughly six feet," Hart said. "Sailors borrowed that span to measure water they couldn't see the bottom of. And eventually the word came to mean something else entirely: to understand a thing completely.

"A name about measuring what you can't see, that grew into a word about understanding," she continued. "For a truck that started with years of trying to understand a specific customer, that was the whole brief in six letters."

Executives have described the five-seater, midsize truck as similar in size to the Maverick, but having more passenger room than the latest Toyota RAV4, the most popular SUV in the United States. Ford has said it will have a 0-60 mph time on the truck to be as fast as the Mustang EcoBoost with more downforce. Like the Tesla Cybertruck, a 48-volt system will replace the traditional 12-volt battery that operates in-vehicle electronics.

Executives have said the pickup will support drivers who need 300 miles of range, similar to the EVs it already has offered but with a third of the battery cells. That, however, is not what the standard-range battery will offer, spokesperson Emma Bergg said. Fathom will have bidirectional power capability that can charge a home without a generator, though the company declined to share for what length of time. The full-size, first-gen electric F-150 Lightning could power a house for up to six days, according to the company.

Every Fathom will be capable of BlueCruise, launching with Ford's Level 2+ hands-free highway driving assistant. The company has said the UEV platform also will support its launch of Level 3 eyes-off-the-road driving in 2028. Plus, a high-resolution touchscreen will have Apple Maps embedded, though consumers still will be able to use Android Auto and Apple CarPlay should they desire. The vehicle will have a digital key.

The truck will be a test for Ford. EV demand has missed expectations as consumers remain wary of their range, cost, speed to charge, and reliability. Mustang Mach-E's U.S. sales are down 50% through July. The elimination of federal tax credits hasn't helped.

But global regulators are pushing for zero-emission vehicle adoption, and Chinese companies are expanding around the world with subsidized, affordable electrified vehicles. Ford CEO Jim Farley has called them an "existential threat."

The UEV is a simplified underpinning developed by Ford's California-based EV hardware and software "skunkworks" team, a group launched in 2022 at a tenth of the size of what Ford typically would hire for this kind of work. The intentional separation of the group was done for the sake of innovation outside of the legacy, bureaucratic system, executives have said.

Ford is investing $2 billion into Louisville Assembly for the UEV and is abandoning the traditional moving assembly line developed by founder Henry Ford in 1913. The new tree-shaped manufacturing design brings together three sub-assemblies and reduces parts by 20%. It will be Ford's most automated assembly plant, and the investment secures 2,200 hourly jobs at Louisville Assembly.

Large, single-piece aluminum unicastings replace dozens of smaller parts so the front and rear of the vehicle can be assembled separately. They then combine with the structural battery, which is assembled independently with seats, consoles and carpeting.

The midsize truck will use batteries from the $3 billion BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall that began pre-production manufacturing earlier this year. It's producing lithium-iron-phosphate batteries, which don't use cobalt or nickel, making them less expensive than traditional EV batteries. They also are less likely to catch fire, though they also are less energy dense. The technology is licensed from China's Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. Ford expects to be the first manufacturer of LFP batteries for automobiles in the United States.

"We wanted to choose a name," Hart said, "to give the vehicle personality, a soul, and make it a character in our customer's life."

text:
RWE will shift investment to gas projects, including Louisiana LNG and US gas power plants

Reuters

German energy company RWE said on Thursday that it had reached a $1.22 billion agreement with the Trump administration to cancel three offshore wind leases in US waters and to direct the funds to LNG and natural gas power plant projects.

The arrangement is the fifth, and largest, the administration has entered into this year as part of its wide-ranging effort to stop development of US offshore wind projects, which US President Donald Trump regards as costly and ugly. His administration has sought to increase domestic fossil fuel production and scrapped policies that support so-called clean energy development.

"Americans deserve an energy system built on common sense, not one dependent on costly subsidies or technologies that can't meet our country’s current demand," Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in a statement welcoming RWE's agreement.

RWE, one of the world's top offshore wind developers, stopped work on its US projects last year due to the administration's efforts to thwart the industry, which included several orders to freeze multibillion-dollar projects under construction.

RWE holds three offshore wind leases in US waters off the coasts of New York, Louisiana and California. Projects associated with the leases had been in very early stages of development and would not have come online until the 2030s.

"After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future," the company said in a statement.

"The company determined that this resolution best serves the interests of its stakeholders and allows it to direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty."

RWE paid $1.1 billion for its lease off the coast of New York at a blockbuster auction held by the Biden administration in 2022. The remaining two leases cost a combined $163 million.

The company said it would spend $900 million to acquire a 16 per cent stake in a Louisiana LNG project. It also signed a $300 million turbine order for its pipeline of 15 natural gas peaker plants across the US.

The company did not disclose the LNG project owner or turbine manufacturer. Australia's Woodside Energy Group is developing a Louisiana LNG terminal.

Not including the RWE agreement, the administration this year has agreed to return about $2.7 billion to offshore wind developers TotalEnergies, Ocean Winds, Invenergy and Duke Energy and cancel nine federal leases. Ocean Winds is a joint venture between Portugal's EDP Renewables and France's ENGIE.

All of those agreements included pledges to direct investments into fossil fuel projects.

A group of 50 US environmental groups in May wrote to RWE CEO Markus Krebber asking him not to cut a similar deal.

Seven states are challenging the TotalEnergies arrangement in court, alleging the administration failed to follow proper administrative processes and misused a government fund reserved for legal settlements even though there was no litigation between the parties.

California has also threatened to sue over the cancellation of an Ocean Winds lease off its coastline.

(Reporting by Nichola Groom; Editing by Mark Porter and Nia Williams)

text:
Companies claiming tax credits for carbon capture technology have been confronting heavy compliance requirements, prolonged waits and uncertainty about being rewarded, according to a new report.

Processing Content

The report, released Thursday by the Government Accountability Office, examined the Carbon Oxide Sequestration Credit, also known as the 45Q credit after that section of the Internal Revenue Code. The tax credit is offered for certain carbon oxides that are captured at emission sources or directly from the air and either stored underground or used to manufacture products. The tax credit dates back to 2008 and has been extended and amended a number of times in various laws, including the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which added new enhancements. More recently, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act created parity in credit values across various uses of captured carbon. As of March 2026, there were 33 carbon capture facilities in the U.S., with more facilities planned. The number of 45Q credit claims more than tripled from 2019 to 2023, according to data from the Internal Revenue Service.

The IRS has taken several actions to administer the 45Q tax credit and avoid potential noncompliance. However, taxpayers using carbon to create products face compliance burdens, delays and uncertainty in claiming the credit, according to the report.

According to stakeholders who talked to the GAO, one problem involves a requirement for pre-approval of a lifecycle analysis combined with the requirement to use direct data through the end of the tax year creates considerable timing challenges that can delay taxpayers from claiming the credit. For example, to claim the credit, a project needs to be in operation and the taxpayer must wait until the end of their tax year, after which the taxpayer will develop the lifecycle analysis report with prior-year production data, submit the LCA report to the Department of Energy and the IRS, and wait for their review and pre-approval.

"The requirement for direct data through the end of the tax year applies regardless of when in the year a facility is placed in service," said the report. "While waiting for pre-approval, taxpayers and their investors must continue to fund years of project development, construction, and operation of their carbon capture and utilization projects. Meanwhile, delays caused by direct data requirements make it difficult to secure investors in developing Carbon Capture Utilization and Sequestration facilities, according to stakeholders we interviewed. The timing of LCA pre-approvals can also prevent taxpayers from benefitting from another 45Q feature, transferability, through which they transfer all or a portion of their credit to an unrelated taxpayer. Transfer elections cannot be made for the first time on an amended return.However, because of the pre-approval timing challenges, many businesses cannot claim the 45Q credit on their originally filed tax return, especially if their initial LCA submission was not approved; instead, they need to submit an amended return."

The GAO identified other areas in the approval process for carbon utilization where the IRS and the Department of Energy may be able to minimize the compliance burden and improve certainty for taxpayers.

"Pursuing such opportunities — for example, streamlining certain processes, or clarifying acceptable datasets that can be used to calculate carbon displaced — could improve the process and help minimize delays for both agencies and taxpayers," said the report. "Multiple potential goals, the lack of a designated agency to evaluate the effectiveness of the credit, and data limitations complicate Congress's ability to understand the performance of the 45Q credit. Even so, periodic reviews of tax expenditures are crucial for informed oversight."

The GAO pointed out it has previously recommended various actions Congress and agencies could take to improve oversight for other tax expenditures, such as identifying what should be analyzed and by whom. In the report, the GAO identified several questions for Congress to consider directing agencies to analyze to help determine the performance of the credit. The key questions are: (1) how well the credit is working to achieve its goals, (2) how efficiently the credit is performing and (3) how the credit compares to other policy tools.

The GAO also made four recommendations to the IRS and two recommendations to the Department of Energy to improve the review process for carbon utilization, by reducing taxpayers' burden while still mitigating potential noncompliance. These include determining a time period of carbon capture data needed to begin claiming the credit, and clarifying datasets acceptable for calculating carbon displaced. The IRS partially agreed with one recommendation; but the IRS and DOE disagreed with the other five. The GAO maintained its recommendations are nevertheless warranted.

"Congress has revised the statute on several recent occasions," wrote IRS CEO Frank Bisignano in response to the report. "Each time, the IRS solicited feedback from taxpayers and other stakeholders and thoughtfully considered their comments when publishing guidance to help taxpayers understand how to meet the requirements to claim the 45Q credit."

Most recently, he noted, the Treasury and the IRS provided a safe harbor for alternative compliance methods to mitigate the effects of anticipated changes in the Environmental Protection Agency's Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program in response to taxpayer concerns that they might potentially lose access to the tax credit because regulations were still tied to the EPA's current reporting regime.

text:
Customer Assistance: 800-292-9555

The MPSC is seeking comment on a straw proposal on that would refine the focus areas of the MPSC’s performance incentive initiative (Case No. U-21400) centered on ways to improve utility reliability performance, customer outcomes, and safety.

The Commission today released a straw proposal to facilitate discussion on the second phase of its performance incentive initiative, which is exploring challenges to utility readiness to accommodate and leverage growth of distributed generation (DG), electric vehicles, and other cost-effective distributed energy resources (DERs).

The Commission’s March 2025 order Commission identified potential focus areas for feedback and consideration for future application of financial incentives and disincentives, including DER interconnection; customer data access and hosting capacity; DER aggregation and non-wires alternatives; 4.8 kilovolt distribution system conversions; and advanced metering infrastructure utilization and grid modernization.

Today’s order reviews initial comments and replies and seeks feedback on refined metrics, scorecards and performance incentive mechanisms, and next steps for this proceeding. Among the updates, the recommendations include more efficient use of the distribution grid, maximizing existing investments and supporting cost-effective additions of aggregated DERs or virtual power plants (VPPs), which aggregate DERs such as rooftop solar, batteries, managed EV charging and smart thermostats to reduce peak grid demand. These efforts can defer or avoid the need for costly new electricity generation and reduce upward pressure on customer utility rates.

This is the second phase of the Commission’s performance incentive initiative, called Reliability-Plus. In the first phase, the Commission in 2025 approved penalties and incentives for utilities, establishing a mechanism through which DTE Electric Co. and Consumers Energy Co, the state’s two largest electric utilities, could qualify for up to $10 million in incentives or penalties for meeting or failing to meet reliability benchmarks. To earn any incentive, the company must meet or exceed all existing Service Quality and Reliability Standards.

Initial comments are due by 5 p.m. Oct. 1, 2026, and may be filed using the MPSC’s E-Dockets, mailed to Executive Secretary, Michigan Public Service Commission, P.O. Box 30221, Lansing, MI 48909, or emailed to mpscedockets@michigan.gov. Reply comments must be filed by 5 p.m. Nov. 5. Comments should reference Case No. U-21400.

Organizations that have participated in the Reliability-Plus proceeding include the Association of Businesses Advocating Tariff Equity; the City of Ann Arbor; Consumers Energy; DTE Electric; the Ecology Center; the Environmental Law & Policy Center; Union of Concerned Scientists; Vote Solar; Michigan Electric and Gas Association; Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council; and Advanced Energy United.

COMMISSION ADDRESSES ISSUES RAISED IN IMPLEMENTATION OF PUBLIC ACT 235 OF 2023

The Commission today released several decisions related to implementation of Public Act 235 of 2023, one of the pieces of the state’s revamped energy laws (Case No. U-21568). The Commission granted a request by Energy Michigan, which represents independent energy producers, for a declaratory ruling that confidential or commercially sensitive information energy providers file in renewable energy dockets is entitled to protection; revised filing requirements related to this matter also were approved. The Commission also responded to requests for declaratory rulings sought by Energy Michigan and Billerud Americas Corp. regarding the interpretation of Sections 28 and 29 of Act 235 by initiating a comment period in Case No. U-21568 so that all interested parties may provide feedback to issues related to renewable energy credits and behind-the-meter generation resources raised by Energy Michigan and Billerud. Individuals or organizations interested in commenting on those issues may do so by 5 p.m. Aug. 27, 2026

MPSC FINDS PROPOSED RATE CASE PROCESS CHANGES LESS EFFICIENT, DECLINES TO ADOPT

The MPSC today opted not to further explore a major change to utility rate case filings, deciding that a draft proposal to create separate stand-alone proceedings on the issues of revenue requirements, cost of service and rate design would not lead to reduced workload for parties involved in cases nor reduce the volume and complexity of rate cases (Case No. U-21637). The Commission had directed MPSC Staff to create a draft proposal exploring the concept of adopting the separate proceedings as a way to address improving the rate case process as rate cases have grown in size and complexity since Michigan’s 2016 energy laws were implemented, reducing the amount of time the MPSC has to review and issue final orders in rate cases to 10 months from 12 months. Public Act 231 of 2023 directed the Commission to investigate opportunities for improving the rate case process. The Commission said it was persuaded by a consensus among commenters in the review of the proposal that separate proceedings would lead to additional filings, create additional expenses, increase inefficiency, pose new burdens for smaller utilities and lead to confusion among customers. While the Commission had previously approved changes to rate case processes relating to consideration of contested rate case settlement agreements, improvements to how demand resources were considered in rate case proceedings and how potential bill impacts should be communicated to customers, today’s order maintains current processes and keeps rate design and cost of service issues as part of rate case proceedings and closes the docket in this matter.

COMMISSION APPROVES UPDATED RULES GOVERNING TELECOMMUNICATIONS PROVIDERS THAT CEASE SERVICE

The MPSC approved updated rules that govern responsibilities for providers of basic local exchange phone service that cease to provide the service (Case No. U-21958). The update mainly repromulgates existing rules that would, under law, have automatically ceased to have effect in March 2027. The updates also simplify existing rules to ensure the Commission and affected customers receive sufficient notice that a provider intends to discontinue service and that the provider meets requirements for discontinuing service. The MPSC in June sought public input on the amended rules, which will be submitted to the Legislative Service Bureau and the Michigan Office of Administrative Hearings for their formal approvals, after which they will be submitted to the Joint Committee on Administrative Rules.

MPSC APPROVES SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT ALLOWING DTE ELECTRIC TO REDUCE COSTS VIA LOWER-COST DEBT FOR SEVERAL MAJOR EXPENSES, SAVING CUSTOMERS $62.5M

The Commission approved a settlement agreement on DTE Electric Co.’s application for a finance order approving securitization of $600.5 million in costs, a move that allows the utility to reduce costs by replacing relatively high-cost debt and equity with lower cost debt (Case No. U-22109). The approval of the settlement agreement reached between the utility and MPSC Staff allows DTE Electric to issue securitization bonds to recover costs including those associated with retirement of coal-handling facilities at the utility’s Belle River plant in St. Clair County transitioning from coal to natural gas ($236.7 million); the related wind-down of the utility’s Midwest Energy Resources Co. subsidiary that shipped coal to the utility ($16 million); and the remainder of DTE Electric’s regulatory asset for a surge in its tree trimming efforts between 2019 and 2025 ($340.2 million). By using securitization to recover these costs, DTE Electric’s customers are projected to save $62.5 million in financing costs.

COMMISSION APPROVES STEAM SALES AGREEMENT BETWEEN DETROIT THERMAL AND DETROIT’S HUNTINGTON PLACE CONVENTION CENTER

The MPSC approved an energy sales agreement between Detroit Thermal LLC and the operators of the Huntington Place convention center in downtown Detroit (Case No. U-22133). The sales agreement between Detroit Thermal and the Detroit Regional Convention Facility Authority to provide steam to the facility formerly known as Cobo Center is through September 14, 2039, with automatic renewal for consecutive 5-year terms unless either party gives notice that it will not renew. Approval of this special contract will not impact rates or costs of service to other customers of Detroit Thermal, which provides steam used for space hearing, hot water heating, absorption chilling and other uses to more than 100 buildings in greater downtown Detroit.

MPSC OKS ACCOUNTING AUTHORITY TO CONSUMERS ENERGY TO DEFER COSTS FROM MARCH 2026 STORMS

The Commission approved an application from Consumers Energy requesting accounting authority to defer significant costs from a series of high-impact storms in mid-March. The storms caused more than 6,700 downed wires and other damage, including the need to replace 515 poles and 1,330 crossarms, costing an estimated $57 million in operations and maintenance costs across lower Michigan (Case No. U-22135). The storms pushed Consumers’ total expense for service restoration from January to April to $111 million, while the utility’s total amount approved for 2026 is $154 million. The Commission’s approval is for accounting treatment only, noting that Consumers must still meet all evidentiary burdens of reasonableness and prudence before the utility can recover restoration costs through rates in a future proceeding. In that regard, the Commission directed Consumers to provide comprehensive storm data and thorough analysis of the storms in its next rate case, as well as demonstrate how its restoration efforts were completed in a cost-effective manner with optimal customer restoration.

COMMISSION APPROVES TEMPORARY AMENDED SERVICE CONNECTION FEES FOR CONSUMERS ENERGY CO. ELECTRIC CUSTOMERS

The MPSC approved temporary revisions sought by Consumers Energy Co. to its electric customer charges for service connection fees (Case No. U-22136). The Commission in March 2026 approved Consumers’ request, in the utility’s previous electric rate case, to update service connection fees to flat fees for both residential and general service customers to reflect inflationary costs since the fees were last updated in 1993. The Commission directed the utility to create a fee structure that covers fixed costs and reflects variable costs in its next general rate case. Reacting to concern from the Home Builders Association of Michigan, Consumers later sought to revise the residential fee to $9.93 per foot and the general service fee to $16.88 per foot, incorporating variability in the interim until the Commission reviews service connection fees in the utility’s pending general rate case, Case No. U-22070.

The following winners from INL were announced Aug. 6 and will be recognized in November at a banquet in Scottsdale, Arizona:

AHA (principal investigator: Timothy Klett)

The All Hazards Analysis (AHA) tool employs machine learning and natural language processing to help analysts identify infrastructure interdependencies. By modeling how failures can propagate, it helps utilities and public entities plan for emergencies and mitigate their effects on essential services such as power, water and healthcare during crisis situations.

ViBRANT (principal investigators: Anthony Crawford)

Visual Benign Reactor as Analog for Nuclear Testing (ViBRANT) is a surrogate nuclear reactor that replaces neutrons with photons to accelerate advanced reactor development. ViBRANT uses an LED-driven core, photodiodes, thermocouples and high-performance software interfaces to help mature advanced reactor instrumentation and control systems, validate models, and facilitate system integration prior to deployment in real-world reactor prototypes.

TMAP8 (principal investigator: Pierre-Clément Simon)

Tritium Migration Analysis Program, Version 8 (TMAP8) tackles fusion energy’s biggest hidden challenge: tritium management. It is the first open-source tritium modeling platform to meet the Nuclear Quality Assurance Level 1 industry standard. The tool combines regulatory rigor; multiscale, multiphysics simulation; and broad industry accessibility and applicability to accelerate safe, commercially viable fusion power.

TELEIOS-BATT (principal investigator: Kevin Gering)

TELEIOS-BATT is an advanced suite of physics-based diagnostic and prognostic tools for batteries. It offers fast, accurate and efficient monitoring, simulation and prediction of battery health and aging, helping maximize safety, reliability and cost efficiency for modern battery-dependent industries.

REFLEX (INL contributors: Samuel Koomson, Wanhua Wang, Zeyu Zhao, Dong Ding)

Developed by the University of Pittsburgh, Idaho National Laboratory, and National Energy Technology Laboratory—Real-time Embedded Feedback and Layered Excitation (REFLEX) transforms passive electrochemical interconnects into intelligent, sensor-enabled components that provide real-time monitoring, active thermal control and digital-twin capabilities for next-generation fuel cells, electrolyzers and hydrogen energy systems.

INL also had one technology announced as a finalist:

FARM (INL contributors: Paul Talbot, Aaron Epiney)

Developed by Argonne National Laboratory and Idaho National Laboratory—Feasible Actuator Range Modifier (FARM) is a tool that helps power plants make better decisions about how to generate energy, ensuring they operate efficiently and avoid unnecessary wear and tear.
