title: In a first, Utah got more power from solar than any other source | Grist
description:
Solar also supports nearly 8,000 jobs in Utah, according to the latest information from the Solar Energy Industries Association.
The state is home to 132 solar companies, including 54 solar developers and 23 solar manufacturers.
The rise of solar power has helped the state wean itself off a dependence on coal.
Turns out, another renewable energy source has seen a surge in generation in the region — wind power.
Most of PacifiCorp’s wind generation comes from facilities in Wyoming, according to Jona Whitesides, a spokesperson with Rocky Mountain Power.
text:
Utah’s solar generation eclipsed all other electricity sources for the first time ever in May, the culmination of a slow but steady years-long shift away from coal. Energy experts are calling it a win for the environment and the state’s economy.

Photovoltaic panels in Utah produced nearly 1 terawatt hour in May 2026. That represented nearly a third of all electricity generated in the state that month, according to data from Ember, a global energy think tank. Natural gas generated 32 percent, coal generated 28 percent, and wind 2 percent.

“The trend of more and more solar in Utah is wonderful news for air quality, it’s wonderful news for the climate, and it’s wonderful news for jobs and the economy,” said Dan Schroeder, a physics professor at Weber State University who regularly checks energy data.

Schroeder attributes the trend to several large solar farms coming online in recent years. The 2,500-acre Green River Energy Center in the central part of the state became operational this spring, and includes 400 megawatts of solar generation and 400 megawatts of battery storage. Excelsior Energy Capital’s Faraday Solar project in Utah County, the state’s second-largest county, started providing up to 685 megawatts for the Meta data center there last fall. The Elektron Solar Project, an 80-megawatt photovoltaic farm, began sending electricity to Salt Lake City, Park City, and Summit County in June 2024.

Solar also supports nearly 8,000 jobs in Utah, according to the latest information from the Solar Energy Industries Association. The state is home to 132 solar companies, including 54 solar developers and 23 solar manufacturers. Investors committed $1.5 billion to Utah’s solar market in 2025 alone.

Oil and gas extraction, by comparison, accounted for 1,291 jobs in the state in 2025, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Coal mining accounted for 1,059 in 2023, the most recent year the bureau has data for that industry. Utah had another 1,905 jobs in coal and petroleum product manufacturing last year.

The rise of solar power has helped the state wean itself off a dependence on coal. In 2017, coal generated between 64 percent and 78 percent of electricity in Utah, depending on the month. By 2023, it started accounting for less than half of the state’s power sources in certain times of the year. This spring, it was less than a third.

Electricity generation is complicated, however, and solar won’t represent a third of Utah’s portfolio every month. But with its sunny, dry climate, “Utah still has room to grow its solar percentage,” Schroeder said.

He pointed to California, which saw nearly 51 percent of its electricity generation come from solar panels in May, the most recent month that Ember has data — showing Utah has much more room to grow.

“We’re going to see milestones like this increasingly happen,” said Logan Mitchell, a climate scientist and energy analyst with Utah Clean Energy.

About 51 percent of the new utility-scale electricity generation added to the country’s grid is expected to come from solar this year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The country is likely to add another 43.4 gigawatts of solar, 24.3 gigawatts of battery storage, and 11.8 gigawatts of new wind power in 2026, compared to just 6.3 gigawatts of natural gas generation and zero new coal capacity.

Some of Utah’s electricity gets exported to other states, and some of its solar farms serve a single customer, like the project in Utah County that has a contract with Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook.

Mitchell pulled the numbers from the state’s largest electricity provider, PacifiCorp, which is the parent company of Rocky Mountain Power. Turns out, another renewable energy source has seen a surge in generation in the region — wind power.

Wind blew past all other energy sources in PacifiCorp’s portfolio for Utah, Wyoming, and Idaho in December and January for the first time, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

“Wind plus solar is on a tear right now,” Mitchell said. “We may have achieved liftoff.”

And the two power sources complement each other, Mitchell said, since wind generation is highest in the winter months, and solar produces the most electricity in the summer.

Most of PacifiCorp’s wind generation comes from facilities in Wyoming, according to Jona Whitesides, a spokesperson with Rocky Mountain Power. He said the recent sweep in wind power likely comes from the company’s investment in new turbines, including 400 megawatts added to the grid last fall at PacifiCorp’s Rock Creek II facility.

“A lot of days we are using more wind,” Whitesides said. “There are no fuel costs there; it’s essentially free.”

The Trump administration is phasing out tax incentives for wind and solar projects, however, calling them “expensive and unreliable.” But renewables combined with battery storage increasingly produce some of the cheapest, cleanest, and most consistent energy sources in the country, Mitchell said, and are not subject to the price spikes and uncertainty brought by global politics. What’s more, burning fossil fuels like coal and natural gas, which is mostly composed of methane, creates pollution and contributes to a warming planet.

Mitchell said he keeps a running list of the ways a warming West is hurting Utahns at home. A record-hot spring followed by a cold snap caused fruit farmers to lose their crops, for example. Utah also saw virtually zero snowpack over the winter, setting the stage for an explosively bad wildfire season and uncertainty about the state’s future water supply. Emergency room visits from tick bites are also on the rise in the West, Axios reports, as milder winters and earlier onset of warm temperatures help the insects thrive.

“In order to reduce those impacts in the future, we need to be reducing our emissions,” Mitchell said. “And we need to be doing it faster.”

Still, the shift in priorities at the federal level caused PacifiCorp to abandon plans to build more wind and solar projects in the next two decades, according to its latest Integrated Resource Plan update. The pivot has earned the utility criticism from renewable advocates like Utah Clean Energy.

Whitesides called the plan a “snapshot in time” that is constantly revised depending on energy costs, along with federal and state policies.

“It didn’t make financial sense to move forward with new renewable resources at this given time,” Whitesides said. “In two years, we could have a different administration. It may bring back more renewables.”

text:
The Sedgwick County Commission denied applications for two massive solar farms just outside Wichita on Wednesday.

The decision came after a nearly 11-hour commission meeting on the Galena Solar Project and the Branch Line Solar Project, two proposed solar farms applying for conditional use permits to develop near Clearwater.

Wednesday’s marathon hearings came amid a six-month moratorium on conditional use permits for solar farms put in place in June and a one-year moratorium on battery energy storage systems issued by the Sedgwick County Commission in March. The developers filed their applications before the moratoriums took effect.

Sedgwick County Commission Chairman Jeff Blubaugh, whose district includes the proposed solar farm sites, moved to deny the permits for several reasons, including that “the character of the neighborhood is not consistent with proposed uses, the zoning uses and nearby properties are not consistent with the proposed use and, lastly, there is significant neighborhood opposition to this application.”

The denials won 4-1 on separate votes, with Commissioner Ryan Baty casting the lone vote in support of keeping the projects moving forward.

“In defense of our farmers and property rights for our landowners, I will be voting no,” Baty said. “Those farmers are hurting, and they have economic opportunity on their land, and I am not going to tell them no. I’m not looking our farmers in the face and telling them that the only thing they can do on their land is farm. I’m not doing it.”

The projects’ permits would have come with more than 40 conditions to regulate development, construction, operation and decommissioning — from setbacks from waterways, to weed control, to limits on capacity and acreage, to an expedited timeline, along with a financial assurance that the developer would cover the cost of decommissioning the solar farm and restoring the site to its original condition.

The developers may apply again in a year or as soon as six months from Wednesday if they make substantial changes to their proposed projects.

The two projects sought to convert a combined nearly 3,000 acres of farmland near Wichita to solar farms and battery energy storage systems that tie into the Evergy transmission grid. Cropland would be converted to solar panel arrays capable of capturing sunlight and converting it to usable energy that’s fed into the power grid.

It’s not clear how the solar farms would affect local property tax revenues, county officials said.

Both projects would be eligible for the state’s 10-year property tax exemptions for renewable-energy-generating properties after completion, although the change in land type from agricultural to commercial could result in additional property taxes collected in the area. Any commercial or industrial machinery and equipment build or installed on site would be exempt from property taxes under a law signed by former Gov. Kathleen Sebelius in 2006.

Brent Shelton, chief financial officer for Sedgwick County, said the county could come to some agreement with the developers at a later date on payment in lieu of taxes through issuance of industrial revenue bonds.

Galena Solar Project by Mission Clean Energy

Mission Clean Energy, the developer for the Galena project, is backed by two primary investors: Wafra, owned by the Public Institution of Social Security of Kuwait, and Orsted, majority-owned by the Danish government.

The Galena Solar Project — a 260-megawatt solar energy project on approximately 1,490 acres west from Ridge to 119th and south of 47th to 71st zoned rural residential, single-family residential and limited commercial — received preliminary approval in June from the Metropolitan Area Planning Commission.

It would be bigger than the largest existing solar farm in the state located near Medicine Lodge but smaller than planned developments in Finney, Coffey and Johnson counties.

Sixty members of the public spoke on the Galena permit application, including nearby residents opposing the project and local union electricians who are backing it.

Concerns included potential negative impacts on nearby property values, energy rates, drainage, dust during construction, soil and groundwater contamination, fire protection and changing the character of the property from “living in the country” to a more industrial feel.

“We’re not opposed to solar,” Stan Evans, who lives in nearby Clearwater, said. “But we are opposed to these solar farms taking out (3,000) acres of productive farmland. There seem to be better places to put it.”

Proponents said the development would provide hundreds of temporary construction jobs, future renewable energy and the potential for increased revenue for landowners who now farm the area.

“We need to diversify our energy portfolio if we are going to meet the demands of an ever-changing technological world and build an energy infrastructure that is ready for what’s going to come next,” Jordan Nolan, president of International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 271, said. “It’s an investment in the people who live here; this project will create opportunities for people to learn a real trade, build a career and make a good living.”

Branch Line Solar Project by TED Renewables

The Sedgwick County Commission spent another three hours Wednesday hearing public comment and debating the future of another solar farm project near Clearwater.

The arguments for and against the Branch Line project were largely the same — with applicants saying farmers need the money offered through lucrative lease agreements and Kansas needs the energy.

Several residents who live nearby said a solar farm would be an inappropriate use of the land, essentially boxing in Clearwater’s future growth and potentially lowering property values on their homes.

Ted Renewables, a wholly owned subsidiary of Tyr Energy developing the Branch Line project, is the North American clean energy division of Japanese conglomerate Itochu Corporation.

The Branch Line Solar Project — a 130-megawatt solar energy project on 1,359.6 acres west of Maize Road to 151st and south of 71st to 87th — received preliminary approval from the MAPC on June 25.

The Clearwater City Council voted to oppose the project in June. In July, Ted Renewables offered Clearwater $3.5 million to be used to fund fire protection for the nearby small town after the County Commission terminated the county’s mutual and automatic fire aid agreements with Clearwater and four other small towns surrounding Wichita. Clearwater heard the proposal but did not approve the agreement, given that the county had not yet approved the permit.

title: UK: Great British Energy announces investment in British innovator Naked Energy
description:
Great British Energy makes its first major solar-thermal investment, backing British innovator Naked Energy to scale UK manufacturing and boost energy security.
'At Great British Energy we are backing UK innovators like Naked Energy and helping to create skilled jobs.
'Great British Energy is supporting well-paid manufacturing jobs for communities, while providing cheaper and secure energy for households and businesses.'
It shows how public and private capital can work together to strengthen UK energy security and grow a domestic renewable energy industry.'
Background Great British Energy is a publicly owned renewable energy company, 100% owned by the British people.
text:
Great British Energy makes its first major solar-thermal investment, backing British innovator Naked Energy to scale UK manufacturing and boost energy security.

The £8.875 million investment, led by Great British Energy and made alongside Barclays Climate Ventures, will fund a new UK manufacturing facility, creating up to 140 jobs and new export opportunities

The British-designed renewable heat technology is already cutting gas bills at iconic UK institutions and will now be manufactured on British soil

Great British Energy and Barclays Climate Ventures have today announced a combined £8.875 million investment in Naked Energy, a British renewable-heat technology company whose solar-thermal systems are already cutting bills and reducing the use of gas at some of the UK's most iconic institutions, including the British Library and the All England Lawn Tennis Club, Wimbledon.

The funding round is led by Great British Energy, which is investing £7.5 million through its Energy Engineered in the UK programme, with Barclays Climate Ventures participating as an existing shareholder. The combined investment will support Naked Energy's plans to establish a new UK-based manufacturing facility for its Virtu solar-thermal technology, creating up to 40 direct skilled jobs and around 100 indirect roles.

In buildings across Britain, gas is still widely used for hot water, space heating and process heat. Cutting that reliance is one of the most important and challenging steps to reducing energy bills and strengthening the UK’s energy security. Naked Energy’s technology generates renewable heat directly at the point of use – reducing gas demand without adding pressure to the electricity grid and helping businesses keep their energy bills stable when gas prices spike.

Dan McGrail, CEO of Great British Energy, said: 'Cutting our reliance on gas is one of the biggest challenges we face, both for energy security and for keeping bills down. Naked Energy has developed a technology that tackles this head on and when you see it working at iconic UK institutions like the British Library and Wimbledon, you understand what is possible.

'At Great British Energy we are backing UK innovators like Naked Energy and helping to create skilled jobs. Through our Energy Engineered in the UK programme we are helping them to manufacture here at home and go further, faster.'

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: 'Homegrown, clean power is an opportunity to reindustrialise Britain as we’re backing UK supply chains to help deliver the energy transition.

'Great British Energy is supporting well-paid manufacturing jobs for communities, while providing cheaper and secure energy for households and businesses.'

The location of the UK manufacturing facility is still to be determined but when up and running, will reduce Naked Energy’s production costs and support its continued growth.

Daniel Hanna, Group Head of Sustainable and Transition Finance, Barclays, said: 'Since our first investment in Naked Energy four years ago, we have worked closely with the business as it has grown, connecting them to our network of partners and clients, leading to the installation of their technology at the All England Lawn Tennis Club.

'Our latest investment will help Naked Energy scale UK manufacturing, create skilled jobs and bring renewable heat to buildings across Britain. It shows how public and private capital can work together to strengthen UK energy security and grow a domestic renewable energy industry.'

The company holds more than 20 patents and unlike conventional solar panels, Naked Energy’s solar-thermal panels can produce both heat and electricity from a single rooftop installation. This is especially useful for buildings and sites with steady heat and cooling demand, such as hotels, leisure centres, hospitals, care homes, manufacturing facilities, residential developments and public buildings.

Its unique, low-profile design allows for around 85% of roof space to be used for energy generation, compared to a typical rate of 50% for conventional tilted solar panels that require spacing between rows to avoid self-shading. This means more energy can be generated from the same space, making it especially useful in cities and on commercial buildings with limited roof space. Notably, it was the only solar energy technology to receive planning permission at the British Library - a Grade I listed building - precisely because its design does not alter the building's roofline or silhouette, unlike many other technologies on the market.

Christophe Williams FEI, Founder and CEO of Naked Energy, said: 'The UK has world-class engineering capability and the opportunity to lead a rapidly growing global market for renewable heat. Great British Energy’s investment will enable us to establish a major UK manufacturing base, reduce production costs and scale a British-designed technology platform that combines advanced solar collectors, system design and digital monitoring.

'Heat is too often overlooked in the energy debate, despite accounting for a major share of fossil-fuel consumption. This investment will help us bring renewable heat to more hospitals, hotels, public buildings and industrial sites in the UK and internationally, while creating skilled jobs and export opportunities here at home.'

Naked Energy is already delivering projects across Europe and North America. The Great British Energy and Barclays joint investment marks a major scale-up phase, enabling Naked Energy to expand its UK production capacity and grow its presence in both domestic and international markets.

This is Great British Energy's first major solar investment and signals its continued commitment to putting public money behind British businesses at critical moments in their growth.

Background

Great British Energy is a publicly owned renewable energy company, 100% owned by the British people. It was established to drive investment in renewable power, create jobs and help deliver the UK's renewable energy ambitions.

Naked Energy is a British renewable-heat technology company headquartered in Crawley. Its Virtu product range includes high-density solar thermal and solar PVT systems that generate renewable heat and, in the case of VirtuPVT, both heat and electricity from the same rooftop footprint. The company also develops digital tools for system design, monitoring and performance optimisation, supporting the deployment of renewable heat across commercial, industrial and public-sector buildings.

Barclays Climate Ventures first invested in Naked Energy in July 2022 and made a follow-up investment in July 2024. Naked Energy has also participated in Barclays' Unreasonable Impact programme, and its technology has been installed at Barclays' Cambridge Eagle Lab and the All England Lawn Tennis Club.

Job figures - up to 40 direct and approximately 100 indirect roles - have been calculated using ONS methodology.

The location of the manufacturing facility has not yet been confirmed. A further announcement is expected in due course.

Great British Energy is investing in the project through its Energy Engineered in the UK programme, which aims to accelerate the commercialisation of British-developed clean energy technologies and build domestic supply chains.

A solar first

The investment marks the organisation's first significant backing of solar-thermal technology, reflecting growing recognition that decarbonising heat will be as important as expanding renewable electricity generation if the UK is to meet its net-zero ambitions.

Across the UK, gas is still commonly used for hot water, space heating and process heat. Cutting that reliance is an important step on the path to reducing energy bills and strengthening the UK’s energy security. Designed to tackle that exact scenario, Naked Energy’s technology generates renewable heat at the point of use.

Great British Energy CEO Dan McGrail said: "Cutting our reliance on gas is one of the biggest challenges we face, both for energy security and for keeping bills down. Naked Energy has developed a technology that tackles this head on and when you see it working at iconic UK institutions such as the British Library and Wimbledon, you understand what is possible.”

McGrail added: "At Great British Energy we are backing UK innovators such as Naked Energy and helping to create skilled jobs. Through our Energy Engineered in the UK programme we are helping them to manufacture here at home and go further, faster.”

British success story

The news was welcomed by the UK's new Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who said: “Homegrown, clean power is an opportunity to reindustrialise Britain as we’re backing UK supply chains to help deliver the energy transition.

"Great British Energy is supporting well-paid manufacturing jobs for communities, while providing cheaper and secure energy for households and businesses.”

The new funding will allow Naked Energy to establish a dedicated manufacturing base in the UK, although the location has yet to be announced. Producing its technology domestically is expected to lower manufacturing costs, strengthen UK supply chains and support the company's continued expansion in both domestic and international markets.

Unlike conventional PV systems, Naked Energy's Virtu technology combines solar thermal and PV generation within a single collector. The design enables both electricity and heat to be produced simultaneously, making it particularly suitable for buildings with year-round demand for hot water or heating, including hospitals, hotels, leisure centres, care homes, industrial facilities and public buildings.

The collectors also offer advantages where roof space is limited. Their low-profile design allows a greater proportion of available roof area to be used for energy generation than conventional tilted solar panels, which require wider spacing to prevent self-shading. UK as a leader

Christophe Williams, founder and CEO of Naked Energy, said: "The UK has world-class engineering capability and the opportunity to lead a rapidly growing global market for renewable heat. text:
CF Industries will begin construction this month on its $4bn Blue Point blue ammonia export project in Louisiana after receiving final construction permits, putting one of the world’s largest low-carbon ammonia plants on track for a 2029 start-up.

The 1.4 million tonne per year Blue Point project, being developed alongside Japanese power and industrial majors Jera and Mitsui, is set to export volumes to Japan and supply CF’s own production network.

CF said the State of Louisiana and the US Army Corps of Engineers issued civil construction permits for the ammonia plant and export infrastructure, clearing the way for work to begin in August.

The project is being developed by a joint venture 40% owned by CF, with Jera and Mitsui holding 35% and 25% stakes. All three have a stake in offtaking volumes from the plant relative to their equity investment.

It will be underpinned by long-term demand from Japan, where Jera and Mitsui were certified as low-carbon hydrogen suppliers by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry, allowing them to import Blue Point ammonia into the country.

Jera intends to supply the ammonia to Japan’s Hekinan Thermal Power Station for blending with coal, while Mitsui plans to supply 280,000 tonnes per year to Hokkaido Electric Power, Mitsubishi UBE Cement and Tosoh Corporation.

This week, the Japan Organisation for Metals and Energy Security said it would subsidise Hokkaido to build an ammonia import and supply facility.

The plant will incorporate autothermal reforming technology to produce hydrogen from natural gas.

It will be equipped with carbon capture technology to remove 95% of the project’s carbon dioxide emissions for transportation and storage by 1PointFive within its Pelican Sequestration Hub in Louisiana.

Industrial gas major Linde will build a $400m air separation unit at the site to supply oxygen and nitrogen for ammonia synthesis.

In Louisiana, CF is investing an additional $550m to build and operate ammonia storage and loading infrastructure.

name: Congress
title: Streamlined permitting threatens the public's voice - The Hill
authors: Adrian Shelley, opinion contributor, Adrian Shelley, opinion contributor
description:
The Trump administration recently pledged to “streamline” permitting for “minor” sources of air pollution.
The move would eliminate the public’s voice in deciding who gets to pollute.
Each state develops and implements its own plan to reduce air pollution, issues permits to pollute, and punishes violators of pollution laws.
In recent years, federal leaders looking to undermine existing environmental laws and regulations have even looked to Texas for guidance.
How can 65 diesel generators be a “minor” source of air pollution?
text:
The Trump administration recently pledged to “streamline” permitting for “minor” sources of air pollution. The move would eliminate the public’s voice in deciding who gets to pollute. Many critics see this as a move that will benefit certain polluting industries.

Don’t let the term “minor” fool you. While these permits are issued to, for example, your neighborhood dry cleaner, they can also apply to much more hazardous facilities, including concrete batch plants and even the gas-burning power plants that power data centers.

What could happen across the country if this so-called “streamlining” is implemented is already happening in Texas.

The Clean Air Act is one of the greatest public health success stories in modern history. During the 30 years beginning in 1990, the act provided $2 trillion in public health benefits for an investment of just $65 billion, a return of more than 30 times the investment.

A hallmark feature of the Clean Air Act is its delegation of authority to the states. Each state develops and implements its own plan to reduce air pollution, issues permits to pollute, and punishes violators of pollution laws.

In business-friendly Texas, state leaders have done the bare minimum, maintaining environmental regulations at the federal floor. In recent years, federal leaders looking to undermine existing environmental laws and regulations have even looked to Texas for guidance. Because Texas regulators work hand in glove with the very industries they are supposed to regulate, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) is quick to offer solutions that make life easier for polluters.

The results speak for themselves. Texas has elevated rates of certain cancers, builds concrete plants next to hospitals and schools, and welcomes data centers in communities that are running out of water. Texas has also failed to meet National Ambient Air Quality Standards in some regions for decades.

This is the context for President Trump’s latest erosion of public rights to enrich corporations and their CEOs. Here’s a real-life example of what that looks like.

On May 28, about 150 people gathered in a hotel ballroom in San Antonio. They participated in the first public opportunity concerning a data center in their community. The data center was already built and operating. It has a gas-fired power plant. It has 32 backup diesel generators, with 33 more proposed. It hums loudly and its lights are on around the clock.

The people in this room were angry. The Spurs were in a playoff game, but they didn’t care. They wanted answers. How does a gas power plant get built in their community with no public notice? How can 65 diesel generators be a “minor” source of air pollution?

What’s the point of a public meeting on a permit for a facility that’s already built and operating?

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality didn’t offer any answers, and neither did the company reps that sat next to them. In Texas, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality allows data centers to obtain low-level permits that don’t trigger public notification requirements to authorize dozens of diesel generators or what it calls electric generating units, gas-powered turbines. Some permits are approved within a day of the application being filed. Other permits don’t even have an approval process -— companies just tell the state they are claiming them.

That’s what Trump’s EPA wants for the rest of the country. No public notice, no process, just “build baby build.”

But even with this approach, how does a massive data center with its own gas plant and 65 backup diesel generators get permitted as a minor source? Auto body shops and dry cleaners are minor sources, not power plants.

Put simply: companies are playing games with the facts in their permit filings. In the San Antonio case, the data center treated its on-site, single-client, behind-the-meter gas power plant as a completely separate source for permitting purposes. Texas let it happen.

The data center, in its permit application, also gave an estimate for the hours of operation of its generators that put its potential to emit pollution just under the major source threshold, which allowed it to avoid triggering the public notice requirement. Again, Texas permitted it.

Finally, it appears that in 2025, when the company realized it would need twice as many backup generators as stated in its initial registration, it just dropped the stated number of operating hours, leaving the potential nitrogen oxide pollution emissions the same — just below the major source threshold. Again, Texas let them do it.

It’s not possible to know whether the entire process was by design. The company may or may not have known all along how many generators it would need. Past practice, though, shows that Texas regulators would allow a company to take steps like these to obtain a permit without triggering the public notice requirement. By the time the public gets involved — when a federal permit is finally needed for a facility that has operated for months with a fistful of minor permits — it’s too late. The facility is built. The generators are operating.

What are you complaining about?

Taking away public notice and participation in permitting will remove a major check on unethical or outright illegal actions by corporations: the public eye. Experts working in the public interest can’t call out phony math if they never see the application. And the stunning success of the Clean Air Act won’t continue without transparency and the public’s input.

Data centers face bipartisan opposition across the country for several reasons. They are noisy, thirsty and hot. They are a physical reminder of Big Tech’s latest intrusion in our lives. Their proponents use sneaky tactics to avoid the local opposition they know is coming.

And now, Trump’s EPA wants to exclude the public’s voice. We can’t let that happen.

Adrian Shelley is the Texas director of Public Citizen.

name: Indiana Environment
title: The problem with going solar in Indiana | News From The States
description:
The average Indiana home uses ~900 kilowatt-hours of energy per month.
Indiana high court sides with utilities on solar power, ending benefits for small owners To cover 100% of those energy needs, a family would need an 8-kilowatt solar system, which costs around $25,000 to install.
This greatly changes the financial math for solar energy in Indiana.
Rather than reducing the previous $152 monthly energy bill for a solar owner to $17, this net metering boondoggle means that the average solar owner in Indiana still pays $85 monthly.
Those savings become profits for Indiana electric utilities and their (mostly) out-of-state shareholders.
text:
Over the past year, I have been noodling over the possibility of installing solar panels on my roof. This simple curiosity eventually turned into action — I got several quotes for what solar installation might cost. It was at that point that I discovered a 2017 Indiana state law that makes installing solar financially difficult for individual homeowners but quite profitable for electric companies.

I like the idea of being more self-sufficient. I like the fact that, once installed, solar panels provide pretty much free energy for my home that is healthier for our planet. And solar technology has become much better and more affordable over time. As climate author Bill McKibben put it on a podcast: “Sometime earlier this decade, we passed some invisible line where it became cheaper to produce energy from the sun and the wind than from setting stuff on fire.”

While it has become less expensive, installing a solar harvesting system is not cheap in the short term; especially after federal lawmakers abruptly eliminated the 30% residential tax credit at the end of last year. I would have to pay a lot up front for the ability to harvest free photons that would otherwise just warm up the shingles on my roof. Under fair economic conditions, that upfront cost pays for itself over time through drastically lower monthly power bills, eventually earning back every dollar spent and saving money for years to come.

Let’s look at what this should look like for an average Hoosier household.

The average Indiana home uses ~900 kilowatt-hours of energy per month. At an average cost of $0.15 per kWh, that equates to an average electricity bill of $135 per month (plus a $17 monthly customer fee, totaling $152 monthly) .

Indiana high court sides with utilities on solar power, ending benefits for small owners

To cover 100% of those energy needs, a family would need an 8-kilowatt solar system, which costs around $25,000 to install.

With fair energy policy, this system would essentially eliminate a family’s electricity charges, leaving them with only the mandatory monthly fee to the electric company required to be connected to the grid. That would drop their $152 monthly energy bill to $17.

At this savings rate, the payoff horizon is 15.4 years. Assuming a 30-year solar panel lifespan, a solar household would save around $23,650 in energy bills over the last 14.6 years of the system. All while releasing zero carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

While that is how it should happen, a 2017 state law ensures that is not how it works in Indiana. Here’s why.

On a sunny afternoon in July, a home solar array typically makes far more power than the house needs, sending the extra electricity back to the neighborhood power lines. At night, when the sun is shining in Australia instead of Indiana, the family has to pull electricity back off the grid to keep the lights on.

Think of the power grid like a bank account: with a solar system you make energy “deposits” during the day, and make energy “withdrawals” at night. The system that tracks these deposits and withdrawals is called “net metering”.

In most states, if you deposit 20 kWh of power during the afternoon (as is usual on a typical sunny day), you get a full 1-to-1 credit to withdraw those same 20 kWh later that night. While states like Florida, Ohio, and Iowa protect 1-to-1 net metering as a matter of property rights and energy freedom, Indiana’s Senate Enrolled Act 309 created an artificial government price control that penalizes Hoosier families for investing in their own homes.

Passed in 2017, the law allows electric companies to harvest those same 20 kWh of afternoon power from you and immediately sell them to your neighbors for $3.00 (the full $0.15/kWh retail price), while crediting you just $0.70 (the discounted $0.035/kWh wholesale rate). When you pull that same power back out of the grid that night, they charge you $3.00 once again. That leaves the homeowner getting back less than 25% of the energy value they deposited just hours earlier.

This greatly changes the financial math for solar energy in Indiana. Rather than reducing the previous $152 monthly energy bill for a solar owner to $17, this net metering boondoggle means that the average solar owner in Indiana still pays $85 monthly. That pushes the payoff horizon to over 31 years, which exceeds the lifespan of the panels entirely. Instead of saving tens of thousands of dollars, Hoosier families actually end up taking a $900 net loss on their investment.

The $23,650 of potential savings that SEA 309 takes from solar households does not disappear into thin air. Those savings become profits for Indiana electric utilities and their (mostly) out-of-state shareholders. Funded out of the pockets of Hoosiers. It’s time for the General Assembly to repeal SEA 309, restore fair 1-to-1 net metering, and give Hoosier families the right to benefit from their own private property investments.

title: How the EV transition is reshaping cost models for international automotive OEMs
description:
The result is a shift from traditional automotive cost models toward more dynamic, region-specific approaches that account for a growing range of variables.
Battery materials, steel, aluminium, energy, logistics, tariffs and compliance costs now play a direct role in vehicle profitability.
EV demand is reshaping investment decisions The EV transition continues to advance, but not uniformly across regions.
Battery materials are now a core margin driver The most significant change in automotive cost structures is the rise of battery materials as a major profitability factor.
A new approach to automotive cost management The EV transition is transforming automotive cost models in fundamental ways.
text:
Key takeaways:

Battery materials like lithium, nickel, and cobalt have become central to vehicle margins, influenced by fluctuating prices and chemistry choices.

Regionalization and trade policies introduce localized supply challenges and tariff impacts, complicating sourcing decisions.

OEMs increasingly adopt data-driven procurement strategies incorporating market intelligence and carbon compliance to navigate complex cost and regulatory landscapes.

The early EV growth story centered on scaling battery production, securing raw material supply and accelerating model launches. Today, however, demand patterns, battery raw material volatility, trade policy and carbon regulation are making manufacturers rethink how they manage profitability.

The result is a shift from traditional automotive cost models toward more dynamic, region-specific approaches that account for a growing range of variables.

Battery materials, steel, aluminium, energy, logistics, tariffs and compliance costs now play a direct role in vehicle profitability. Managing those factors effectively has become critical for OEMs to maintain margins throughout the EV transition.

EV demand is reshaping investment decisions

The EV transition continues to advance, but not uniformly across regions. In Europe, battery-electric vehicles (BEVs) captured around 20% market share during the first five months of 2026, while hybrid vehicles remained the largest powertrain category. At the same time, growth remains concentrated in Western European markets, highlighting significant regional differences in adoption rates.

This fragmentation is changing how OEMs forecast demand and allocate capital.

Rather than relying on a single global EV growth trajectory, manufacturers increasingly need to plan by geography, powertrain mix, battery chemistry and vehicle segment. A premium European BEV, a North American hybrid strategy and an entry-level Asian EV each carry different raw material and cost exposures.

North America illustrates how market conditions can alter investment plans.

Honda recently suspended aspects of its North American EV strategy, citing uncertainty over EV business viability and shifting its focus toward hybrid and internal combustion engine vehicles. The company’s decision underscores how automakers are reassessing whether planned EV investments align with actual market demand.

Battery materials are now a core margin driver

The most significant change in automotive cost structures is the rise of battery materials as a major profitability factor.

While OEMs have long managed exposure to steel and aluminium, electrification has introduced additional dependence on lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, manganese and other battery materials. These are highly sensitive to supply-chain constraints, refining capacity and rapidly evolving market dynamics.

Lithium demonstrates how dramatically market conditions can shift. Fastmarkets reported that lithium hydroxide prices exceeded $80 per kg in late 2022 before falling to around $8 per kg by 2025 as supply expanded and demand growth underperformed earlier expectations.

While lower lithium prices have supported OEM margins in the short term, they also create uncertainty around future supply investment. Prolonged low prices often can delay new projects, increasing the risk of tighter supply if EV demand accelerates again. As a result, procurement teams must monitor not only current pricing but longer-term supply fundamentals.

Battery chemistry choices are also becoming a cost-management tool. The growing adoption of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which generally rely on lithium carbonate rather than lithium hydroxide, has altered previous assumptions about raw material demand.

For many automakers, chemistry selection now involves balancing performance, affordability and commodity price exposure.

Want to learn more about what is happening at the cutting-edge of critical minerals and battery raw materials? Listen to our Fast Forward podcast series for insight, debate and news from the major players.

Localization introduces new automotive cost challenges

Government policies such as the USMCA and the Inflation Reduction Act have encouraged OEMs to localize sourcing and manufacturing across North America. While domestic supply chains can reduce logistics risks, they do not eliminate commodity exposure.

In many cases, localization creates new challenges, including tighter regional supply, local price premiums and greater exposure to domestic policy changes.

Fastmarkets analysis notes that steel and aluminium markets are becoming increasingly fragmented as tariffs, supply restrictions and regional regulations reshape pricing dynamics.

Honda reported significant profit losses linked to tariffs while also facing Section 232 steel duties, automobile tariffs and anti-dumping measures.

For international OEMs, this means sourcing decisions can no longer be based solely on headline commodity prices. Tariffs, incentives, logistics costs, policy stability and supply availability must all be incorporated into cost models when evaluating production locations and supplier networks.

Carbon and compliance costs are gaining importance

Alongside material costs, carbon and compliance considerations are becoming increasingly important in automotive procurement strategies. European OEMs must now manage battery material costs while also addressing a more complex regulatory environment and rising sustainability expectations.

Carbon-related pricing mechanisms are also beginning to influence trade flows and sourcing decisions. While regulatory impacts vary by region, automotive manufacturers increasingly need visibility into the emissions profile of materials alongside their financial cost.

This is particularly relevant for steel and aluminium, where decarbonization efforts can significantly influence pricing and supplier selection.

As a result, many OEMs are moving toward cost frameworks that evaluate commodities based on both financial and carbon performance rather than price alone.

Automotive procurement is becoming data-driven

Greater cost volatility is driving a shift toward more sophisticated procurement and risk-management strategies. OEMs increasingly require independent benchmarks, market forecasts and exposure analysis to support sourcing decisions and supplier negotiations.

Fastmarkets’ lithium risk-management framework illustrates this trend. By using Cash Flow at Risk (CFaR) methodologies, companies can quantify the financial impact of potential commodity price movements and establish predefined hedging triggers when exposure exceeds acceptable limits.

The broader battery materials industry is also evolving. Discussions at the Fastmarkets Global Lithium, Battery and Critical Materials Conference highlighted how battery raw materials are now influenced not only by EV demand but also by growth in energy storage, AI infrastructure and national security initiatives.

These new demand drivers increase competition for future supply and reinforce the importance of long-term supply planning.

A new approach to automotive cost management

The EV transition is transforming automotive cost models in fundamental ways.

First, battery materials have become central to vehicle profitability.

Second, trade policy and localization strategies are fragmenting global sourcing economics.

Third, volatility is forcing procurement, finance and strategy teams to rely on shared market intelligence and risk-management frameworks rather than static annual budgets.

For international OEMs, the challenge is no longer simply scaling EV production. It is doing so profitably while navigating volatile commodity markets, shifting policy frameworks and evolving consumer demand.

The manufacturers best positioned for success will be those that combine cost visibility, procurement agility and robust market intelligence to make faster, more informed decisions in an increasingly complex automotive landscape.

FIRST ON FOX: Senate Republicans are launching a multi-front effort targeting the legal framework they say allows California to exert outsized influence over vehicle and equipment emissions standards beyond its borders, creating economic and consumer consequences.

Republicans argue California has become the nation's de facto emissions regulator — as manufacturers rarely create separate product lines for the Golden State and instead are inclined to build to California’s standards, creating implicit national requirements.

Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo. — a top member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (EPW) — is leading the effort alongside Sens. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., Jon Husted, R-Ohio, and Pete Ricketts, R-Neb. They argue EPA waivers granted to California during the Obama and Biden administrations under the Clean Air Act have turned narrow environmental exceptions into de facto climate regulation, advancing the state's sweeping climate agenda.

"California's climate zealots have run roughshod over the rest of the country for too long," Lummis told Fox News Digital.

CALIFORNIA SUES TRUMP EPA OVER MOVE TO SUBJECT STATE VEHICLE EMISSIONS WAIVERS TO CONGRESSIONAL REVIEW

"Under Governor Newsom, Sacramento has decided it can dictate what Wyoming families drive and what equipment our small businesses use. That ends today."

Last year, lawmakers successfully rescinded three Biden-era EPA waivers allowing California to create emissions standards for trucks, cars and buses that they said gave the state outsized regulatory control. Thursday’s package goes a step further by targeting earlier EPA decisions they say laid the legal foundation for those now-rescinded regulations.

Each resolution uses the Congressional Review Act (CRA) to nullify a different EPA waiver. The CRA gives Congress the power to check agencies' executive power.

NEWSOM, WALZ URGE CONGRESS TO BLOCK ANTI-CLIMATE BILL IN THEIR ‘WOKE’ CRUSADE

Because the CRA bars agencies from issuing rules that are "substantially the same" without new authorization from Congress, Republicans argue overturning the waivers would prevent future administrations from simply reinstating them — which targets the legal foundation of such carveouts.

Collectively, the package targets California's authority over gas-powered lawn equipment, passenger vehicle emissions standards, the Advanced Clean Cars program and the original 2009 EPA waiver allowing Sacramento to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from automobiles.

In the 1960s, the Clean Air Act gave California a narrow carve-out to seek EPA waivers for emissions rules that could be stricter than federal standards — but critics say the exemption, originally intended to address severe Los Angeles smog, has been weaponized to force manufacturing changes that reverberate across the country.

Andrew Bray, an executive with the National Association of Landscape Professionals, whose members rely on small off-road engines affected by the waivers, said he supports a responsible transition to lower-emission equipment — but underlined that it must come from "practical innovation" and not government mandates.

TRUMP’S REINDUSTRIALIZATION AGENDA FACES ITS BIGGEST HURDLE — AMERICANS

"This resolution is a critical step in securing the flexibility businesses need while technology continues to advance," Bray said. Michael Lee of the Golf Course Superintendents Association of America added that the legislative process, not state-specific fiats with "nationwide consequences," is the way to address the situation.

The four lawmakers leading the fight said in a release that California regulators have "abandoned any pretense of addressing local air quality and turned the waiver process into a backdoor for imposing a radical climate agenda on the entire country… without a single vote in Congress."

Lummis' resolution would rescind a 2025 waiver granted just before President Donald Trump took office that she said allowed California to phase out gas-powered small engines such as chainsaws and leaf blowers.

In doing so, manufacturers would no longer be inclined to transition to electric or zero-emission models.

TRUMP'S EPA CHIEF PUSHES BACK ON CLIMATE SKEPTICS BEING LABELED 'SCIENCE DENIERS'

Lummis' resolution targets a 2025 EPA waiver that allowed California to move toward phasing out new gas-powered small engines such as chainsaws, leaf blowers and lawn mowers. Supporters say repealing the waiver would remove regulatory pressure encouraging manufacturers to transition those products toward zero-emission technology.

Husted’s resolution targets a 2022 EPA waiver that restored California’s authority to continue its Advanced Clean Cars program.

"Ohioans shouldn’t be forced to follow California’s lead when it comes to policies that make everyday life more expensive and less convenient," he told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

Ricketts said the situation is proof that the Obama-Biden era of "overregulation and red tape" continues to cost Nebraskans and Americans writ large millions of dollars, citing his state's massive agricultural industry as an example of regulatory reverberations from Sacramento.

EUROPE'S 'GREEN IDEOLOGY' CLIMATE AGENDA RISKS CRUSHING ITS INDUSTRY, ENVIRONMENT MINISTER WARNS

"They used California policies as a backdoor EV mandate and even tried to control how we cut our grass," he said. His CRA resolution targets an Obama-era waiver originally authorizing the clean car program, while Schmitt seeks repeal of a waiver granted just months after President George W. Bush left office that allows California to enforce greenhouse gas emissions standards for new passenger vehicles beginning with the 2009 model year.

Schmitt said the waivers allow Sacramento to "continue to punish" manufacturers around the country and affect consumer choice and costs through their "climate alarmist rules."

Together, Republicans say the four resolutions represent Congress' broadest effort yet to unshackle states and manufacturers from California's emissions framework by targeting not only individual regulations but the EPA decisions they argue made those regulations possible.

Why GAO Did This Study The 45Q credit was created in 2008 to incentivize the development of carbon capture technology and reduce carbon emissions.
This report assesses (1) IRS’s administration of the 45Q credit, and (2) the challenges in evaluating the effectiveness of the credit.
text:
Carbon capture technology can reduce carbon in the atmosphere by storing it underground or using it to make products like concrete or jet fuel.

The 45Q tax credit was created to incentivize development of this technology. But some taxpayers have difficulty claiming it. Those who use captured carbon to make products face the biggest hurdles—long delays for approval and a high rejection rate, for example.

No agency is tasked with measuring results and the law didn't set clear goals, so it's hard to know if the 45Q tax credit is working.

We made recommendations to Congress and agencies to improve oversight and administration of the tax credit.

Industrial carbon capture and storage facility with tall metal towers, and pipes.

What GAO Found

The Carbon Oxide Sequestration Credit (45Q) is a tax credit provided for certain carbon oxides that are captured at emission sources or directly from the air and either stored underground or used to produce products. The credit has been amended multiple times, including by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), which added new credit features. More recently, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act created parity in credit values across uses of captured carbon. As of March 2026, there were 33 carbon capture facilities in the U.S., with additional facilities planned. The number of 45Q credit claims more than tripled from 2019 to 2023, according to IRS data.

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) has taken several actions to administer the 45Q credit and mitigate potential noncompliance. However, taxpayers using carbon to produce products face compliance burdens, delays, and uncertainty in claiming the credit. GAO identified areas in the approval process for carbon utilization where IRS and the Department of Energy (DOE) could potentially minimize compliance burden and improve certainty for taxpayers. Pursuing such opportunities—for example, streamlining certain processes, or clarifying acceptable datasets that can be used to calculate carbon displaced—could improve the process and help minimize delays for both agencies and taxpayers.

Multiple potential goals, the lack of a designated agency to evaluate the effectiveness of the credit, and data limitations complicate Congress’s ability to understand the performance of the 45Q credit. Even so, periodic reviews of tax expenditures are crucial for informed oversight. GAO has previously recommended various actions Congress and agencies could take to improve oversight for other tax expenditures, such as identifying what should be analyzed and by whom. In this report, GAO identified key questions for Congress to consider directing agencies to analyze to help determine the performance of the credit. These key questions are: (1) how well the credit is working to achieve its goals, (2) how efficiently the credit is performing and (3) how the credit compares to other policy tools.

Why GAO Did This Study

The 45Q credit was created in 2008 to incentivize the development of carbon capture technology and reduce carbon emissions. Carbon capture involves complex and novel technology, and the 45Q credit could result in potentially substantial revenue expenditures.

The IRA includes a provision for GAO to review the distribution and use of IRA funds. This report assesses (1) IRS’s administration of the 45Q credit, and (2) the challenges in evaluating the effectiveness of the credit. GAO reviewed agency policies and procedures and interviewed officials from IRS, DOE, and the Environmental Protection Agency. GAO also interviewed selected external stakeholders knowledgeable about the 45Q credit, representing advocacy, research, and industry. GAO also conducted two site visits to carbon capture sites in Houston, Texas.

text:
Illinois is one step closer to building its first new nuclear reactors in nearly 40 years.

Though the state leads the nation in nuclear energy generation, a recently lifted moratorium on new nuclear power plant construction means the race is on to bring new plants online — a task that can take years.

As Illinois looks for the right sites to build, several communities have already said “yes” to new plants.

Planning for these new reactors is happening in a different context from the last time they were built in the state in the 1970s and ‘80s. Reactor technology has advanced, but so has wind and solar power. And with energy demands rising quickly, construction time and costs are sure to play a big part in the trajectory of nuclear power.

A Winding Path to New Plants

This is just the latest step in the state’s long history with nuclear technology.

University of Chicago scientists built the world’s first nuclear reactor under the stands of the school’s football field in 1942. After World War II, the federal government opened Argonne National Laboratory to continue research into civilian uses for nuclear power.

Today, Illinois leads the nation in generating nuclear energy, with 11 plants pumping out half of the state’s total electricity. But of these existing plants, the last one came online in 1988.

A statewide moratorium on new construction lasted from the late 1980s until this January, when it was lifted as part of an energy omnibus bill. Gov. JB Pritzker wasted little time getting the ball rolling on new projects.

“The economic opportunity of building new, clean power is enormous,” Pritzker said in his February budget address, announcing an executive order intended to speed up the construction of new nuclear facilities.

“We can take years off of the development and launch of new base load energy production,” Pritzker said.

Read More:

These 9 Illinois Communities Say They’re Interested in New Nuclear Facilities

What Does Pritzker’s Nuclear Energy Executive Order Do in Illinois?

Pritzker Signs Major Energy Reform Bill Amid Projected Shortages

The order directed state agencies to create a framework for the evaluation, financing and safety regulation of new nuclear power plants. Importantly, the order also directed those agencies to request information from communities interested in hosting a new facility.

Now, the responses are in. Nine communities, plus the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, submitted initial comments.

Many came from communities that host existing nuclear plants, like Grundy County. In addition to the Dresden Generating Station within the county lines, the LaSalle Generating Station is a 40-minute drive to the west, and the Braidwood Generating Station is about 25 minutes south.

“We have a comfort with nuclear, we have the workforce for nuclear, we have the safety mechanisms in place,” said Nancy Norton, president of the Grundy County Economic Development Council.

“And frankly, (we have) the infrastructure and transmission to get power out to the customers,” Grundy said.

Then there are places like Peoria County, which is navigating a new energy landscape after the closure of a coal-fired power plant in 2022.

“Where we separate ourselves is we’ve been very supportive and agnostic of all the alternative energy sources,” said Scott Sorrel, the Peoria County administrator.

Peoria County is one of the state leaders in approving utility-scale solar power projects and is planning two utility-scale wind power projects, according to Sorrel.

“At this point in time, we’re not closing a door to nuclear, but making sure that door stays open,” Sorrel said. “And if the opportunity presents itself, to walk through that door.”

Time and Money Shape the Clean Energy Transition

Nuclear power is considered “clean” energy, since it does not emit the greenhouse gases that cause climate change. It can also output energy around the clock. But the role it can play in the transition away from fossil fuels is still a matter of debate.

The two most recent nuclear plants to come online in the United States, at the Vogtle Generating Plant in Georgia, opened seven years behind schedule and $17 billion over budget.

With energy demand rapidly rising, environmental advocates point to the relatively cheap and fast deployment of renewable sources like solar and wind projects.

While nuclear power still provides Illinois with about half of its electricity, the share provided by renewables has tripled in the past decade — growing to 16% in 2025, according to the Illinois Power Agency.

That’s at least the current status of nuclear power in Illinois, generated at large facilities with the familiar hourglass-shaped cooling towers. But Norton and Sorrel both acknowledged that the technology is changing, and the next generation of reactors could look and operate differently.

Advancing Reactor Designs

One place to look for what modern nuclear reactors might accomplish is the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. There, the university is working in partnership with the company NANO Nuclear Energy to build a prototype of a “microreactor” on campus.

While this would produce around 1% of the energy made by traditional large reactors, James Walker, the NANO Nuclear Energy CEO, said the advantage is in how it can be built and operated.

“All the components will be shipped to site as a modular system, assembled there, and begin to immediately output power,” Walker said.

So far, no commercial small modular reactors (SMRs) have been completed in the United States, and the industry is split between dozens of different designs. The NANO Nuclear reactor, which would fit on a 2-acre plot of land adjacent to an existing power plant, is the first of its size to be submitted for federal approval from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

But even though the designs are new, Walker said the technology isn’t the main bottleneck for quickly deploying reactors like the University of Illinois project.

“It’s having all of the components to be able to mass manufacture the reactors, that’s going to be the challenge,” Walker said.

And since new reactors of any size haven’t been built in decades, one remaining question is where the workforce and expertise might come from.

For Norton, the answer is right down the street.

“We have the construction workers that have been maintaining these nuclear plants,” Norton said.

“In our region, we probably have a couple thousand employees who understand how nuclear reactions and nuclear reactors work,” Norton said. “So I don’t know that to scale up would be that difficult for us.”

Capitol News Illinois contributed to this report.
