text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger said she’ll intervene in the proposed $67 billion merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy in a move she said is aimed at lowering energy costs and protecting jobs.

Spanberger wrote in The Washington Post about the action she said is a first for a Virginia governor.

“As a Virginian, I am deeply skeptical about whether selling our primary, state-regulated utility to an out-of-state company is good for the commonwealth,” she said. “I have serious questions about what this deal would mean for us. And as governor, I intend to get answers and be a voice for Virginians in the process.”

Spanberger said she will request to be a party to the case.

NextEra Energy is seeking to acquire Dominion Energy in an all-stock deal, creating a massive power company as the energy needs of artificial intelligence drive demand higher in the U.S.

It is one of the biggest proposed mergers so far this year and would create the world’s biggest regulated electric utility business by market capitalization, the companies said this spring.

The combined company would serve approximately 10 million utility customer accounts across Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Florida.

Prior reporting contributed by the Associated Press.

Stay with NBC Washington for more details on this developing story.

On an adjusted basis, second-quarter 2026 earnings were $762 million or $1.16 per diluted share, compared to $583 million or $0.89 per diluted share in 2025.

"Across our management team, there is a consistent emphasis on execution, and our progress through the first half of the year is reflected in strong financial performance," said Jeffrey W. Martin, chairman and CEO of Sempra. "I could not be more proud of our employees and their commitment to innovation and continuous improvement, as we look to find new and better ways to serve customers."

The reported financial results reflect certain significant items as described on an after-tax basis in the following table of GAAP earnings, reconciled to adjusted earnings, for second-quarter 2026 and 2025.

Advancing Value Creation Initiatives

During the second quarter, Sempra continued executing on a series of value creation initiatives to further its mission of building America's leading utility growth business. Taken together, these initiatives are designed to simplify the company's strategy, strengthen its financial position and support long-term utility growth.

In the first half of 2026, Sempra's businesses invested capital expenditures of over $6 billion to support safe, reliable and affordable energy for the communities we serve. These investments are part of Sempra's record five-year 2026-2030 capital plan of approximately $65 billion, with 95% allocated to investments at our Texas and California utilities.

Sempra Texas

Sempra continues to see strong growth opportunities in Texas through its investment in Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor). During the quarter, Oncor's new base rates became effective June 1. In addition, Oncor filed the surcharge that was approved through its recent base rate review. The surcharge, which took effect August 1, recovers the difference between the new base rates and the rates in effect from January 1 to June 1, 2026. The updated base rates better align Oncor's cost structure with today's operating environment, strengthen its financial profile and support continued infrastructure investments to meet Texas' growing energy needs.

Texas continues to experience unprecedented growth in electric demand as evidenced by Electric Reliability Council of Texas' (ERCOT) new all-time peak load of 91 gigawatts (GW) set in July. Continued growth in demand is leading to a series of new opportunities to invest in the electric grid.

Earlier this year, ERCOT endorsed a series of high-voltage transmission projects expected to require more than $7 billion of incremental investment, supporting approximately 16 GW of new electric demand with anticipated in-service dates between 2026 and 2034. Oncor expects to construct the majority of those projects, which are subject to regulatory approval.

Also, the Public Utility Commission of Texas recently approved ERCOT's Batch Zero process, establishing a standardized framework intended to streamline large-load interconnections and support growing demand across the electric grid. While the timeline of the Batch Zero process remains to be determined, approximately 44 GW of large-load requests in Oncor's service territory are expected to be eligible as base or studied load, consisting of approximately 27 GW of base load and 17 GW of studied load. The referenced 44 GW also includes 8 GW of existing interconnected large load that is ramping up to its authorized capacity. The projects reflect significant customer commitment through financial security, site control and other ERCOT qualification requirements, reinforcing the substantial demand for infrastructure investment across Oncor's service territory. For context, if fully realized, these requests would represent over 140% growth relative to Oncor's current system peak load of 31 GW.

Sempra California

In California, Sempra's utilities remained focused on advancing safety, reliability and affordability for customers. During the quarter, San Diego Gas & Electric (SDGE) and Southern California Gas Company (SoCalGas) filed their 2028 General Rate Case (GRC) applications. Together, these GRC applications demonstrate a balanced approach to advancing critical safety and reliability investments supporting wildfire risk reduction, electric reliability and resilience, and pipeline safety, while maintaining disciplined cost management and a focus on customer affordability.

Regulatory momentum continued in the quarter, including the approval by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission of SDGE's electric transmission rate, or TO6, settlement. The settlement provides a constructive outcome for SDGE's transmission business, including an authorized base return on equity of approximately 10.28% and a supportive regulatory framework for continued transmission investment. Additionally, the California Independent System Operator's 2025–2026 Transmission Plan included over $160 million of reliability-driven projects for SDGE, further supporting grid resilience.

Sempra California also continued to advance innovation and deliver meaningful benefits for customers. SoCalGas estimates that its energy efficiency programs helped customers save more than $100 million on their utility bills last year, while SDGE expanded its battery energy storage capacity in the second quarter to support grid reliability. In addition, SDGE launched a collaboration with Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. and the University of California San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography to develop edge-based artificial intelligence technology aimed at enhancing extreme-weather response capabilities. In combination, these efforts reflect Sempra California's broader commitment to safety, innovation and long-term system reliability.

Sempra Infrastructure Partners Strategic Updates

The transaction to sell a 45% equity interest in Sempra Infrastructure Partners to affiliates of KKR remains on track and is expected to close in the third quarter of 2026, subject to required approvals and customary closing conditions. The planned sale of Ecogas México, S. de R.L. de C.V. continues to advance following the recent approval without condition by Mexico's antitrust authority and is expected to close in August. These transactions further Sempra's capital recycling program with a view toward simplifying the company's strategy, strengthening its financial position and supporting long-term utility growth.

Sempra is updating its full-year 2026 GAAP earnings-per-common share (EPS) guidance range to $5.02 to $5.55, reflecting actual results through the second quarter, affirming its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance range of $4.80 to $5.30 and affirming its full-year 2027 EPS guidance range of $5.10 to $5.70. Sempra is also affirming a 7% to 9% projected long‑term EPS growth rate.

Six of the 10 judges on the panel said the EPA could not terminate the program "based solely on a policy disagreement."

According to Lawrence, "The court leaves open what the EPA can do next, stating it is evenly divided on whether the temporary restrictions on the EPA should continue based on the remaining legal arguments presented to them."

text:
Long-duration energy storage startup Ore Energy announced that it has raised $43 million in a Series A funding round, with proceeds aimed at scaling its iron-air battery technology for multi-day storage of wind and solar energy, to enable fully renewable power systems.

Energy storage is considered a key enabler of the clean energy transition, helping address the intermittent nature of renewable energy sources such as wind and solar while meeting around-the-clock electricity demand and supporting growing power needs from sectors including transportation electrification and AI-driven computing. Duration remains a key challenge to energy storage systems, with most lithium-ion solutions becoming uneconomical beyond a few hours.

Founded in 2022 by CEO Aytac Yilmaz, and COO Rutil Özdemir, Amsterdam-based Ore Energy develops long-duration iron-air battery technology designed to provide low-cost energy storage for renewable energy. The company said that its batteries, built from iron, water and air, can store electricity for up to 100 hours, enabling electricity grids to continue operating through multi-day periods of low wind and sun.

Iron-air batteries store electricity by reversing the rusting process, as charging converts iron oxide back into metallic iron, while discharging re-oxidizes the iron using oxygen from the air.

The company said that the new capital will support the commercialization of its technology and the construction of its first manufacturing facility, as it works towards GWh-scale manufacturing by 2028.

Aytac Yilmaz, co-founder and CEO of Ore Energy, said,

“Affordable, renewable baseload power is the foundation for the next generation of manufacturing, AI infrastructure and industrial growth globally. Ore Energy’s long-duration storage is an essential part of that future. This funding will help us build our first manufacturing facility and put us on the path to gigawatt hour-scale production, making renewable electricity available whenever and wherever needed.”

The funding round was led by Plural and HV, with the participation of Positron.

title: Can President Trump End U.S. Reliance On Chinese Rare Earth Minerals?
description:
President Trump wants to end U.S. reliance on Chinese critical minerals by January 1, 2027, but it is unlikely American miners and processors will be ready by then.
The United States has reserves of most critical minerals, but it lacks the capacity to mine and process many of them.
In February, the Trump administration launched Project Vault, a $12 billion effort to stockpile critical minerals for American manufacturers.
​It is buying an existing U.S. magnet producer.
Conclusion President Trump wants the United States to mine and process its own critical minerals by January 1, 2027, and stop purchasing from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea.
text:
President Trump wants to end U.S. reliance on Chinese critical minerals by January 1, 2027, but it is unlikely American miners and processors will be ready by then. The Trump administration has spent tens of billions of dollars on nearly 150 minerals companies to loosen China’s hold on supply chains for weapons and other strategic products essential for the nation. The January 1, 2027, deadline is the date under federal regulations to ‌stop purchasing rare earths, magnets, tungsten, molybdenum, and tantalum from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea. The United States has been trying to limit critical mineral imports for years but has had to grant companies waivers because U.S. industries involved have been unable to meet demand. Recently, President Trump signed an executive order making it even harder for defense contractors to obtain waivers. According to Trump’s executive order, waivers can only be issued if a contractor shows an “exhaustive effort” to avoid Chinese material and has a timeline for weaning itself off such supply.

The difficulty of weaning the U.S. off dependence on Chinese supplies can be seen in the following example. In 2025, U.S. demand for the most common type of rare ​earth magnet was about 48,000 metric tons while domestic sources supplied 300 metric tons. U.S. firms are now on track to have the capacity to produce 5,000 metric tons by year-end, but that is a far cry from the amount of demand. Rare earths, ​which are among the 60 minerals considered critical by the government, must be processed before they are turned into magnets used to make weapons, automobiles, computers and other products. That processing is resource-intensive and an area where China dominates, thanks to its cheap coal power and lax environmental regulations.

Further, U.S. firms have not produced tungsten since 2015 and ⁠tantalum since 1959. Guardian Metal Resources is working to open a U.S. tungsten mine by 2028, while Lion Rock Resources is developing a tantalum mine in South Dakota, with no timeline for opening, but both are beyond the 2027 date.

The United States has reserves of most critical minerals, but it lacks the capacity to mine and process many of them. ​China grew to dominate the minerals-refining industry in the late 20th century and controls more than 80% of the sector today. The International Energy Agency warned recently that $6.5 trillion of global manufacturing is at risk if China imposes export restrictions on rare earths, as it has done periodically in recent years. U.S. rare earths investment has been hindered by persistently low prices because China has been subsidizing its producers and flooding the market with cheap products, thus making American projects unprofitable. Control of markets allows China to respond to the opening of a U.S. mine or processing facility by flooding the market with its own material, which drives down world prices and renders the new facility uneconomic. Technological breakthroughs can help drive price drops when they occur.

Ucore Rare Metals, a minerals-refining startup backed by the War Department, has developed a processing technology known as RapidSX that is similar to, but faster, cleaner, and cheaper than, the industry-standard solvent extraction. Ucore had planned to start refining by 2025, but production will not begin until 2027 at the earliest, as it had to rework its plans due to changing demands from the War Department, according to the company.

In February, the Trump administration launched Project Vault, a $12 billion effort to stockpile critical minerals for American manufacturers. Later, officials acknowledged that they will need to initially buy minerals from abroad, including China. Defense contractor Lockheed Martin provided the Department of War with a list of minerals it would like stockpiled, as defense contractors need to place orders. Nick Myers, CEO of Massachusetts-based Phoenix Tailings, a minerals ​startup that recently received a $500 million loan from the War Department to build ​a processing facility, said, “Defense contractors have just assumed they can keep buying Chinese products. The defense industry is never going to stop if ⁠you keep giving waivers.”

The complexity of mineral refining has slowed U.S. projects. Among the biggest U.S. companies is MP Materials, which is financially supported by the War Department. The company spent years calibrating its solvent extraction processing equipment, part of what CEO Jim Litinsky described ​as a “painstaking” process. MP built a magnet ⁠facility in Texas and expects to have magnets approved for its first customer, General Motors, by the end of the year. A separate magnet facility that MP is building for the Department of War is slated to open in 2028.

In Marion, Indiana, ReElement Technologies plans to process minerals using a technology common in the pharmaceutical industry known as chromatography. The technology has never been used to process large volumes of minerals. ReElement is planning to build the capacity to process 10,000 metric tons of germanium or other minerals this year. According to ReElement CEO Mark Jensen, the company’s ⁠germanium production is “profitable ​at any volume.” ReElement received a $25 million investment from the Department of War.

Another company, USA Rare Earth, spent more than five years studying chromatography before pivoting to solvent extraction. USA Rare Earth is building a South Carolina magnet facility. Energy Fuels, which recently received a $725 million loan from the Department of War, plans to be processing small amounts of rare earths by the end of the year and 6,000 metric tons annually by 2029. ​It is buying an existing U.S. magnet producer. Ucore, Energy Fuels and ReElement have each agreed to supply rare earths to magnet maker Vulcan Elements, which is building a North Carolina manufacturing plant, slated to open by 2030.

Conclusion

President Trump wants the United States to mine and process its own critical minerals by January 1, 2027, and stop purchasing from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. But U.S. miners and processors are not ready to supply the quantity needed to meet demand due to the complexity of processing and the challenges of getting mining operations of that magnitude up and running, particularly amid changing requirements. The United States will still need to rely on China, which has dominated the minerals industry by subsidizing its producers and undercutting American mineral prices.

title: The future of freight: Electrify more, optimise better - ET Auto
authors: Pawan Mulukutla, Dr. O.P. Agarwal, ET Auto, www.ETAuto.com
description:
Road freight keeps our cities well supplied, responsive and economically alive.
Freight is an increasingly significant source of urban congestion, energy use and road transport emissions.
Despite being less than 3 percent of India’s vehicular population, road freight accounts for 64 percent of the nation’s diesel consumption and contributes to 34 percent of road transport emissions.
Passenger and freight transport have traditionally been treated as two separate systems.
Instead of deploying more freight vehicles into already congested cities, existing autorickshaws could transport goods during periods when passenger demand is low.
text:
Every city has a hidden circulatory system that keeps it running. Long before we open an app, collect medicines from a pharmacy, or receive groceries at our doorstep, thousands of vehicles, drivers, loaders, warehouse teams and logistics operators are already at work. Road freight keeps our cities well supplied, responsive and economically alive.

Freight is an increasingly significant source of urban congestion, energy use and road transport emissions. Despite being less than 3 percent of India’s vehicular population, road freight accounts for 64 percent of the nation’s diesel consumption and contributes to 34 percent of road transport emissions. As commerce expands and consumers increasingly expect faster deliveries, the number of freight trips will only grow. The challenge is not just to transition to electric freight, but also to ensure that every vehicle already on the road is used more efficiently.

Advt

Recognising the need to accelerate the transition, the Government of India launched the PM E-DRIVE Scheme in 2024. With an outlay of ₹10,900 crore, this is one of the biggest pushes towards clean mobility, supporting electric vehicle adoption, charging infrastructure and domestic manufacturing.

Electric trucks, three-wheelers and other low emission delivery vehicles can reduce tailpipe emissions, improve air quality and help India advance its climate goals. But for electrification to deliver its full potential, it must be supported by adequate charging infrastructure, affordable financing, reliable supply chains, robust manufacturing capacity and forward-looking policy support.

This transition must also work for the people who move goods every day. Across India, most commercial drivers and small fleet operators work on narrow margins. For many, transitioning to an electric vehicle is a daunting financial undertaking. Improving the earning potential of existing assets can strengthen operators' financial resilience and make the transition to cleaner vehicles more feasible.

Passenger and freight transport have traditionally been treated as two separate systems. India has one of the world's largest autorickshaw fleets, yet most of these vehicles remain dedicated exclusively to passenger transport. Many autorickshaws spend a significant part of the day underutilised. Allowing the same vehicle to transport passengers and goods at different times can unlock substantial efficiency gains.

Advt

A WRI India research paper indicates passenger autorickshaws can effectively transport goods weighing between 30 and 300 kg, a segment that currently falls between two-wheelers and larger cargo vehicles. Instead of deploying more freight vehicles into already congested cities, existing autorickshaws could transport goods during periods when passenger demand is low. This approach can help meet growing freight demand and improve utilisation of vehicles already in service.

The economics are equally compelling. The research further found that many autorickshaw drivers spend between one and four hours each day waiting for passengers. Freight demand follows a different rhythm. Passenger trips peak during the morning and evening commute, while freight demand is concentrated through the middle of the day. That creates a natural opportunity for drivers to carry freight during otherwise idle hours without affecting passenger services.

The result is a potential 15% increase in driver incomes while improving vehicle utilisation from an estimated 30-35% to nearly 60%. Vehicles that otherwise run empty can carry freight instead, reducing dead mileage and improving overall efficiency. Electric autorickshaws, with a lower centre of gravity and better weight distribution than conventional ICE vehicles, are also well suited for carrying both passengers and moderate freight. For many drivers operating on thin margins and often servicing vehicle loans, the additional income can improve household resilience, accelerate debt repayment and strengthen their ability to invest in cleaner vehicles in the future.

One of urban freight's biggest inefficiencies is not the type of vehicle itself, but how effectively it is utilised. Empty return trips, poor route planning, fragmented deliveries and low load utilisation continue to drive up fuel consumption, operating costs and emissions. Digital freight companies and emerging technologies can play a critical role in addressing these challenges.

Better route optimisation, data-enabled trip planning, dynamic load matching and demand forecasting can reduce empty miles, improve load utilisation and consolidate consignments across operators. These are improvements cities can achieve today, without waiting for complete fleet electrification.

While governments continue investing in cleaner vehicles and the infrastructure that supports them, logistics companies must also embrace digital tools that maximise asset utilisation. Simultaneously decision makers should explore innovative business models, such as the dual use of vehicles already on the road, that improve efficiency without adding more vehicles to city streets. Most importantly, every intervention must place drivers and small operators at its centre, ensuring that those who power the freight economy are beneficiaries of the transition.

The future of urban freight will not be built through electrification alone, nor can it be built without it. It will require clean vehicles, smarter logistics, intelligent technology and innovative business models that allow every vehicle to deliver greater environmental, economic and social value.

Dr. OP Agarwal is ex-joint secretary, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, Government of India, and is currently a professor of practice at the Indian School of Public Policy. Pawan Mulukutla is Executive Director - Integrated Transport, Clean Air & Hydrogen, WRI India. Views expressed are personal.

title: Hopes Grow for Higher Ethanol Blend With Inclusion in U.S. Senate Farm Bill
description:
Supporters of year-round E15 availability say it would strengthen the farm economy and make the country more energy independent.
Without a law authorizing year-round E15, summertime sales require a federal waiver.
The farm bill is multi-year legislation that determines federal agriculture, food and nutrition policies.
The Senate Agriculture Committee included year-round E15 when it released its version of the farm bill last week ahead of the committee’s hearing this Thursday.
The last farm bill was signed into law in 2018 and has been extended after Congress failed to pass a new version.
text:
By Makenzie Huber

South Dakota’s congressional delegation is hopeful that year-round, nationwide approval of E15 — a gasoline blend with 15% ethanol — will clear Congress this year, bolstered by its inclusion in the latest Senate version of the farm bill.

Ethanol is a fuel additive made primarily from corn, and a lower E10 blend is already available year-round. Supporters of year-round E15 availability say it would strengthen the farm economy and make the country more energy independent. Without a law authorizing year-round E15, summertime sales require a federal waiver.

Opponents point to research showing emissions from higher blends could worsen summer smog while encouraging the conversion of grasslands for corn farming. Some lawmakers from oil-producing and refining states also oppose the expansion.

The House pulled year-round E15 from its version of the farm bill earlier this year, instead approving it as separate legislation amending the Clean Air Act.

The farm bill is multi-year legislation that determines federal agriculture, food and nutrition policies. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, voted in favor of both bills.

The Senate Agriculture Committee included year-round E15 when it released its version of the farm bill last week ahead of the committee’s hearing this Thursday. The House’s standalone E15 bill awaits a hearing in another Senate committee.

The last farm bill was signed into law in 2018 and has been extended after Congress failed to pass a new version. Johnson spoke to South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday at the Sioux Empire Fair in Sioux Falls about the legislation’s progress, including the Senate version.

“In general, I don’t think the House is going to love this version compared to what we passed, but at some point we’ll figure out a way to get to yes, collectively,” Johnson said. “We need to. This is really important if we care about American energy dominance, and we just can’t get there without E15.”

Year-round E15 sales have been a longstanding goal of the ethanol industry. Ethanol plants process more than half of South Dakota-grown corn.

Rising gas prices this summer and the ongoing war with Iran have drawn attention to the United States’ continued reliance on liquid fuels in cars and airplanes — and its entanglement in Middle East oil markets, Johnson said.

“I would rather wake up every morning worried about the price of corn in a South Dakota field than worried about the price of oil in an Iranian oil field,” said Johnson, who will leave Congress in January after his failed run for governor.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, said in a statement that year-round E15 is a boost for agriculture and rural communities across South Dakota and the country.

“I remain committed to getting the farm bill and E15 to the president’s desk to secure these critical wins for South Dakota’s farmers and ranchers,” Thune said.

South Dakota Republican Sen. Mike Rounds has also spoken in support of year-round E15.

name: Clean Energy
title: Fossil fuel occupations show high transferability across the wider economy - Nature
description:
Routine manual occupations are often closely tied to fossil fuel production activities, while non-routine cognitive occupations frequently require specialized technical expertise specific to fossil fuel industries.
Even in traditional energy-producing states—such as Texas, Pennsylvania, and Colorado, where fossil fuel employment is relatively concentrated—employment in fossil fuel industries still represents only a small fraction of employment in non-fossil fuel industries.
To address the concern that fossil fuel-specific occupations (e.g., coal miners) may face worse transition prospects than occupations common in non-fossil fuel industries (e.g., administrative assistants), we follow the classification of Zaussinger et al.20 to further disaggregate occupations in fossil fuel industries into fossil fuel specific and non-fossil fuel specific occupations.
Identifying fossil fuel industries Fossil fuel industries comprise upstream (exploration and extraction of oil, gas, and coal), midstream (processing, transportation, and storage), and downstream (refining, conversion, and distribution) segments.
Let \(F\) denote the set of fossil fuel origin sectors, and let \(J2{J}_{{ij}}\) denote the number of job-to-job transitions from fossil fuel sector \(i\in F\) to destination sector \(j\).
text:
The Paris Agreement’s 2 °C goal accelerates a global shift from fossil fuels to low-carbon energy1. Although crucial for climate mitigation, workers currently in the fossil fuel industries will face involuntary job displacement. Around 13 million jobs in fossil fuel-related industries are at risk by 2030 as estimated by International Energy Agency (IEA)’s Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario2. This underscores the critical need for a just transition that provides targeted support to fossil fuel workers and communities3,4,5, ensuring the energy transition does not perpetuate disparities between winners and losers and deepen social inequity. However, achieving this requires clearly identifying at-risk workers and positioning alternative employment pathways for effective just transition policies and broader labor market interventions.

Current research has largely concentrated on transition pathways for routine manual workers in fossil fuel industries (e.g., coal miners) moving into green sectors6,7,8,9,10, neglecting the equally pressing challenges confronting managerial and high-skilled professionals in fossil fuel industries. Petroleum engineers, geologists, and project managersspecializing in coal, oil and gas face particular difficulties, as their specialized knowledge and skills often don’t align neatly with renewable energy sectors’ requirements2,11,12,13,14,15. Moreover, green jobs frequently present impractical transition options due to three key barriers: geographic dislocation from traditional energy hubs6,16,17,18, fundamental skill mismatches19,20, and many workers’ preference to remain in familiar industrial sectors. This raises critical questions about whether fossil fuel workers have broader transition possibilities across all industries.

To address these challenges, our study investigates economy-wide transition opportunities for all occupations within fossil fuel industries. We identify viable pathways from fossil fuel sectors to all non-fossil fuel sectors by integrating skill similarity metrics and realistic inter-industry labor transition. By expanding the scope of occupational alternatives from green sectors to include all economic activities—which exist in every region, we overcome the geographical barrier6. We use job transition data from 2010 to 2023 Current Population Survey (CPS) surveys to employ skill similarity metrics to identify high-transferability occupation matches (0.85 ≤ similarity < 1) and viable reskilling pathways (0.8 ≤ similarity < 0.85), tackling the skill mismatch problem19,20. When analyzing destination industries, we incorporate realistic inter-industry labor mobility data to identify transition opportunities within industrial ecosystems that are already familiar to workers. By adopting this comprehensive “dirty-to-all” framework—rather than limiting options to green sectors—we maximize potential pathways for displaced workers.

We identify 399 distinct occupations across fossil fuel industries, spanning the full value chain of coal, oil, and gas sectors—from upstream extraction through midstream processing to downstream distribution. Based on Cortes et al.21, we categorize these occupations into 187 routine manual (RM) occupations (e.g., roof bolters), 141 non-routine cognitive (NRC) occupations (e.g., petroleum engineers), 44 routine cognitive (RC) occupations (e.g., office clerks), and 27 non-routine manual (NRM) occupations (e.g., security guards). Although originally developed in the context of routine-biased technological change, this task-based framework is equally applicable to occupation transition analysis. Cortes et al.21 characterize occupations by their routine task intensity, distinguishing between standardized, codifiable tasks and more complex, non-routine activities. Routine tasks are more structured and rule-based, whereas non-routine tasks tend to rely on context-specific knowledge. Drawing on Gathmann and Schönberg22, the task-based framework can be used as an indirect proxy for skill transferability: routine-intensive workers possess task profiles that overlap more broadly across a wide range of roles, whereas workers in non-routine cognitive occupations rely on abstract, context-specific knowledge that is less readily redeployed outside their origin occupation.

Using detailed skill information from the O*NET database, we find that 77.4% of occupations in fossil fuel industries exhibit high transferability (0.85 ≤ similarity < 1) to non-fossil fuel roles, primarily in RM fields, while 11.3% of occupations can gain high transferability to occupations in non-fossil fuel sectors through reskilling (0.8 ≤ similarity < 0.85), particularly in RM occupations. When fossil fuel workers transition to non-fossil fuel industries, the most probable destination industries are Accommodation and Food Services; Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting; Professional, Scientific and Technical Services sectors when disregarding realistic inter-industry labor transition, versus Accommodation and Food Services; Administrative, Waste Management and Remediation Services; Professional, Scientific and Technical Services when such labor transition is considered. However, these transitions are frequently associated with wage reductions, as about 67% of occupations in non-fossil fuel industries offer lower wages compared to their fossil fuel counterparts when workers transition to their identical occupations considering geographic factors. Cross-occupational transitions reduce wage loss risks to 65% and expand the upper bound of potential wage gains from 400% to 600% when workers move to occupations with high skill similarity after reskilling.

To capture the full scope of occupations in fossil fuel industries, including roles such as petroleum engineers and office clerks, we use 2023 National Employment Matrix from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Based on 25 six-digit NAICS codes classified as fossil fuel industries (see Supplementary Table 1), we identify 399 unique occupations within these sectors. We analyze the occupational composition of fossil fuel industries using the Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) taxonomy. Classifying occupations by task types is essential, as task requirements fundamentally define occupational characteristics and reveal critical heterogeneity in transition potential. We follow established literature in labor economics21,23 to classify occupations into four types: non-routine cognitive (NRC), routine cognitive (RC), non-routine manual (NRM), and routine manual (RM). This classification is highly relevant in the context of the energy transition because it captures cross-sector transferability among different occupational types in fossil fuel industries. Routine manual occupations are often closely tied to fossil fuel production activities, while non-routine cognitive occupations frequently require specialized technical expertise specific to fossil fuel industries. Both are therefore harder to transfer across sectors. By contrast, routine cognitive occupations tend to involve more general administrative tasks that are widely used across industries and non-routine manual occupations are more prevalent in non-fossil fuel industries, making their cross-sector transition more feasible.

Figure 1 provides an overview of employment structure in fossil fuel industries. Figure 1A maps the geographic distribution of fossil fuel employment across U.S. states. Fossil fuel employment is concentrated in a small number of states, with Texas standing out as by far the largest employer in fossil fuel industries, consistent with its dominant position in U.S. oil and gas production24. Other states with notable fossil fuel employment include California, Pennsylvania, and Colorado, reflecting the broader spatial footprint of oil, gas, and coal extraction and processing across the country.

Figure 1B compares the employment structure of fossil fuel and non-fossil fuel industries. Fossil fuel industries are dominated by RM (43.9%) and RC (35.5%) employment, together accounting for nearly 80% of sectoral employment. In contrast, non-fossil fuel industries exhibit a more balanced distribution across RM (30.9%), NRC (30.6%), RC (23.8%), and NRM (14.8%). This composition reflects the fossil fuel sector’s reliance on physical extraction processes and standardized administrative tasks. Importantly, the proportion of RM occupations is significantly higher in fossil fuel industries (43.9%) than in non-fossil fuel industries (30.9%). This disparity indicates a greater reliance on routine manual tasks—such as mining and oil extraction—within the fossil fuel sector, a finding consistent with existing literature6,25 suggesting that workers in routine manual roles are disproportionately vulnerable to disruptions from the energy transition.

However, it is crucial to note that over 50% of at-risk workers in fossil fuel industries fall outside the RM category. This substantial segment includes a significant share of RC occupations (35.5%, e.g., office clerks), NRC roles (18.0%, e.g., petroleum engineers), NRM positions (2.6%, e.g., security guards). While their tasks are not routine manual, these workers equally face the brunt of transition risks as their industries phase down. Our analysis extends beyond the existing literature emphasis on routine manual workers6,7,8,9,10 to encompass all occupations within fossil fuel industries. These workers often possess broader external options, but their sheer scale and realistic transition pathways remain insufficiently understood, pointing to the need for an economy-wide framework that distinguishes occupation-specific risk intensity from workforce-wide transition needs.

To assess opportunities and challenges for same-occupation transitions, we identify occupations that have the highest prevalence in non-fossil fuel industries and highest concentration in fossil fuel industries. Fossil fuel sectors employ both specialized roles (e.g., gas plant operators) and generalist roles (e.g., accountants). Generalists transition more easily to non-fossil fuel industries due to high prevalence of their occupations, while specialists face greater challenges due to limited job opportunities. We calculate the occupation prevalence and concentration using the industry-occupation matrix and 2023 U.S. employment data from BLS. Prevalence refers to the commonality of an occupation across non-fossil fuel industries, while concentration measures the proportion of an occupation’s total national employment located within the fossil fuel sector.

Figure 1C shows that occupations in general management, accounting, human resources, and office work exhibit high prevalence in non-fossil fuel industries. This widespread distribution indicates a strong potential for workers in these roles to undertake same-occupation transitions outside the fossil fuel industry. Maintenance and repair workers—a routine manual occupation—also show considerable prevalence in non-fossil fuel sectors. In contrast, the most concentrated occupations within the fossil fuel sector are mostly routine manual roles, including roof bolters and gas plant operators. Certain NRC occupations, such as petroleum engineers, geological technicians, and emergency management directors, also exhibit significant concentration within fossil fuel industries (see Supplementary Fig. 1). Their high degree of sectoral specialization and limited presence in other industries highlights a significant transition challenge.

As identical-occupation transitions can be challenging, we investigate the potential of cross-occupation transitions based on skill similarity. To understand the transition feasibility of different occupations, we use occupational skill profiles from the O*NET database from the U.S. Department of Labor to calculate skill similarity between occupations in fossil fuel industries and all other occupations. We compare the skill similarity using the Jaccard similarity (see Methods). The similarity ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater similarity between sets of skills and higher potential of cross-occupation transitions.

Figure 2A presents the distribution of similarity scores between occupations in fossil fuel industries and their paired matches in other sectors. We calibrate the transferability thresholds using longitudinal CPS monthly data (2010–2023). For the training-switch group, we track each worker’s training month, record the last occupation observed before training, and identify the first occupation observed after training. For the no-training-switch group, we treat each month-to-month occupational change as an independent occupational transition event and exclude any event in which the individual has any prior training record (see Methods). In both cases, we compare the skill similarity between origin and destination occupations and examine the distribution of similarities. We use the 90th percentile to ensure a stringent threshold for feasible occupational transitions. The 90th percentile of the similarity distribution is ~0.85 for the no-training group and 0.82 for the training group (see Supplementary Fig. 2). We accordingly consider that fossil fuel workers exhibit high transferability to occupations with similarity exceeding 0.85 and achieve comparable transferability to roles with similarity ranging from 0.8 to 0.85 after a few months of reskilling. Based on CPS longitudinal tracking, the average interval between a worker’s last recorded occupation before training and their first new occupation afterward is about 2.5 months, suggesting that the reskilling period typically spans 2–3 months.

Figure 2B shows that 77.4% of occupations in fossil fuel industries exhibit high transferability to other sectors and are mainly concentrated in the RM type. 11.3% of occupations can achieve comparable transferability after reskilling, also primarily for RM occupations. About 11.3% of occupations are categorized as low transferability (similarity < 0.8). Supplementary Fig. 3 shows distribution of transition potential across occupational types using employment data. 91.8% of employment in fossil fuel industries exhibits high transferability to other sectors. In both cases, RM occupations account for the largest share within fossil fuel industries, indicating that routine manual jobs constitute the core of the fossil fuel workforce. NRC and RC occupations also represent a substantial part of employment, whereas NRM occupations remain relatively limited.

Figure 2C illustrates the matched occupation pairs between fossil fuel and non-fossil fuel industries based on different similarity thresholds categorized by occupational type. We focus on cross-occupation transition pathways (excluding similarity = 1). RC occupations show a notable transition feasibility to NRC roles, particularly at the threshold of 0.8 ≤ similarity < 1. Conversely, RM occupations predominantly remain within the same category across both thresholds. The findings highlight a divergence in adaptability—RC roles demonstrate a higher potential to evolve into higher-skilled NRC positions, whereas RM roles face greater barriers to such transitions due to skill disparities.

When occupations in fossil fuel industries achieve high transferability to their matched occupations with minor training, the number of available occupational pairs for each type increases significantly (Fig. 2D). For example, when skill similarity is constrained to 0.85, RM occupations have only on average about 10.1 viable transition options. However, after reskilling, the average number of feasible occupational pairs increases to 63.4. Supplementary Fig. 4 presents the case of gas plant operators, showing that without reskilling they can only transition to 20 other RM occupations (0.85 ≤ similarity < 1). After reskilling, the range expands to 100 matched occupations (0.8 ≤ similarity < 1), underscoring the importance of reskilling for cross-occupation mobility.

Figure 3 further illustrates potential transition destination industries for fossil fuel workers. As fossil fuel industries face varying degrees of structural decline due to the net zero transition, identifying potential destination sectors for displaced workers is important. We model a scenario in which fossil fuel workers transition either to the same occupation in a non-fossil fuel industry or a different occupation with high transferability after reskilling (0.8 ≤ similarity ≤ 1). The employment of distinct matched occupation pairs in non-fossil fuel industries serves as a proxy for estimating the transition probability for fossil fuel workers. Figure 3A shows that, without considering realistic labor mobility between industries, fossil fuel workers exhibit high transition potential to industries such as Accommodation and Food Services; Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting; Professional, Scientific and Technical Services sectors. These sectors are typically characterized by broad labor demand and relatively diverse occupational structures, which makes them highly viable to absorb displaced fossil fuel workers. In particular, Accommodation and Food Services and Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting contain a large number of routine manual jobs, while Professional, Scientific and Technical Services offers a wider range of cognitive occupations.

To approximate realistic transition opportunities, we weight occupational mobility flows by destination-industry workforce. This adjustment ensures that transition potential reflects not only skill similarity between origin and destination occupations, but also considers the real-world mobility flows. Furthermore, industries with stronger occupational mobility linkages tend to be more geographically co-located26. Identifying such industries can address the dual barriers of geographic dislocation and worker preference, thereby enabling more practical and effective transition pathways. We measure realistic inter-industry labor mobility flows using U.S. Job-to-Job Origin-Destination (J2JOD) data (see Methods). Considering both skill similarity and realistic inter-industry labor mobility, the top non-fossil fuel industries that fossil fuel workers are able to transition into are Accommodation and Food Services; Administrative, Waste Management and Remediation Services; Professional, Scientific and Technical Services (Fig. 3B).

Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services emerges as a pivotal destination industry in both scenarios, underscoring their critical role in absorbing displaced fossil fuel workers. Specifically, NRC occupations in fossil fuel industries—such as engineers and geoscientists—demonstrate transition potential into Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services industries, highlighting a viable pathway into other innovation-driven segments of the economy. Notably, RM workers exhibit transition potential into Accommodation and Food Services; Administrative, Waste Management, and Remediation Services, suggesting that RM workers have relatively strong potential to transition into labor-intensive service sectors. In particular, their transition potential into Administrative, Waste Management and Remediation Services reflects the fact that their specialized technical skills—for example, in equipment maintenance and operation—remain highly valuable due to close industrial linkages and shared technical foundations between these sectors.

Figure 4 provides complementary evidence that non-fossil fuel industries retain capacity to absorb workers displaced from fossil fuel industries. Figure 4A shows the ratio of employment in fossil fuel to non-fossil fuel industries in each state in 2023. In nearly all states, employment in fossil fuel industries represents only a small share of employment in non-fossil fuel industries, implying that local non-fossil fuel sectors generally have sufficient labor market space to absorb workers transitioning out of fossil fuel industries. Even in traditional energy-producing states—such as Texas, Pennsylvania, and Colorado, where fossil fuel employment is relatively concentrated—employment in fossil fuel industries still represents only a small fraction of employment in non-fossil fuel industries. Supplementary Fig. 5A shows the similar pattern with the ratio of employment in fossil fuel industries to matched occupations (0.8 ≤ similarity ≤ 1) in non-fossil fuel industries by state in 2023.

Figure 4B and Supplementary Fig. 5C–F show that the net employment change gap is positive for the vast majority of fossil fuel occupations, indicating that the matched occupations in non-fossil fuel industries generally exhibit stronger projected employment growth than the corresponding fossil fuel occupations over 2024–2034 for all occupational types. Supplementary Fig. 5B further reinforces this conclusion from the employment perspective. While employment in fossil fuel industries remains relatively small and fairly stable throughout 2013–2023, non-fossil fuel industries employ more than one million workers and continue to expand overall. This large and persistent employment gap suggests that non-fossil fuel industries have ample labor market space to accommodate workers from fossil fuel sectors.

To address the concern that fossil fuel-specific occupations (e.g., coal miners) may face worse transition prospects than occupations common in non-fossil fuel industries (e.g., administrative assistants), we follow the classification of Zaussinger et al.20 to further disaggregate occupations in fossil fuel industries into fossil fuel specific and non-fossil fuel specific occupations. Zaussinger et al.20 employ an expert-validated method based on the European Skills, Competencies, Qualifications and Occupations (ESCO) taxonomy to identify occupations predominantly associated with the production and processing of fossil fuels (coal, oil, and gas). To apply this classification in our study, we map ESCO occupations to the O*NET occupation taxonomy via the ESCO–O*NET crosswalk provided by U.S. BLS (see Supplementary Table 3). Figure 4C shows that the net employment change gap remains positive for the large majority of fossil fuel-specific occupations, with a magnitude and distribution broadly comparable to that of non-fossil fuel-specific occupations in Fig. 4D. This indicates that skill-similar occupations outside the fossil fuel sectors exhibit sufficient employment growth to absorb displaced fossil fuel specific workers, mitigating the concern that these workers face a uniquely constrained set of external options in terms of labor demand.

Beyond analyzing transition potential, it is crucial to consider the welfare implications of occupational transitions. We investigate how transitions affect wages of fossil fuel workers by comparing wages between occupations in fossil fuel industries and their matched occupations in other sectors in the same state (see Methods). Wage analysis includes identical transitions into a non-fossil fuel industry and different occupations with high transferability after reskilling (0.8 ≤ similarity ≤ 1), as identical transitions also entail wage changes due to industry-level pay differences. We obtain 2023 annual median wages for each six-digit SOC occupation in different states from the 2023 BLS OEWS. Figure 5A shows that when fossil fuel workers transition to the same occupations in non-fossil fuel industries, 33% of matched roles offer higher wages, while 67% offer lower wages than their fossil fuel industry counterparts. When workers move to different occupations with high transferability (Fig. 5B), the share of matched occupations associated with wage gains rises slightly to 34%. Moreover, the scope for wage improvement becomes greater after reskilling. As shown in Fig. 5C, when workers transition into occupations with high transferability after reskilling, 35% of matched occupations offer higher wages, and the upper bound of potential wage gains reaches 600% of pre-transition wages, suggesting that reskilling can not only improve access to better-paid opportunities, but also lead to larger potential wage gains. This underscores the importance of reskilling programs for achieving a just transition.

We further compare wage changes by occupational type. Figure 5D shows that NRC and RM workers are more likely to experience wage decrease when they transition to non-fossil fuel industries. In contrast, RC and NRM workers show the potential to increase their wages after transitioning to non-fossil fuel sectors. These findings are supported by t-tests (Fig. 5E). This disparity may be explained by the highly specialized skill profiles of NRC and RM occupations within the fossil fuel sectors. NRC workers (e.g., petroleum engineers) possess knowledge and skills that are deeply specialized and tightly bound to fossil technologies. Similarly, RM workers (e.g., roof bolters) are trained in sector-specific manual tasks. Although these skills are transferable to some extent, they are often less valued in non-fossil fuel sectors. In contrast, RC workers (e.g., accountants) possess skills that are widely applicable across industries. NRM workers (e.g., security guards, cleaners) have higher demand in non-fossil fuel industries, especially the service sectors, which may explain their potential for wage growth.

To examine whether these wage patterns are stable over time, we extend the analysis to BLS OEWS data from 2014, 2017, and 2020 (Supplementary Fig. 6). For identical-occupation transitions, the share of matched roles offering higher wages declined modestly from 28% in 2014 to 25% in 2020, before recovering to 33% in 2023, a rebound likely reflecting accelerated wage growth in non-fossil fuel industries after Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. While the Inflation Reduction Act stimulated clean energy investment and labor demand, it also exacerbated displacement pressures in fossil fuel industries27. Reskilling raises the wage-gain share and expands the upper bound of potential wage gains across all periods.

BLS OEWS and employment projections data

Employment and wage data for the United States are obtained from two BLS datasets: the Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) program and the Employment Projections (EP) program. The OEWS program is a large-scale establishment survey conducted jointly by BLS and state workforce agencies, providing annual occupation-by-industry data of employment and wages across all U.S. states. Although OEWS reports industry detail across multiple NAICS levels, the most granular and consistently available disaggregation is at the 4-digit NAICS level. The EP program, by contrast, is developed by BLS in collaboration with the U.S. Department of Labor and provides an industry-occupation employment matrix with more detailed industry breakdowns, including employment counts at the 6-digit NAICS level for 2023. We therefore use EP data to measure employment in narrowly defined 6-digit fossil fuel industries in 2023, while relying on OEWS data for state-level and multi-year analyses of employment and wages.

Identifying fossil fuel industries

Fossil fuel industries comprise upstream (exploration and extraction of oil, gas, and coal), midstream (processing, transportation, and storage), and downstream (refining, conversion, and distribution) segments. We identify 25 six-digit NAICS codes as fossil fuel industries (see Supplementary Table 1). The coverage of fossil fuel industries is primarily in line with Lim et al. and Raimi et al.6,25.

We identify occupations in fossil fuel industries using the 2023 National Employment Matrix from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), an industry-occupation matrix based on the 2022 NAICS and the 2018 SOC system. After removing duplicates, we identify a total of 399 unique six-digit occupations within the 25 fossil fuel industries.

Occupation skill data

We use occupation skill profiles from the O*NET database. This database contains a rich set of variables that describe work and worker characteristics, including skill requirements, which is widely used by the U.S. Department of Labor, policy makers, and researchers to study skills in the workforce23,32. O*NET identifies 35 different skills for 1016 occupations defined by the SOC taxonomy and rates each skill importance in an occupation on a continuous range of 1–5. We normalize skill importance level to a continuous range of 0 to 1, where 1 is the most important skill for a given occupation.

Occupational type

Existing studies have categorized occupations into four major types based on two dimensions of job tasks: cognitive versus manual and routine versus non-routine23,33,34,35. The cognitive-manual distinction reflects the relative emphasis on mental versus physical activities. Routine occupations involve tasks that follow well-defined procedures and instructions, whereas non-routine occupations require flexibility, problem-solving, and interpersonal skills. As such, the four occupational types are: non-routine cognitive (NRC), routine cognitive (RC), routine manual (RM) and non-routine manual (NRM). Cortes et al.21 categorized NRC, RC, NRM, and RM occupations based on the 2010 Census Coding System. Following Cortes et al.21 we map the 2010 Census Coding System to the 2018 O*NET taxonomy using the correspondence provided by U.S. BLS (see Supplementary Table 2). In this paper, we exclude observations for those working in the military occupations.

Measuring skill similarity

We use \({{raw}}_{k,s}\) to denote the original O*NET importance score of skill \(s\in S\) for occupation \(k\), which ranges from 1 to 5, with higher values indicating greater importance. To make skill profiles comparable across occupations, for each occupation, the raw skill scores are normalized into the \([0,1]\) interval as

$${{onet}}_{k,s}=\frac{{ra}{w}_{k,s}-\,{\min }_{{{s}}{\prime} \in S}{ra}{w}_{k,s{\prime} }}{{\max }_{{s}{\prime} \in S}{ra}{w}_{k,s{\prime} }-{\min }_{{s}{\prime} \in S}{ra}{w}_{k,s{\prime} }}$$

(1)

so that \({{onet}}_{k,s}\) captures the ralative weight of skill \(s\) within occupation \(k{\prime}\) s skill. Based on these normalized skill weights, we calculate the skill similarity for a pair of occupations \(k\) and \({k}_{1}\) according to the real-valued Jaccard similarity:

$${similarity}\,(k,{k}_{1})=\frac{{\sum }_{s\in S}min ({{onet}}_{k,s},{{onet}}_{{k}_{1},s})}{{\sum }_{s\in S}max ({{onet}}_{k,s},{{onet}}_{{k}_{1},s})}$$

(2)

Note that \({similarity}\,(k,{k}_{1})=1\) when occupations \(k\) and \({k}_{1}\) require the exact same skills while \({similarity}\,(k,{k}_{1})=0\) when occupations \(k\) and \({k}_{1}\) require completely different skills.

Identifying threshold of high transferability, high transferability after reskilling and low transferability

We calibrate the transferability thresholds using longitudinal monthly CPS data from 2010 to 2023. We construct two groups of observed occupational transitions. For the training-switch group, we identify each worker’s first month of training-related search, record the last occupation observed before that month, and then identify the first occupation observed after a subsequent occupational switch. For the no-training-switch group, we treat each month-to-month occupational change as an independent transition event and exclude any event for which the worker had any prior training record. This procedure yields 336,045 no-training-switch transitions and 945 training-switch transitions.

For both groups, we map CPS occupation codes to SOC occupations and calculate the skill similarity between origin and destination occupations. We then examine the distribution of observed transition similarities and use the 90th percentile as a stringent benchmark for feasible occupational mobility. The 90th-percentile similarity is about 0.85 in the no-training-switch group and 0.82 in the training-switch group (Supplementary Fig. 2). Based on this benchmark, we classify occupations with similarity above 0.85 as exhibiting high transferability, occupations with similarity between 0.80 and 0.85 as exhibiting high transferability after reskilling, and occupations with similarity below 0.80 as exhibiting low transferability. This classification reflects realistic transition behavior in the labor market and imposes a conservative standard for identifying feasible occupational transition.

Identifying viable non-fossil fuel industries for fossil fuel occupation transitions

To identify the most probable destination industries for fossil fuel workers, we assess transition probability using two components: (1) employment of matched occupations in non-fossil fuel industries, (2) inter-industry job-to-job flows. In Fig. 3A when not accounting for realistic inter-industry labor mobility, we use only component (1) as a proxy; with mobility consideration in Fig. 3B, we use both components. We focus on transitions where fossil fuel occupations exhibit high transferability to other occupations after reskilling or can move seamlessly to identical occupations in non-fossil fuel industries (0.8 ≤ similarity ≤ 1).

In Fig. 3B, to estimate the inter-industry job-to-job flows, we use the 2023 Job-to-Job Origin-Destination (J2JOD) data and aggregate labor transitions at the two-digit NAICS sector level (the most detailed available industry breakdown). Since fossil fuel industries in our study are defined at the six-digit level, we define fossil fuel sectors by extracting the first two digits of each fossil fuel industry code, including 21 (Mining, Quarrying, and Oil and Gas Extraction), 22 (Utilities), 23 (Construction), 31–33 (Manufacturing), 42 (Wholesale Trade), 44–45 (Retail Trade), and 48–49 (Transportation and Warehousing).

To capture the inter-industry mobility, for each destination sector \(j\), we calculate the total number of workers flowing from fossil fuel industries into that sector in 2023. Let \(F\) denote the set of fossil fuel origin sectors, and let \(J2{J}_{{ij}}\) denote the number of job-to-job transitions from fossil fuel sector \(i\in F\) to destination sector \(j\). The total observed outflow to destination sector \({{{\rm{j}}}}\) is:

$${Flo}{w}_{j}={\sum}_{i\in F}J\,2{J}_{{ij}}$$

(3)

We then convert this into a destination-specific labor-flow share:

$${Shar}{e}_{j}=\frac{{Flo}{w}_{j}}{{\sum}_{j}F{lo}{w}_{j}}$$

(4)

\({Shar}{e}_{j}\) measures the ratio of fossil fuel workers transitioning into non-fossil fuel sectors \({{{\rm{j}}}}\) to total fossil fuel workers outflow. \({N}_{j}\) denotes employment of matched occupations (0.8 ≤ similarity ≤ 1) in non-fossil fuel sectors \(j\). Transition probability \({P}_{j}\) of fossil fuel workers moving into the non-fossil fuel sectors \(j\), considering realistic inter-industry labor transition, is given by:

$${P}_{j}={N}_{j}\times {Shar}{e}_{j}$$

(5)

Analyzing wage changes

We obtain 2023 annual median wages for each six-digit SOC occupation in different four-digit industries from BLS OEWS data (the most detailed available industry breakdown) from the U.S. BLS. Since fossil fuel industries in our study are defined at the six-digit level but BLS data are reported at the four-digit level, we match wages by extracting the first four digits of each fossil fuel industry code and link them to the corresponding BLS industry wage data. We then construct state-level wage comparisons for each matched occupation pair: for each state, we calculate the mean wage of a six-digit SOC occupation within fossil fuel industries and compare it with the mean wage of its matched occupation within non-fossil fuel industries. This allows us to measure wage differences for occupation transitions considering geographic factors.

text:
(Indianapolis, IN) – Gov. Mike Braun declared a new statewide energy emergency on Wednesday and extended Indiana’s gas tax holiday another 30 days.

“New conditions that continue to disrupt global energy distribution provide a new basis for a suspension of gas taxes. Affordability is my top priority, and my gas tax suspensions delivered the cheapest gas in America for Hoosiers all summer,” Gov. Braun said. “I’m keeping those savings going for Hoosier families, and my recommended budget will tap our reserves to keep state and local infrastructure projects fully funded.”

This latest energy emergency is prompted by new disruptions to global oil shipping lanes in recent weeks, in the Black Sea/Kerch Strait as the Russia-Ukraine conflict has escalated into maritime drone battles and the disruption to the Alberta Oil Sands Region from Canadian wildfires.

Braun said these disruptions have created new pressures on fuel prices that are driving the price of gas for Hoosiers to unnatural levels outside the norm of standard economic conditions.

Gov. Braun first suspended the Gasoline Usage Tax in April and expanded the relief in May to include the Gasoline Excise Tax.

The new emergency takes effect Friday (August 7) in all 92 counties and provides a 120-day window of authority.

Both gas taxes will be suspended through September 5.

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita backed Braun’s authority to create a new energy emergency.

“Nothing in Indiana’s emergency powers statutes prohibits the governor from declaring separate emergencies based upon different factors,” Rokita said. “It is within the Governor’s authority to give Hoosiers temporary and much-needed relief at the pump based upon changed conditions.”

Braun said he has reached an agreement with House and Senate fiscal leadership to use reserve funds during next year’s budget session, covering money lost from the gas tax pause.

The reserve balance is currently on track to be over $5 billion.

name: American Energy
title: Some data centers are building their own power plants. In Oklahoma, most want to plug into the grid
description:
"You're going to be building your own data centers, and you're going to be building your own electric plants," said President Donald Trump.
The legislature also passed Senate Bill 480 last year, allowing data centers to build power plants behind the meter, bypassing utilities.
But so far, most data centers with plans in Oklahoma are opting to plug into the grid.
Why Oklahoma isn't seeing an influx of behind-the-meter projects for data centers Data centers typically have backup generators on site, should they temporarily lose connection.
Large proposed data centers, including the Luther Horizon Technology Park, Project Mustang in Claremore, IREN's Kiowa Data Center and more, plan to work with local utilities.
text:
Last month, Gov. Kevin Stitt and some Oklahoma electric utilities signed a federal pledge to protect household ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Pledge directs data center developers to pay their own way and invest in surrounding communities.

Part of the document states companies must buy the massive amount of electricity they require, add more power to the grid or supply it on-site.

"You're going to be building your own data centers, and you're going to be building your own electric plants," said President Donald Trump. "You're essentially becoming a utility."

The pledge is one of many ways officials are responding to public pushback against hyperscale data centers.

Oklahoma has its own version of a ratepayer protection pledge, a law requiring electricity suppliers to create separate terms and conditions for large-scale energy consumers like data centers and increase transparency. State regulators are currently reviewing large-load tariffs from utilities intended to prevent households from shouldering grid connection costs for companies like Google and Meta.

The legislature also passed Senate Bill 480 last year, allowing data centers to build power plants behind the meter, bypassing utilities. Rep. Brad Boles, R-Marlow, co-authored the legislation.

"What we realized is in Oklahoma, our state law is kind of vague; it doesn't really say that companies can provide their own power generation," Boles, who is running for a seat on the Corporation Commission, said. "It doesn't say they can't either, but it doesn't say that they can."

" So we wanted to provide clarity that if a large load comes to Oklahoma and they want to provide their own power generation, that they would have the ability to do that," he said.

The bill was expected to generate billions of dollars in private investment and alleviate pressure from the electric grid. Growing demand, supercharged by large-load consumers like data centers, is expected to outpace supply within the Southwest Power Pool's territory. The organization operates the electric grid in Oklahoma and 16 other states.

But so far, most data centers with plans in Oklahoma are opting to plug into the grid. Experts say the state's grid system is likely more reliable than depending on behind-the-meter generation. Building a power plant is costly and can take years to complete.

" I don't readily, actually, believe that any data center company wants to also be in the power business," said Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin.

Still, some AI companies are investing in behind-the-meter natural gas plants in states like neighboring Texas to accelerate the pace of buildout. Those plants are expected to emit significant amounts of pollution, an analysis from the Texas Tribune and Floodlight shows.

Why Oklahoma isn't seeing an influx of behind-the-meter projects for data centers

Data centers typically have backup generators on site, should they temporarily lose connection. Some companies are adding power to the grid with new energy projects.

Google and Oklahoma Gas & Electric announced a deal in the spring to power the tech company's three data centers in Muskogee and Stillwater. Google is building two solar farms to add energy generation.

Christi Woodworth, OG&E's chief communications officer, said companies are eyeing the state's relatively low electricity costs and reliability.

"They've got to make a decision about if they want to build or bring their own generation," she said. "That effectively puts them on an island, right? They take on all of that risk themselves, and they have to decide if that's something that they want to do."

"The folks we're talking with are very interested in connecting to the grid."

The company is in "a handful" of other discussions with large-load projects, Woodworth said, but no plans are public yet.

Last year, officials announced a project in Chickasha and celebrated the state's new behind-the-meter law. The Chickasha Airport Industrial Park could one day be home to a data center and power plant, but no firm plans have been made public. A manufacturing firm in the Tulsa Port of Catoosa announced early this year it plans to build its power on-site. A news release says the company specializes in aerospace, energy and advanced manufacturing.

Large proposed data centers, including the Luther Horizon Technology Park, Project Mustang in Claremore, IREN's Kiowa Data Center and more, plan to work with local utilities.

The Kiowa facility is the state's largest proposed data center, according to energy analytics firm Cleanview. In an email, Jason Date, associate director of development, said the company plans to secure its power through Public Service Company of Oklahoma.

"Like the vast majority of homes and businesses, IREN's facilities use grid power because it is the most efficient and reliable way to source electricity," he said.

A delay in critical infrastructure delivery is also an obstacle for data center developers. Getting a natural gas plant, the typical energy source for behind-the-meter data center projects, can currently take years.

"If you're not in line right now, you're probably not getting one until the 2030s," Rhodes said.

Some companies instead are turning to used products to avoid the mile-long backlog.

" I've heard of companies looking to buy used cruise ship engines," Rhodes said. "I heard one the other day of someone trying to string together a bunch of used helicopter engines."

Oklahoma's behind-the-meter law requires developers to have natural gas as part of their plant. Other sources, including solar and wind, could be used in conjunction. When asked about the natural gas requirement, Boles said it was included to support the oil and gas industry.

"We felt like, as Oklahomans, it's important to ensure that natural gas has a seat at the table," he said.

According to an analysis from Cleanview, Oklahoma has fewer than 30 data centers planned for the state as of early August. Texas has hundreds in its queue, Rhodes said, meaning more developers are racing to supply power. Should tech companies continue showing interest in Oklahoma, it's possible more behind-the-meter projects could be announced.

Boles said he expects more interest in the future.

"Like anything, it takes time," Boles said. "If you're to build a facility with behind-the-meter, it may take three to five years to get the power infrastructure built."

"I think we're not going to really know for sure how many companies are utilizing this until a few years down the road."

title: The geopolitical case for geothermal as a domestic energy resource - SLB
description:
Advancing toward the full potential of geothermal Geothermal is unique.
Tapping only 1% of the thermal energy stored in the Earth’s crust at depths of up to 5 km could theoretically meet current global energy demand for 3,500 years.
The US Department of Energy projects that geothermal power could meet 12% of US energy demand by 2050.
Where geothermal differs from oil and gas Although subsurface understanding has advanced considerably in recent decades, uncertainty remains over how a geothermal resource will perform once developed.
